lessons.title: Physics, Physical Quantities and SI Units
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Quantities

A physical quantity is a quantity that can be measured. Some quantities have their own base units and are called fundamental quantities. Mass, time and luminous intensity (luminosity) are fundamental quantities in this sense.

Supplementary Quantities

Besides the fundamental quantities there are supplementary quantities. The plane angle and the solid angle are supplementary quantities.

  • Plane angle — a supplementary quantity; its unit is the radian
  • Solid angle — the three-dimensional angle subtended at a point; a supplementary quantity

SI Units Named in This Unit

QuantitySI Unit
Solid anglesteradian (sr)
Timesecond (s)
Masskilogram (kg)
Luminous intensitycandela (cd)

The second, kilogram and candela are the units of time, mass and luminous intensity respectively, while the steradian belongs to the solid angle alone.

Time — the Same Unit in All Systems

Length is measured in metre, centimetre or foot and mass in kilogram, gram or pound in different systems, so their units change from system to system. Time is different: the second is used as the unit of time in the CGS, MKS and FPS systems alike, so time is the quantity having the same unit in all systems of units.

Quantities With a Unit but No Dimensions, and Without Either

  • Plane angle — has a unit (radian) but no dimensions, because it is a ratio of arc length to radius
  • Strain — has neither a unit nor dimensions, because it is a ratio of two lengths

Constants — With and Without a Unit

  • Universal gravitational constant G — a constant which has a unit, N m^2 / kg^2
  • The number π — a constant which has no unit, because it is a pure ratio of circumference to diameter

These examples show that having a unit and having dimensions are two separate ideas: a quantity or constant may have one, both, or neither.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a supplementary quantity?
mcqs.why: Solid angle is a supplementary quantity, like the plane angle. Mass, time and luminous intensity are fundamental quantities with their own base units.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of solid angle?
mcqs.why: The solid angle, the three-dimensional angle subtended at a point, is measured in steradian (sr). Candela is for luminous intensity, kilogram for mass and second for time.

mcqs.q: The candela (cd) is the SI unit of which quantity?
mcqs.why: Luminous intensity is measured in candela (cd). Time uses the second, mass uses the kilogram and solid angle uses the steradian.

mcqs.q: Which quantity has the same unit in the CGS, MKS and FPS systems alike?
mcqs.why: Time uses the second in the CGS, MKS and FPS systems alike. Length changes between metre, centimetre and foot, and mass between kilogram, gram and pound, so their units differ by system.

mcqs.q: Which quantity has a unit but no dimensions?
mcqs.why: Plane angle has the unit radian but no dimensions because it is a ratio of arc length to radius. Strain has neither a unit nor dimensions, while displacement and force both have dimensions.

mcqs.q: Strain is an example of a quantity that has:
mcqs.why: Strain has neither a unit nor dimensions because it is a ratio of two lengths, so the lengths cancel. Plane angle, by contrast, has a unit (radian) but no dimensions.

mcqs.q: Which constant has a unit?
mcqs.why: The universal gravitational constant G has the unit N m^2 / kg^2, so it is a constant with a unit. The number pi has no unit because it is a pure ratio of circumference to diameter.

mcqs.q: Why does the number pi have no unit?
options: It is a pure ratio of circumference to diameter
mcqs.why: Pi has no unit because it is a pure ratio of circumference to diameter, and a ratio of two lengths carries no unit. It is a constant without a unit, not a measured quantity.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of plane angle?
options: Degree only, with no SI unit
mcqs.why: Plane angle is a supplementary quantity whose unit is the radian. The steradian belongs to solid angle alone, and candela belongs to luminous intensity.

mcqs.q: Mass, time and luminous intensity are classified in the notes as:
options: Derived quantities with no base unit
mcqs.why: Mass, time and luminous intensity are fundamental quantities because they have their own base units: kilogram, second and candela. Plane angle and solid angle are the supplementary quantities.

lessons.title: Measurement Techniques and Instruments
lessons.notes_html:
Least Count

The least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can make reliably. The least count decides how precise an instrument is: the smaller the least count, the more precise the instrument.

Vernier Caliper

For a Vernier caliper the least count is one main scale division minus one Vernier scale division, commonly 1 mm − 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.

To read a Vernier caliper: read the main scale just before the zero of the Vernier scale, then add the coinciding Vernier division multiplied by the least count of 0.01 cm, and finally apply any zero correction.

Micrometer Screw Gauge

For a micrometer screw gauge the least count is the pitch of the screw divided by the number of divisions on the circular scale, commonly 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm, so the micrometer is the more precise instrument.

To read a micrometer: read the exposed sleeve (main scale) reading in millimetres, add the thimble division in line with the reference line multiplied by the least count of 0.01 mm, and apply any zero correction.

Comparing the Two Instruments

InstrumentLeast Count (common)
Vernier caliper0.01 cm
Micrometer screw gauge0.001 cm (0.01 mm)

Worked Example 1

An aeroplane travels at 850 km/h. How long does it take to travel 1.00 km?

Step 1: Convert the speed to m/s, 850 × 1000 / 3600 = 236.1 m/s

Step 2: Convert the distance, 1.00 km = 1000 m

Step 3: Use time = distance / speed

Step 4: Substitute, time = 1000 / 236.1 = 4.24 s

The aeroplane takes about 4.23 s to travel 1.00 km.

Worked Example 2

A rectangular holding tank 25.0 m in length and 15.0 m in width is used to store water for a short period of time in an industrial plant. If 2980 m^3 of water is pumped into the tank, what is the depth of the water?

Step 1: Write the volume relation, volume = length × width × depth

Step 2: Rearrange for depth, depth = volume / (length × width)

Step 3: Substitute, depth = 2980 / (25.0 × 15.0) = 2980 / 375

Step 4: Calculate, depth = 7.95 m

The depth of the water is 7.95 m.

Worked Example 3

Find the volume of a rectangular underground water tank having dimensions 1.9 m by 1.2 m by 0.8 m.

Step 1: Write the formula, volume = length × width × height

Step 2: Substitute, volume = 1.9 × 1.2 × 0.8

Step 3: Multiply in stages, 1.9 × 1.2 = 2.28, and 2.28 × 0.8 = 1.824

The volume of the tank is 1.824 m^3.

Worked Example 4

One hectare is defined as 10^4 m^2. One acre is 4 × 10^4 ft^2. How many acres are in one hectare? (Hint: 1 m = 3.28 ft.)

Step 1: Convert one square metre to square feet, 1 m^2 = (3.28)^2 ft^2 = 10.76 ft^2

Step 2: Convert one hectare to square feet, 10^4 × 10.76 = 1.076 × 10^5 ft^2

Step 3: Divide by the size of one acre, number of acres = 1.076 × 10^5 / (4 × 10^4) = 2.69

One hectare is about 2.69 acres.

Worked Example 5

The diameter of the Moon is 3480 km. What is the volume of the Moon? How many Moons would be needed to create a volume equal to that of Earth? (Hint: Radius of Earth = 6380 km)

Step 1: Find the volume of the Moon, V = (4 / 3) π r^3, with radius of Moon = 1740 km = 1.74 × 10^6 m

Step 2: Substitute, V = 1.333 × 3.1416 × (1.74 × 10^6)^3 = 4.189 × 5.27 × 10^18 = 2.2 × 10^19 m^3

Step 3: For the number of Moons, use the ratio of volumes, which is the cube of the ratio of radii, (6380 / 1740)^3

Step 4: Calculate the ratio, 6380 / 1740 = 3.667, and 3.667^3 = 49.3

The volume of the Moon is about 2.2 × 10^19 m^3, and about 49.3 Moons would make up the volume of Earth.

mcqs.q: The least count of an instrument is best defined as:
options: The largest measurement it can make
The smallest measurement it can make reliably
mcqs.why: The least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can make reliably, and it decides how precise the instrument is. It is not the maximum range or the zero error.

mcqs.q: How does a smaller least count affect an instrument?
options: It makes the instrument more precise
It makes the instrument less precise
It has no effect on precision
mcqs.why: The smaller the least count, the more precise the instrument is, because it can reliably detect smaller changes. That is why the micrometer, with the smaller least count, is more precise than the Vernier caliper.

mcqs.q: For a Vernier caliper with 1 main scale division = 1 mm and 1 Vernier division = 0.9 mm, the least count is:
mcqs.why: Least count = 1 main scale division - 1 Vernier division = 1 mm - 0.9 mm = 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm. The value 0.01 mm belongs to the micrometer screw gauge, not the Vernier caliper.

mcqs.q: A micrometer screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on the circular scale. Its least count is:
mcqs.why: Least count = pitch / number of circular scale divisions = 0.5 mm / 50 = 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm. Dividing the pitch by the divisions, not multiplying, gives this small value.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is more precise, and why?
options: The Vernier caliper, because its least count is larger
The micrometer screw gauge, because its least count of 0.001 cm is smaller than 0.01 cm
The Vernier caliper, because it reads the main scale first
mcqs.why: The micrometer screw gauge is more precise because its least count, 0.001 cm (0.01 mm), is smaller than the Vernier caliper least count of 0.01 cm, and a smaller least count means greater precision.

mcqs.q: To read a Vernier caliper correctly, you should:
options: Read only the coinciding Vernier division
Read the sleeve reading, then the thimble division
Read the main scale just before the Vernier zero, add the coinciding division times the least count, then apply zero correction
Multiply the pitch by the number of divisions
mcqs.why: For a Vernier caliper: read the main scale just before the zero of the Vernier scale, add the coinciding Vernier division multiplied by the least count of 0.01 cm, and finally apply any zero correction. Sleeve and thimble readings belong to the micrometer.

mcqs.q: To read a micrometer screw gauge correctly, you should:
options: Read the exposed sleeve reading in mm, add the thimble division in line with the reference line times 0.01 mm, then apply zero correction
Read the main scale before the Vernier zero only
Subtract one Vernier division from one main scale division
Read the coinciding Vernier division times 0.01 cm
mcqs.why: For a micrometer: read the exposed sleeve (main scale) reading in millimetres, add the thimble division in line with the reference line multiplied by the least count of 0.01 mm, and apply any zero correction.

mcqs.q: An aeroplane travels at 850 km/h. How long does it take to travel 1.00 km?
mcqs.why: Convert speed: 850 x 1000 / 3600 = 236.1 m/s. Distance = 1000 m. Time = distance / speed = 1000 / 236.1 = 4.24 s, about 4.23 s.

mcqs.q: A tank 25.0 m long and 15.0 m wide holds 2980 m^3 of water. What is the depth of the water?
mcqs.why: Depth = volume / (length x width) = 2980 / (25.0 x 15.0) = 2980 / 375 = 7.95 m. Using volume = length x width x depth and rearranging gives the depth directly.

mcqs.q: One hectare is 10^4 m^2 and one acre is 4 x 10^4 ft^2, with 1 m = 3.28 ft. How many acres are in one hectare?

lessons.title: Errors, Uncertainty and Significant Figures
lessons.notes_html:
Significant Figures — Counting Them

All non-zero digits are significant, and zeros between non-zero digits are also significant, as in 203 which has three significant figures. Leading zeros before the first non-zero digit are not significant, as in 0.003 which has one, while trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant, as in 2.50 which has three. In scientific notation only the digits before the power of ten are counted.

For example, 23.023 has five significant figures, because all five digits are significant, including the zero between non-zero digits; 0.0003 has only one significant figure, because the leading zeros are not significant; and 2.1 × 10^-3 has two significant figures, because only the digits 2 and 1 are counted.

Rules for Calculations

  • Addition and subtraction — the answer keeps the fewest decimal places of the data
  • Multiplication and division — the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the data

Considering significant digits in the product or quotient of two measurements is necessary, because the result of a calculation cannot be more precise than the least precise measurement used in it. For example, 4.16 × 2.0 must be written as 8.3, not 8.32, otherwise the answer would claim an accuracy that the data do not have.

Exact Numbers Do Not Limit Significant Figures

If the radius of a wheel is measured as 4.16 cm and multiplied by 2 to get the diameter, the result is written as 8.32 cm, not 8 cm. The number 2 here is an exact count, not a measurement, so it has unlimited significant figures and does not limit the answer. The measured radius has three significant figures, so the diameter must also keep three significant figures; writing 8 cm would wrongly throw away measured precision.

Accuracy and Precision

AccuracyPrecision
How close a measured value is to the true value of the quantityHow close repeated measurements are to one another

A result can be precise without being accurate, for example when a faulty instrument gives nearly the same wrong reading every time. Good measurement needs both: closeness to the true value and consistency between readings.

Systematic Error and Random Error

Systematic ErrorRandom Error
Caused by a fault in the instrument, a wrong zero, or a fixed flaw in the methodCaused by unpredictable small changes in conditions or in the observer's judgement
Shifts every reading in the same direction by a similar amount; it can be either positive or negative for a given set-upMakes readings scatter on both sides of the true value; positive in some readings and negative in others
Removed by correcting (eliminating) the causeReduced by taking a number of observations and their mean, so the errors partly cancel

For example, a zero error of a scale may add to every reading or subtract from every reading — that is why a systematic error can be either positive or negative. Care and better instruments reduce random errors, but averaging repeated observations is the standard way to minimise their effect.

Uncertainty

A measurement is written with its absolute uncertainty, for example 3.67 ± 0.25 m. The percent uncertainty compares that absolute uncertainty with the measured value itself.

percent uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) × 100

Worked Example 1

What is the percent uncertainty in the measurement 3.67 ± 0.25 m?

Step 1: Write the formula, percent uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) × 100

Step 2: Substitute the values, percent uncertainty = (0.25 / 3.67) × 100

Step 3: Calculate, 0.25 / 3.67 = 0.0681, and 0.0681 × 100 = 6.81 percent

The percent uncertainty is about 6.8 percent.

Worked Example 2

What is the area, and its approximate uncertainty, of a circle with radius 3.7 × 10^4 cm?

Step 1: Find the area, A = π r^2, taking the uncertainty in r as half of the last quoted digit, 0.05 × 10^4 cm

Step 2: Substitute, A = 3.1416 × (3.7 × 10^4)^2 = 3.1416 × 1.369 × 10^9 = 4.30 × 10^9 cm^2

Step 3: Find the fractional uncertainty in r, 0.05 / 3.7 = 0.0135, and because A depends on r^2, the fractional uncertainty in A is doubled, 2 × 0.0135 = 0.027

Step 4: Find the absolute uncertainty, 0.027 × 4.30 × 10^9 = 0.12 × 10^9 cm^2, approximately 0.11 × 10^9 cm^2

The area is (4.3 ± 0.11) × 10^9 cm^2.

Worked Example 3

A watch factory claims that its watches gain or lose not more than 10 seconds in a year. How accurate is this watch, expressed as a percentage?

Step 1: Convert one year to seconds, 365 × 24 × 3600 = 3.15 × 10^7 s

Step 2: Write the formula, percentage accuracy error = (error / total time) × 100

Step 3: Substitute, (10 / 3.15 × 10^7) × 100 = 3.17 × 10^-5 percent

The watch is accurate to about 3.16 × 10^-5 percent.

mcqs.q: The numbers of significant figures in 23.023, 0.0003 and 2.1 x 10^-3 are respectively:
mcqs.why: 23.023 has 5 significant figures because all digits including the zero between non-zero digits count. 0.0003 has 1 because leading zeros are not significant, and 2.1 x 10^-3 has 2 because only 2 and 1 before the power of ten are counted.

mcqs.q: How many significant figures are in the measurement 2.50?
mcqs.why: 2.50 has three significant figures because trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant. This differs from leading zeros before the first non-zero digit, which are not significant.

mcqs.q: In addition and subtraction, the answer should keep:
options: The fewest significant figures of the data
The fewest decimal places of the data
The most decimal places of the data
mcqs.why: For addition and subtraction the answer keeps the fewest decimal places of the data. For multiplication and division, by contrast, the answer keeps the fewest significant figures of the data.

mcqs.q: The product 4.16 x 2.0 should correctly be written as:
mcqs.why: 4.16 x 2.0 = 8.32 before rounding, but 2.0 has only two significant figures, so the result keeps two significant figures: 8.3. Writing 8.32 would claim more precision than the least precise measurement allows.

mcqs.q: A wheel radius is measured as 4.16 cm. Multiplying by the exact number 2 to get the diameter gives:
options: 8 cm, because 2 has one significant figure
8.3 cm, because the answer keeps two figures
8.32 cm, because 2 is exact and does not limit the answer
mcqs.why: The diameter is 8.32 cm. The number 2 is an exact count with unlimited significant figures, so it does not limit the answer; the measured radius has three significant figures, so the diameter also keeps three.

mcqs.q: Accuracy of a measurement means:
options: How close the measured value is to the true value
How close repeated measurements are to one another
How small the least count is
How large the percent uncertainty is
mcqs.why: Accuracy is how close a measured value is to the true value of the quantity. Precision is different: it is how close repeated measurements are to one another.

mcqs.q: A faulty instrument gives nearly the same wrong reading every time. This result is:
options: Neither accurate nor precise in any sense
mcqs.why: This is precise without being accurate: the readings are close to one another (precise) but far from the true value (not accurate) because the instrument is faulty. Good measurement needs both accuracy and precision.

mcqs.q: Systematic error is removed by:
options: Taking the mean of many observations
Using a larger sample of random readings only
Ignoring the zero of the instrument
mcqs.why: Systematic error is caused by a fault in the instrument, a wrong zero or a fixed flaw in the method, so it is removed by correcting (eliminating) the cause. Taking a mean reduces random error instead.

mcqs.q: A systematic error in a given set-up can be:
mcqs.why: A systematic error shifts every reading in the same direction by a similar amount, but that direction can be either positive or negative. For example, a zero error may add to every reading or subtract from every reading.

mcqs.q: What is the percent uncertainty in the measurement 3.67 +/- 0.25 m?
mcqs.why: Percent uncertainty = (absolute uncertainty / measured value) x 100 = (0.25 / 3.67) x 100. 0.25 / 3.67 = 0.0681, and 0.0681 x 100 = 6.81 percent, about 6.8 percent.

lessons.title: Dimensional Analysis and Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
Dimensions of Common Quantities

  • Work — force × distance, so [MLT^-2] × [L] = [ML^2T^-2]
  • Energy — the same dimensions as work, [ML^2T^-2], because energy is the capacity to do work
  • Power — work divided by time, so [ML^2T^-3]
  • Momentum — mass × velocity, so [M] × [LT^-1] = [MLT^-1]
  • Force — mass × acceleration, so M × LT^-2 = [MLT^-2]
  • Displacement — [L]; strain — dimensionless; pressure — [ML^-1T^-2]

Kinetic energy, (1/2) m v^2, has dimensions [M] × [LT^-1]^2 = [ML^2T^-2], exactly the dimensions of work, so work and all forms of energy share the same dimensions.

Pairs With the Same Dimensions

Impulse and momentum have the same dimensions. Impulse is force × time, [MLT^-2] × [T] = [MLT^-1], and momentum is mass × velocity, [M] × [LT^-1] = [MLT^-1]. Checking dimensions in this way is a quick test of whether two quantities can be equal or added.

Every Term in an Equation Must Match

Every term in an equation must have the same unit as the quantity it is added to. For example, if y = a + b t + c t^2, where y is in metres and t in seconds, then the term c t^2 must be measured in metres. Since t^2 has the unit s^2, c must have the unit metre divided by s^2, i.e. m / s^2 — in other words, c has the unit of acceleration.

Deriving a Relation — Period of a Mass on a Spring

Suppose the period T depends on the mass m and the spring constant k, so T is proportional to m^a k^b. The dimensions of k are force divided by length, that is [MT^-2], so writing [T] = [M]^a [MT^-2]^b gives a + b = 0 for mass and −2b = 1 for time, hence b = −1/2 and a = 1/2. Therefore T is proportional to √(m / k), and experiment fixes the dimensionless constant as 2π, giving:

T = 2π √(m / k)

Uses of Dimensional Analysis

  • Checking an equation — if the dimensions of both sides are not equal, the equation must be wrong
  • Deriving a relation — as in finding that the period of a pendulum depends on √(l / g)
  • Converting units — changing a quantity from one system of units to another by using the conversion factors of the fundamental units
  • Checking consistency of units — preventing the mixing of, for example, centimetres and metres in one formula

Limitations of Dimensional Analysis

  • It cannot determine dimensionless constants such as 2π or 1/2 in a formula, because such numbers have no dimensions
  • It cannot distinguish between different quantities that have the same dimensions, such as work and torque
  • It cannot deal with trigonometrical, exponential or logarithmic functions
  • It cannot derive relations involving more than three fundamental quantities or quantities added or subtracted in a sum

Worked Example 1

Two students derive the following equations, in which x refers to distance travelled, v to the speed, a to the acceleration, t to the time and the subscript (o) means a quantity at time t = 0: (a) x = v t^2 + 2 a t and (b) x = v_o t + 2 a t^2. Which of these could possibly be correct according to a dimensional check?

Step 1: Check part (a), term by term: [v t^2] = LT^-1 × T^2 = LT, which is not L, and [2 a t] = LT^-2 × T = LT^-1, which is also not L, so part (a) is dimensionally incorrect

Step 2: Check part (b), term by term: [v_o t] = LT^-1 × T = L, which is correct, and [2 a t^2] = LT^-2 × T^2 = L, which is also correct

Step 3: Compare the two results: every term in (b) has the dimension of length, while no term in (a) does

(a) is incorrect and (b) could possibly be correct.

Graphs — Variables

  • Independent variable — the quantity that the experimenter changes deliberately, one step at a time, in order to study its effect; it is the cause
  • Dependent variable — the quantity that responds to that change and is measured during the experiment; it is the effect

For example, in studying how the length of a pendulum affects its period, length is independent and period is dependent.

Types of Graph

A graph is a visual plot of the dependent variable against the independent variable, and it shows their relationship at a glance.

TypeUse
Line graphContinuous change, such as displacement against time
Bar graphComparing separate categories, such as the marks of different subjects
Pie chartShares of a total
Scatter graphLooking for a correlation between two measured quantities

For example, a straight line on a velocity-time graph shows uniform acceleration, its slope gives the acceleration and the area under it gives the displacement.

Extrapolation

Extrapolation means extending a graph or a trend beyond the range of the measured data in order to predict a value outside that range. In the graphical method the plotted curve is extended smoothly in the same trend, and the required value is read off it; in the formula method the equation fitted to the data is used with a value of the variable outside the measured range. Extrapolation assumes that the observed trend continues unchanged, so its predictions become less reliable the farther they go from the data.

mcqs.q: The dimensions of work are:
mcqs.why: Work = force x distance, so [MLT^-2] x [L] = [ML^2T^-2]. Energy has the same dimensions as work, while [ML^2T^-3] is power and [MLT^-1] is momentum.

mcqs.q: The dimensions of power are:
mcqs.why: Power = work / time, so [ML^2T^-2] / [T] = [ML^2T^-3]. Work itself is [ML^2T^-2], momentum is [MLT^-1] and pressure is [ML^-1T^-2].

mcqs.q: Momentum has dimensions:
mcqs.why: Momentum = mass x velocity, so [M] x [LT^-1] = [MLT^-1]. Force is [MLT^-2] and work is [ML^2T^-2], so neither of those matches momentum.

mcqs.q: Kinetic energy, (1/2) m v^2, has the same dimensions as:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy has dimensions [M] x [LT^-1]^2 = [ML^2T^-2], exactly the dimensions of work, [MLT^-2] x [L] = [ML^2T^-2]. So work and all forms of energy share the same dimensions.

mcqs.q: Which pair has the same dimensions?
options: Work and torque only, with no other example in the notes
mcqs.why: Impulse = force x time = [MLT^-2] x [T] = [MLT^-1], and momentum = mass x velocity = [M] x [LT^-1] = [MLT^-1], so impulse and momentum have the same dimensions.

mcqs.q: Which statement about dimensions is correct?
options: Displacement is dimensionless and strain is [L]
Strain is dimensionless while displacement is [L]
mcqs.why: Displacement has dimension [L], while strain is dimensionless because it is a ratio of two lengths. Pressure is [ML^-1T^-2], not [MLT^-1].

mcqs.q: The dimensions of the spring constant k, defined as force divided by length, are:
mcqs.why: k = force / length, so its dimensions are [MLT^-2] / [L] = [MT^-2]. This result is used in deriving the period of a mass on a spring by dimensional analysis.

mcqs.q: If y = a + b t + c t^2, with y in metres and t in seconds, the unit of c is:
mcqs.why: Every term must have the unit of y, the metre, so c t^2 is in metres. Since t^2 has unit s^2, c must have unit metre / s^2, i.e. m/s^2, the unit of acceleration.

mcqs.q: By dimensional analysis, the period T of a mass m on a spring of constant k is proportional to:
mcqs.why: Writing [T] = [M]^a [MT^-2]^b gives a + b = 0 for mass and -2b = 1 for time, so b = -1/2 and a = 1/2. Therefore T is proportional to sqrt(m/k), and experiment fixes the constant as 2pi.

mcqs.q: Which equation passes a dimensional check, where x is distance, v is speed, a is acceleration and t is time?
mcqs.why: For x = v_o t + 2 a t^2: [v_o t] = LT^-1 x T = L and [2 a t^2] = LT^-2 x T^2 = L, so every term is a length. For x = v t^2 + 2 a t the terms give LT and LT^-1, so that equation fails.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a use of dimensional analysis listed in the notes?
options: Checking whether an equation can be correct
Deriving a relation such as the pendulum period depending on sqrt(l/g)
Finding the exact value of dimensionless constants such as 2pi
Converting a quantity from one system of units to another
mcqs.why: Dimensional analysis is used for checking equations, deriving relations and converting units, but it cannot determine dimensionless constants such as 2pi or 1/2 because such numbers have no dimensions.

mcqs.q: Which is a limitation of dimensional analysis?
options: It cannot check the dimensions of both sides of an equation
It cannot distinguish quantities with the same dimensions, such as work and torque
It cannot be used to convert units
It can handle trigonometrical and exponential functions fully
mcqs.why: A limitation is that dimensional analysis cannot distinguish between different quantities that have the same dimensions, such as work and torque. It also cannot deal with trigonometrical, exponential or logarithmic functions.

mcqs.q: In an experiment on how pendulum length affects period, the dependent variable is:
options: The period, because it is the effect that is measured
The length, because it is the cause
mcqs.why: The independent variable is the cause changed deliberately (pendulum length), and the dependent variable is the effect measured in response (the period). So the dependent variable is the period.

mcqs.q: A scatter graph is best used for:
options: Comparing separate categories such as subject marks
Looking for a correlation between two measured quantities
Showing continuous change such as displacement against time
mcqs.why: A scatter graph is used for looking for a correlation between two measured quantities. A pie chart shows shares of a total, a bar graph compares separate categories, and a line graph shows continuous change.

mcqs.q: Extrapolation means:
options: Repeating measurements and taking their mean
Correcting a zero error on an instrument
Reading a value between two measured points only
Extending a graph or trend beyond the measured data to predict a value outside that range
mcqs.why: Extrapolation means extending a graph or trend beyond the range of measured data to predict a value outside that range. It assumes the trend continues unchanged, so predictions become less reliable the farther they go from the data.

lessons.title: Vectors, Scalars and Resolution of a Vector
lessons.notes_html:
Displacement as a Vector

Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so displacements are combined as vectors, not by simple addition of their magnitudes. Two displacement vectors of 6 m and 8 m give different resultants according to the angle between them: parallel vectors give 14 m, antiparallel vectors give only 2 m, and perpendicular vectors give √(6^2 + 8^2) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 m.

Parallelogram Law of Addition

When two vectors are drawn from the same point, their resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed on them. For two forces F1 and F2 with angle θ between them:

R = √(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos θ)

Dot Product

The dot (scalar) product of two vectors A and B has magnitude A B cos θ, where θ is the angle between them.

  • If the dot product of two non-zero vectors vanishes, the vectors are perpendicular to each other, because A B cos θ can vanish for non-zero vectors only when cos θ = 0, that is θ = 90°

Cross Product

The cross (vector) product of two vectors A and B has magnitude A B sin θ.

When Dot and Cross Products Are Equal

The magnitudes A B cos θ and A B sin θ are equal when sin θ = cos θ, that is tan θ = 1. This happens at θ = 45°, so the angle at which the dot product becomes equal to the cross product is 45°.

ProductMagnitudeSpecial Case
Dot productA B cos θZero when θ = 90° (perpendicular)
Cross productA B sin θEqual to dot product when θ = 45°

Worked Example 1

Two tug boats are towing a ship, each exerts a force of 6000 N, and the angle between the two ropes is 60°. Calculate the resultant force on the ship.

Step 1: Write the parallelogram law, R = √(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos θ)

Step 2: Substitute, R = √(6000^2 + 6000^2 + 2 × 6000 × 6000 × cos 60°)

Step 3: Calculate inside the root, 3.6 × 10^7 + 3.6 × 10^7 + (7.2 × 10^7 × 0.5) = 1.08 × 10^8

Step 4: Take the square root, R = √(1.08 × 10^8) = 10392 N

The resultant force on the ship is 10392 N, acting along the bisector of the angle between the ropes.

mcqs.q: Two displacement vectors of 6 m and 8 m are perpendicular to each other. Their resultant is:
mcqs.why: For perpendicular vectors, R = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(36 + 64) = sqrt(100) = 10 m. Parallel vectors would give 14 m and antiparallel vectors only 2 m.

mcqs.q: According to the parallelogram law, the resultant of forces F1 and F2 with angle theta between them is:
options: R = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos theta)
R = F1 + F2 in all cases
R = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 - 2 F1 F2 sin theta) only
mcqs.why: When two vectors are drawn from the same point, their resultant is the diagonal of the parallelogram formed on them: R = sqrt(F1^2 + F2^2 + 2 F1 F2 cos theta). Simple addition F1 + F2 holds only when they are parallel.

mcqs.q: Two tug boats each exert 6000 N with 60 deg between the ropes. The resultant force on the ship is:
mcqs.why: R = sqrt(6000^2 + 6000^2 + 2 x 6000 x 6000 x cos 60 deg). Inside the root: 3.6 x 10^7 + 3.6 x 10^7 + 7.2 x 10^7 x 0.5 = 1.08 x 10^8. sqrt(1.08 x 10^8) = 10392 N, along the bisector of the angle.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the dot (scalar) product of vectors A and B with angle theta between them is:
mcqs.why: The dot product has magnitude A B cos theta, where theta is the angle between the vectors. The cross product, by contrast, has magnitude A B sin theta.

mcqs.q: If the dot product of two non-zero vectors vanishes, the vectors must be:
mcqs.why: Dot product = A B cos theta can vanish for non-zero vectors only when cos theta = 0, that is theta = 90 deg, so the vectors are perpendicular to each other.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the cross (vector) product of A and B is:
options: Equal to the dot product at 90 deg
mcqs.why: The cross product has magnitude A B sin theta, where theta is the angle between the vectors. The dot product uses cos theta instead, and the two become equal at 45 deg, not 90 deg.

mcqs.q: At what angle are the magnitudes of the dot product and the cross product equal?
mcqs.why: A B cos theta = A B sin theta requires sin theta = cos theta, i.e. tan theta = 1, which happens at theta = 45 deg. So the dot and cross product magnitudes are equal at 45 deg.

mcqs.q: Two 6 m and 8 m displacements in the same direction (parallel) combine to give:
mcqs.why: Parallel vectors in the same direction add by magnitude: 6 m + 8 m = 14 m. Antiparallel vectors give only 8 - 6 = 2 m, and perpendicular vectors give 10 m.

mcqs.q: Why must displacements be combined as vectors rather than by simply adding magnitudes?
options: Because displacement is a scalar quantity
Because displacement has both magnitude and direction
Because displacement is measured only in metres
mcqs.why: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, so displacements are combined as vectors, not by simple addition of magnitudes. The resultant depends on the angle between them: 14 m parallel, 2 m antiparallel, 10 m perpendicular for 6 m and 8 m.

mcqs.q: For the two equal tug-boat forces, the resultant acts:
options: Along the bisector of the angle between the ropes
mcqs.why: The resultant force of 10392 N acts along the bisector of the angle between the ropes. For two equal forces the parallelogram is symmetric, so its diagonal bisects the angle between them.

lessons.title: Motion Graphs and Instantaneous Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
Speed and Velocity in Daily Life

Speed is used whenever only the rate of covering distance matters, for example the speedometer of a car, speed limits on roads, the speed of a ceiling fan or of an internet connection. Velocity is used when the direction also matters, for example in navigation of ships and aircraft, in weather reports giving wind movement, and in sports where a ball must be sent in a chosen direction. In short, speed tells how fast, while velocity tells how fast and in which direction.

Average Velocity and Average Speed

  • Average velocity — displacement divided by time
  • Average speed — total distance divided by time

Displacement can never be greater than the distance travelled, so the ratio of the numerical values of average velocity and average speed is always unity or less: it is 1 for straight motion in one direction and less than 1 whenever the path is not straight.

Instantaneous Velocity and Uniform Velocity

The instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant. If the average velocity of a body becomes equal to its instantaneous velocity, the body is moving with uniform velocity: the velocity does not change at any instant, so the velocity at every instant is the same as the average over any interval. In all other cases the instantaneous velocity keeps differing from the average value.

As an illustration of changing velocity: if a particle has velocity 10 m/s at an instant and 20 m/s after 5 s, its uniform acceleration is (20 − 10) / 5 = 2 m/s^2, and 3 s before that instant its velocity was 10 − (2 × 3) = 4 m/s.

Velocity-Time Graph — Slope

On a velocity-time graph the slope gives the acceleration of the body.

Velocity-Time Graph — Area

The area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement of the body during that time interval. This is because a thin strip of the area has height v and width dt, and v × dt is the small displacement in that short interval. The rule holds for uniform as well as accelerated motion, and in addition the slope of the same graph gives the acceleration.

A straight line on a velocity-time graph shows uniform acceleration: its slope gives the acceleration and the area under it gives the displacement — the same two readings used when the equations of motion are derived from the graph in the next lesson.

mcqs.q: A car speedometer, road speed limits and the speed of a ceiling fan are examples of the use of:
options: Speed, because only the rate of covering distance matters
Velocity, because direction is essential in each case
mcqs.why: Speed is used whenever only the rate of covering distance matters, as with a speedometer, speed limits, a ceiling fan or an internet connection. Velocity is used when direction also matters, as in navigation and wind reports.

mcqs.q: Average velocity is defined as:
options: Change in speed divided by time
mcqs.why: Average velocity = displacement / time, while average speed = total distance / time. Because displacement can never exceed distance travelled, the two averages are generally different.

mcqs.q: The ratio of the numerical values of average velocity to average speed is always:
mcqs.why: Average velocity uses displacement and average speed uses total distance. Displacement can never be greater than distance travelled, so the ratio is unity or less: 1 for straight motion in one direction and less than 1 otherwise.

mcqs.q: The ratio of average velocity to average speed equals 1 when:
options: The body moves in a straight line in one direction
The body returns to its starting point
mcqs.why: The ratio is 1 for straight motion in one direction, because then displacement equals distance travelled. Whenever the path is not straight, displacement is smaller than distance and the ratio is less than 1.

mcqs.q: Instantaneous velocity means:
options: The average velocity over a long interval
The total displacement divided by total time
The velocity at a particular instant
The speed shown averaged over a journey
mcqs.why: Instantaneous velocity is the velocity at a particular instant. If it stays the same at every instant and equals the average velocity, the body moves with uniform velocity.

mcqs.q: If the average velocity of a body becomes equal to its instantaneous velocity, the body moves with:
mcqs.why: The body moves with uniform velocity: the velocity does not change at any instant, so the velocity at every instant is the same as the average over any interval. In all other cases instantaneous velocity keeps differing from the average.

mcqs.q: On a velocity-time graph, the slope gives:
options: Instantaneous speed at one point only
mcqs.why: On a velocity-time graph the slope gives the acceleration of the body, while the area under the graph gives the displacement. A straight line on this graph shows uniform acceleration.

mcqs.q: The area under a velocity-time graph gives:
mcqs.why: The area under a velocity-time graph gives the displacement, because a thin strip has height v and width dt, and v x dt is the small displacement in that interval. The slope of the same graph gives acceleration.

mcqs.q: A straight line on a velocity-time graph shows:
options: That the body is at rest
Uniform acceleration, with slope giving acceleration and area giving displacement
mcqs.why: A straight line on a velocity-time graph shows uniform acceleration: its slope gives the acceleration and the area under it gives the displacement. These are the same two readings used to derive the equations of motion.

mcqs.q: A particle has velocity 10 m/s at an instant and 20 m/s after 5 s, with uniform acceleration. Its velocity 3 s before that instant was:
mcqs.why: Acceleration = (20 - 10) / 5 = 2 m/s^2. Going 3 s back: velocity = 10 - (2 x 3) = 10 - 6 = 4 m/s. The forward change must be reversed when going backwards in time.

lessons.title: Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion
lessons.notes_html:
The Three Equations

v = u + a t

s = u t + (1/2) a t^2

v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s

Together they connect the five quantities u, v, a, t and s for motion with constant acceleration.

How the Equations Are Derived

  • First equation — v = u + a t comes directly from the definition of acceleration, a = (v − u) / t, rearranged for v
  • Second equation — s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 comes from the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a rectangle of area u t plus a triangle of area (1/2) a t^2
  • Third equation — v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s is obtained by eliminating t between the first two equations

Starting From Rest

An object can have an initial velocity of zero and still experience uniformly accelerated motion. Acceleration depends on the force acting on the body, not on its starting velocity, so a body dropped from rest starts with zero velocity but falls with the uniform acceleration g. Similarly, a car starting from rest with a steady engine force moves with roughly uniform acceleration in its first moments. Zero initial velocity only means the body begins from rest; it says nothing about how its velocity will change afterwards.

Upward Throw — Time to Return

A ball thrown upwards with a velocity of 100 m/s, taking g = 10 m/s^2, takes the total time of flight 2u / g = (2 × 100) / 10 = 20 s to reach the ground again. The ball spends 10 s rising and the same 10 s falling back to the ground.

Distance in the nth Second

s_n = u + (a / 2)(2n − 1)

Worked Example 1

A car starts from rest and moves with a constant acceleration. During the 5th second of its motion, it covers a distance of 36 metres. Calculate: (a) the acceleration of the car, (b) the total distance covered by the car during this time.

Step 1: Use the formula for distance in the nth second, s_n = u + (a / 2)(2n − 1), with n = 5

Step 2: Substitute, 36 = 0 + (a / 2)(9), so 36 = 4.5 a

Step 3: Solve part (a), a = 36 / 4.5 = 8 m/s^2

Step 4: For part (b), use s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 with t = 5 s, giving s = 0 + (1/2) × 8 × 25 = 100 m

The acceleration is 8 m/s^2 and the total distance covered in 5 s is 100 m.

Worked Example 2

A helicopter is ascending at the rate of 12 m/s. At a height of 80 m above the ground, a package is dropped. How long does the package take to reach the ground?

Step 1: Take upward as positive, so the displacement to the ground is s = −80 m and the acceleration is a = −10 m/s^2; the initial velocity of the package is u = +12 m/s, the same as the helicopter

Step 2: Use s = u t + (1/2) a t^2, giving −80 = 12 t − 5 t^2

Step 3: Rearrange into a quadratic, 5 t^2 − 12 t − 80 = 0

Step 4: Solve, t = [12 + √(144 + 1600)] / 10 = [12 + √1744] / 10 = [12 + 41.76] / 10 = 5.38 s, rejecting the negative root

The package takes about 5.4 s to reach the ground.

mcqs.q: The first equation of motion, v = u + a t, is obtained from:
options: The area under the velocity-time graph
Eliminating t between the other two equations
The definition of acceleration, a = (v - u) / t, rearranged for v
The formula for distance in the nth second
mcqs.why: v = u + a t comes directly from the definition of acceleration, a = (v - u) / t, rearranged for v. The second equation comes from the area under the velocity-time graph, and the third by eliminating t.

mcqs.q: The second equation, s = u t + (1/2) a t^2, comes from:
options: The area under the velocity-time graph: rectangle u t plus triangle (1/2) a t^2
Eliminating s between the other equations
mcqs.why: s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 comes from the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a rectangle of area u t plus a triangle of area (1/2) a t^2. Together the three equations connect u, v, a, t and s for constant acceleration.

mcqs.q: The third equation, v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, is obtained by:
options: Measuring the slope of a displacement graph
Eliminating t between the first two equations
Taking the area of a triangle only
mcqs.why: v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s is obtained by eliminating t between v = u + a t and s = u t + (1/2) a t^2. It links v, u, a and s without needing the time.

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown upwards with velocity 100 m/s, taking g = 10 m/s^2. The total time to return to the ground is:
mcqs.why: Total time of flight = 2u / g = (2 x 100) / 10 = 20 s. The ball spends 10 s rising and the same 10 s falling back to the ground.

mcqs.q: Can a body starting from rest (u = 0) still have uniformly accelerated motion?
options: No, zero velocity means zero acceleration
Yes, for example a dropped body falls with uniform acceleration g
Only if its velocity stays zero
Only for a car, not for a falling body
mcqs.why: Yes. Acceleration depends on the force acting, not on the starting velocity, so a body dropped from rest starts with zero velocity but falls with uniform acceleration g. Zero initial velocity only means the body begins from rest.

mcqs.q: The distance covered in the nth second is given by:
mcqs.why: Distance in the nth second is s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1). This is the formula used for the car covering 36 m in its 5th second, giving a = 8 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A car starts from rest and covers 36 m during its 5th second. Its acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Use s_n = u + (a/2)(2n - 1) with u = 0, n = 5: 36 = 0 + (a/2)(9) = 4.5 a, so a = 36 / 4.5 = 8 m/s^2. The total distance in 5 s is then 100 m.

mcqs.q: For the same car (starting from rest, a = 8 m/s^2), the total distance covered in 5 s is:
mcqs.why: s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 = 0 + (1/2) x 8 x 25 = 100 m. The 36 m figure is only the distance covered during the 5th second alone, not the total.

mcqs.q: A package is dropped from a helicopter ascending at 12 m/s at a height of 80 m (g = 10 m/s^2). It reaches the ground in about:
The three equations of motion together connect which set of quantities for constant acceleration?
options: u, v, a, t and s
mcqs.why: The equations v = u + a t, s = u t + (1/2) a t^2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s together connect the five quantities u, v, a, t and s for motion with constant (uniform) acceleration.

lessons.title: Projectile Motion
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Projectile?

A kicked football, a cricket ball hit by the bat, a basketball thrown towards the basket, water from a garden hose and a stone thrown from a cliff are all projectiles once they leave the hand or the bat and move under gravity alone.

The motion of an aeroplane in normal flight is not projectile motion, because its engines provide thrust and its wings provide lift, so forces other than gravity act on it throughout. Only an object dropped or released from the aeroplane behaves as a projectile.

Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion

The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile take place independently of each other, each obeying its own equations. Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the velocity stays u cos θ, while vertically gravity produces the acceleration g and the velocity changes as in free fall. The two motions are linked only by the common time t, which is why the combination of steady horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion produces the parabolic path.

Horizontal Component of Velocity

The horizontal component, v_x = u cos θ, remains constant throughout the flight when air resistance is neglected. This is because no force acts in the horizontal direction, so there is no horizontal acceleration. The projectile therefore covers equal horizontal distances in equal times, and its horizontal motion is exactly like uniform motion in a straight line.

Acceleration at the Top of the Trajectory

Throughout the flight the only acceleration acting on a projectile is the acceleration due to gravity, acting vertically downward. At the top only the vertical component of velocity becomes zero for an instant; the acceleration remains g.

Range and Horizontal Distance

They are closely related but not exactly the same idea. The range is the specific horizontal distance between the point of projection and the point where the projectile lands at the same level. The phrase horizontal distance is general and can mean the horizontal separation at any stage of the flight or between any two points. So range is one particular horizontal distance, the total one for the complete flight.

R = (u^2 sin 2θ) / g

H = (u^2 sin^2 θ) / (2 g)

Effect of Launch Angle and Velocity

Increasing the launch velocity increases everything: the range and maximum height grow with u^2 and the time of flight grows with u. The launch angle divides the velocity into components: a larger angle gives more height and time of flight but less horizontal speed, while a smaller angle gives a flatter, faster flight. The range is greatest at 45°, and two complementary angles give the same range with different heights and times.

For the same speed, projectiles fired at 60° and 30° have the same range, because the range depends on sin 2θ and sin 120° = sin 60°. Their heights and times of flight differ, because those depend on sin θ and sin^2 θ, which are not equal for 30° and 60°.

Effect of Air Resistance

Air resistance opposes the motion at every instant, so it reduces both the horizontal and the vertical component of velocity. As a result the maximum height, the range and the speed of landing all become smaller than their ideal values, and the trajectory is no longer a symmetric parabola, the falling part becoming steeper. The time of flight also changes, and strictly the horizontal velocity is no longer constant.

Worked Example 1

Show that the ranges of a projectile at complementary angles are the same, with examples.

Step 1: Write the range for the complementary angle (90° − θ), R' = (u^2 sin 2(90° − θ)) / g = (u^2 sin(180° − 2θ)) / g

Step 2: Use the identity sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ, so R' = (u^2 sin 2θ) / g = R

Step 3: Give an example: for the same speed u, angles 30° and 60° give sin 60° and sin 120°, and both sines equal 0.866, so both ranges are equal

Projectiles projected at complementary angles, such as 30° and 60°, have the same range.

Worked Example 2

At what angle does the range of a projectile become equal to the height of the projectile?

Step 1: Equate the two expressions, (u^2 sin 2θ) / g = (u^2 sin^2 θ) / (2 g), and cancel u^2 / g

Step 2: Write sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ, so 2 sin θ cos θ = (sin^2 θ) / 2

Step 3: Divide both sides by sin θ cos θ, giving tan θ = 4

Step 4: Find the angle, θ = arctan(4) = 76°

The range equals the maximum height when the angle of projection is about 76°.

Worked Example 3

A mortar shell is fired at a ground level target 500 m distance with an initial velocity of 90 m/s. What is the launch angle?

Step 1: Write the range formula, R = (u^2 sin 2θ) / g

Step 2: Rearrange, sin 2θ = R g / u^2

Step 3: Substitute, sin 2θ = (500 × 9.8) / (90)^2 = 4900 / 8100 = 0.605

Step 4: Find 2θ, 2θ = sin^-1(0.605) = 37.2° or 180 − 37.2 = 142.8°, so θ = 18.6° or 71.4°

The launch angle is 71.4° for the high trajectory (the shell can also reach the target at the complementary angle of 18.6°).

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT projectile motion?
options: The normal flight of an aeroplane
A stone thrown from a cliff
mcqs.why: An aeroplane in normal flight is not a projectile because its engines provide thrust and its wings provide lift, so forces other than gravity act throughout. A football, hose water and a thrown stone move under gravity alone once released.

mcqs.q: The independence of horizontal and vertical motion in a projectile means:
options: The two motions are independent, each obeying its own equations, linked only by the common time t
Horizontal motion stops when vertical motion starts
Gravity acts horizontally as well as vertically
The path is a straight line
mcqs.why: The horizontal and vertical motions take place independently, each obeying its own equations, linked only by the common time t. Steady horizontal motion plus accelerated vertical motion produces the parabolic path.

mcqs.q: The horizontal component of velocity of a projectile, v_x = u cos theta, during flight (no air resistance):
options: Becomes zero at the top and stays zero
mcqs.why: v_x = u cos theta remains constant throughout the flight when air resistance is neglected, because no force acts horizontally, so there is no horizontal acceleration and equal horizontal distances are covered in equal times.

mcqs.q: At the top of the trajectory, the vertical component of velocity is:
mcqs.why: At the top only the vertical component of velocity becomes zero for an instant. The horizontal component u cos theta continues, and the acceleration remains g downward.

mcqs.q: At the top of the trajectory, the acceleration of the projectile is:
mcqs.why: Throughout the flight the only acceleration is g acting vertically downward, including at the top. Only the vertical component of velocity becomes zero there; the acceleration remains g.

mcqs.q: The range of a projectile launched with speed u at angle theta is:
options: R = u^2 / g in all cases
mcqs.why: Range R = (u^2 sin 2 theta) / g. The expression (u^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g) is the maximum height H, not the range, so the two formulas must not be swapped.

mcqs.q: The maximum height of a projectile is:
mcqs.why: Maximum height H = (u^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g), which depends on sin^2 theta. The range formula uses sin 2 theta instead, which is why complementary angles share a range but not a height.

mcqs.q: For a given launch speed, the range is greatest at a launch angle of:
mcqs.why: The range is greatest at 45 deg, because R depends on sin 2 theta and sin 90 deg = 1 is the maximum value. At 76 deg the range instead equals the maximum height.

mcqs.q: Two projectiles fired with the same speed at 30 deg and 60 deg have:
mcqs.why: They have the same range because R depends on sin 2 theta and sin 120 deg = sin 60 deg (both 0.866). Their heights and times of flight differ because those depend on sin theta and sin^2 theta.

mcqs.q: Why do the 30 deg and 60 deg projectiles (same speed) have different heights despite equal ranges?
options: Height depends on sin theta and sin^2 theta, which are not equal for 30 deg and 60 deg
Height depends on sin 2 theta, like the range
Air resistance acts differently at the two angles in the ideal case
Gravity is larger for the 60 deg launch
mcqs.why: Height and time of flight depend on sin theta and sin^2 theta, which are not equal for 30 deg and 60 deg, so they differ. Only the range, depending on sin 2 theta, is the same for complementary angles.

mcqs.q: The range of a projectile equals its maximum height when the launch angle is about:
mcqs.why: Setting R = H gives (u^2 sin 2 theta)/g = (u^2 sin^2 theta)/(2g), which reduces to tan theta = 4, so theta = arctan(4) = about 76 deg.

mcqs.q: A mortar shell fired at 90 m/s must hit a target 500 m away (g = 9.8 m/s^2). The high-trajectory launch angle is:
mcqs.why: sin 2 theta = R g / u^2 = (500 x 9.8) / 8100 = 4900 / 8100 = 0.605, so 2 theta = 37.2 deg or 142.8 deg, giving theta = 18.6 deg or 71.4 deg. The high trajectory uses 71.4 deg.

mcqs.q: When air resistance is taken into account, what happens to a projectile?
options: Maximum height, range and landing speed all become smaller, and the falling part becomes steeper
Its horizontal velocity stays exactly constant
Its trajectory stays a symmetric parabola
mcqs.why: Air resistance opposes the motion at every instant, reducing both velocity components, so maximum height, range and landing speed all become smaller, the trajectory is no longer a symmetric parabola (the falling part is steeper), and horizontal velocity is no longer constant.

mcqs.q: Increasing the launch velocity u (at a fixed angle) affects the projectile as follows:
options: Range and height grow with u^2, and time of flight grows with u
Time of flight decreases as u increases
mcqs.why: Increasing launch velocity increases everything: range and maximum height grow with u^2 (both formulas contain u^2) and time of flight grows with u. Nothing decreases when u increases at a fixed angle.

mcqs.q: How is range different from horizontal distance in general?
options: They are exactly the same in every situation
Range is any horizontal separation at any stage of flight
Range is the specific horizontal distance from projection to landing at the same level, while horizontal distance is the general term
mcqs.why: Range is the specific horizontal distance between the point of projection and the point where the projectile lands at the same level. Horizontal distance is general and can mean the separation at any stage of flight, so range is one particular horizontal distance.

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion, Inertia and Weight
lessons.notes_html:
Mass and Inertia

The term mass refers to the same physical concept as inertia. Mass is the measure of the inertia of a body, that is, of its resistance to any change in its state of rest or motion. A body of greater mass is harder to start, stop or turn, while weight is a force that depends on gravity and is a different quantity.

Force and Acceleration

The laws of motion show the relationship between force and acceleration. Newton's second law, F = m a, states that the acceleration produced in a body is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to its mass. The laws of motion are therefore fundamentally a statement of how force and acceleration are related for a given mass.

For example, a 3 kg bowling ball experiencing a net force of 15 N has acceleration a = F / m = 15 / 3 = 5 m/s^2, and the acceleration acts in the direction of the net force on the ball.

Types of Forces

Forces may be contact forces or field forces acting at a distance.

  • Contact forces — the push or pull of a hand, friction, tension in a string, the normal reaction of a surface and air resistance
  • Field forces — the gravitational force (weight), the electric force and the magnetic force, which act without touching the body

In every case a force can change the speed, the direction or the shape of the object.

Friction — a Self Adjusting Force

Frictional force is also called a self adjusting force. Static friction adjusts its own magnitude to match the applied force, up to its limiting value, so that the body stays at rest. Tension, weight and thrust do not change themselves in this self adjusting way.

How Friction Influences Motion

Friction opposes the relative motion, or the tendency of motion, between surfaces in contact, so it slows a moving object and can bring it to rest. It wastes part of the kinetic energy as heat, which is why extra force is needed to keep an object moving at constant speed on a rough surface. At the same time friction is useful, because walking, braking of vehicles and gripping of objects are all impossible without it.

Calculating Net Force

First list all the forces acting on the body and show them on a free body diagram, with their directions. Then add the forces as vectors, taking forces in one chosen direction as positive and those in the opposite direction as negative, or resolving them into x and y components when they are not in a line. The vector sum so obtained is the net force, and it alone decides the acceleration through F_net = m a.

Weight and Mass

Weight is a force, found from the mass by W = m g, so mass is obtained from a known weight as m = W / g. This conversion is the first step in the two worked examples below.

Worked Example 1

A car weighing 9800 N is moving with a speed of 40 km/h. On the application of brakes it comes to rest after travelling a distance of 50 metres. Calculate the average retarding force.

Step 1: Find the mass, m = W / g = 9800 / 9.8 = 1000 kg

Step 2: Convert the speed, 40 km/h = 40 × 1000 / 3600 = 11.11 m/s

Step 3: Use v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, so 0 = (11.11)^2 + 2 a (50), giving 0 = 123.4 + 100 a

Step 4: Solve for the retardation, a = −123.4 / 100 = −1.235 m/s^2

Step 5: Find the force, F = m a = 1000 × 1.235 = 1235 N in magnitude (using more exact figures, 1234.57 N)

The average retarding force is about 1234.57 N, acting opposite to the motion.

Worked Example 2

A helicopter weighs 3920 N. Calculate the force on it if it is ascending up at the rate of 2 m/s^2. What will be the force on the helicopter if it is moving up with a constant speed of 4 m/s?

Step 1: Find the mass, m = W / g = 3920 / 9.8 = 400 kg

Step 2: For accelerated ascent, the lifting force must overcome weight and also provide m a, so F = m (g + a)

Step 3: Substitute, F = 400 × (9.8 + 2) = 400 × 11.8 = 4720 N

Step 4: At a constant speed of 4 m/s the acceleration is zero, so the lifting force only balances the weight, F = W = 3920 N

The force is 4720 N while accelerating upward, and 3920 N while rising at constant speed.

mcqs.q: The term mass refers to the same physical concept as:
mcqs.why: Mass is the measure of the inertia of a body, that is, its resistance to any change in its state of rest or motion. Weight is a different quantity, a force that depends on gravity.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following forces is also called a self adjusting force?
mcqs.why: Static friction adjusts its own magnitude to match the applied force, up to its limiting value, so the body stays at rest. Tension, weight and thrust do not adjust themselves in this self adjusting way.

mcqs.q: The laws of motion show the relationship between:
mcqs.why: Newton's second law, F = m a, states that the acceleration produced is directly proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass, so the laws of motion relate force and acceleration for a given mass.

mcqs.q: A 3 kg bowling ball experiences a net force of 15 N. What will be its acceleration?
mcqs.why: From F = m a, the acceleration is a = F / m = 15 / 3 = 5 m/s^2, and it acts in the direction of the net force on the ball.

mcqs.q: A car weighs 9800 N. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, the mass of the car is:
mcqs.why: Mass is obtained from a known weight by m = W / g = 9800 / 9.8 = 1000 kg. This conversion is the first step before the mass can be used in F = m a.

mcqs.q: A car weighing 9800 N is moving at 40 km/h. On applying the brakes it comes to rest after travelling 50 m. The average retarding force is about:
mcqs.why: Working: m = 9800 / 9.8 = 1000 kg and u = 40 km/h = 11.11 m/s. From v^2 = u^2 + 2 a s, 0 = 123.4 + 100 a, so a = -1.235 m/s^2. Then F = m a = 1000 x 1.235 = about 1235 N, acting opposite to the motion.

mcqs.q: A helicopter weighs 3920 N. The force on it while it is ascending with an acceleration of 2 m/s^2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: m = W / g = 3920 / 9.8 = 400 kg. For accelerated ascent the lifting force must overcome the weight and also provide m a, so F = m (g + a) = 400 x (9.8 + 2) = 400 x 11.8 = 4720 N.

mcqs.q: The same helicopter (weight 3920 N) rises with a constant speed of 4 m/s. The lifting force on it is then:
mcqs.why: At constant speed the acceleration is zero, so the lifting force only has to balance the weight: F = W = 3920 N, whatever the steady speed of rising happens to be.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a field force, acting at a distance without touching the body?
mcqs.why: The gravitational force (weight), like the electric and magnetic forces, is a field force that acts without touching the body. Friction, tension and the normal reaction are contact forces.

mcqs.q: The weight of a body of mass 5 kg, taking g = 9.8 m/s^2, is:
mcqs.why: Weight is a force found from W = m g = 5 x 9.8 = 49 N. The mass remains 5 kg; the weight is the force and is measured in newtons.

lessons.title: Momentum, Impulse and Newton's Second Law
lessons.notes_html:
Newton's Second Law of Motion

Newton's second law states that the acceleration of a body is directly proportional to the resultant force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass, and it takes place in the direction of the force. In symbols:

F = m a

where F is the net force in newtons, m the mass in kilograms and a the acceleration in m/s^2. It also has the more general form that force is the rate of change of momentum.

Force as Rate of Change of Momentum

The rate of change of linear momentum of a body is called a linear force. By Newton's second law, the resultant force acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its linear momentum:

F = Δp / Δt

Impulse is force multiplied by time, and power is the rate of doing work, so neither of them is a rate of change of momentum.

How Mass Affects Acceleration

For the same applied force, a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration, because a = F / m and acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration if the force is unchanged. This is why a loaded truck speeds up much more slowly than an empty one driven with the same engine force.

The second law means a bigger push speeds a body up faster, while a heavier body responds more slowly to the same push. For example, a force of 20 N gives a 2 kg trolley an acceleration of 10 m/s^2, but the same force gives a 5 kg trolley only 4 m/s^2. The law also explains everyday facts such as why a loaded vehicle needs a stronger engine force to accelerate like an empty one.

Impulse

Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts, and it is equal to the change in momentum of the body:

J = F × Δt = m v − m u

A large force acting for a short time can therefore produce the same impulse as a small force acting for a long time. This is why extending the time of impact, as with a fielder pulling his hands back while catching a ball, reduces the force experienced.

The impulse-momentum theorem states that the impulse is exactly equal to the change in momentum, F × Δt = m v − m u. So whenever a force acts for some time, it changes the momentum of the body by a definite amount. A cricketer catching a fast ball pulls the hands backwards to increase the stopping time, so the same change of momentum is produced by a smaller, safer force on his hands.

Momentum and Kinetic Energy

Kinetic energy can be written in terms of momentum as:

K.E. = p^2 / (2 m)

  • Because kinetic energy grows with the square of the momentum, if momentum is increased by 20 percent the momentum becomes 1.20 times and 1.20^2 = 1.44, which is a 44 percent increase in kinetic energy
  • For a body of mass 2 kg and momentum of 2 N s, K.E. = 2^2 / (2 × 2) = 4 / 4 = 1 J — a relation useful whenever the momentum and mass are known instead of the velocity
  • For the same kinetic energy, momentum is p = √(2 m × K.E.), so the momentum is larger for the larger mass; among an electron, a proton, a deuteron and an alpha particle, the alpha particle is the heaviest (about four times as heavy as a proton), so it carries the greatest momentum for the same kinetic energy

Worked Example 1

A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second into a target. Each bullet weighs 20 gram and had a speed of 1500 m/s. Find the necessary force to hold the gun in position.

Step 1: Find the momentum carried away by one bullet, p = m v = 0.02 × 1500 = 30 kg m/s

Step 2: Find the momentum carried away per second, 10 × 30 = 300 kg m/s per second

Step 3: Force equals rate of change of momentum, so the gun experiences a backward force of 300 N, and an equal forward force must be applied to hold it

A force of 300 N is necessary to hold the gun in position.

mcqs.q: The rate of change of linear momentum of a body is called a:
mcqs.why: By Newton's second law, the resultant force acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its linear momentum, F = delta p / delta t, and this is called a linear force. Impulse is force multiplied by time, and power is the rate of doing work.

mcqs.q: In its more general form, Newton's second law states that the resultant force acting on a body is equal to:
options: the rate of change of its linear momentum
the product of force and time
mcqs.why: The general form of the second law is F = delta p / delta t: the resultant force equals the rate of change of linear momentum, and it takes place in the direction of the force.

mcqs.q: Impulse is equal to:
options: the kinetic energy of the body
the change in momentum of the body
the power delivered to the body
the force acting on the body
mcqs.why: Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts, J = F x delta t, and the impulse-momentum theorem states that it is exactly equal to the change in momentum, m v - m u.

mcqs.q: A force of 20 N acts on a trolley of mass 5 kg. The acceleration of the trolley is:
mcqs.why: Working: a = F / m = 20 / 5 = 4 m/s^2. The same 20 N force gives a lighter 2 kg trolley an acceleration of 10 m/s^2, showing that acceleration falls as mass rises.

mcqs.q: If the mass of a body is doubled while the applied force stays the same, its acceleration:
mcqs.why: Since a = F / m, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration if the force is unchanged, which is why a loaded truck speeds up much more slowly than an empty one with the same engine force.

mcqs.q: A machine gun fires 10 bullets per second. Each bullet has mass 20 g and speed 1500 m/s. The force necessary to hold the gun in position is:
mcqs.why: Working: the momentum of one bullet is p = m v = 0.02 x 1500 = 30 kg m/s. Ten bullets per second carry away 10 x 30 = 300 kg m/s per second, and force equals the rate of change of momentum, so a forward force of 300 N must be applied to hold the gun.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass 2 kg and momentum of 2 N s is:
mcqs.why: Working: kinetic energy in terms of momentum is K.E. = p^2 / (2 m) = 2^2 / (2 x 2) = 4 / 4 = 1 J. This relation is useful whenever momentum and mass are known instead of velocity.

mcqs.q: If the momentum of a body is increased by 20 percent, its kinetic energy increases by:
mcqs.why: Working: K.E. = p^2 / (2 m), so kinetic energy grows with the square of the momentum. A 20 percent increase makes the momentum 1.20 times, and 1.20^2 = 1.44, which is a 44 percent increase in kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: For the same kinetic energy, the momentum is maximum for:
mcqs.why: For a fixed kinetic energy, momentum is p = sqrt(2 m x K.E.), so the momentum is larger for the larger mass. The alpha particle is the heaviest of the four, about four times as heavy as a proton, so it carries the greatest momentum.

mcqs.q: A cricketer pulls his hands backwards while catching a fast ball. This works because it:
options: increases the force on his hands
increases the stopping time, so the same change of momentum is produced by a smaller force
decreases the change of momentum of the ball
increases the impulse given to the ball
mcqs.why: Pulling the hands back increases the stopping time delta t. Since F x delta t must equal the same change of momentum, a longer time means a smaller and safer force on the hands.

lessons.title: Conservation of Momentum, Collisions and Rocket Propulsion
lessons.notes_html:
Law of Conservation of Momentum

The law states that when no external force acts on a system, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant. In other words, the total momentum before a collision or an explosion is equal to the total momentum after it, even though individual bodies may exchange momentum. This law follows from Newton's second and third laws.

In a closed system with no external force, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after it. A clear everyday example is the recoil of a gun: before firing, the gun and bullet together have zero momentum, and after firing the forward momentum of the bullet is balanced by the equal backward momentum of the gun. The same principle is seen when a person jumps from a small boat and the boat moves backwards in the opposite direction.

Rocket Propulsion

The motion of a rocket in space is according to the law of conservation of linear momentum. The rocket throws exhaust gases backwards with momentum in one direction, so the rocket gains equal momentum in the forward direction. The total momentum of the rocket and gases stays constant, which is why a rocket works even in empty space.

Explosions

Conservation of momentum also governs an explosion from rest. For example, when a bomb of mass 12 kg, initially at rest, explodes into two pieces of masses 4 kg and 8 kg and the 8 kg mass moves at 6 m/s, conservation of momentum gives 4 × v = 8 × 6, so the 4 kg piece moves at v = 12 m/s, and its kinetic energy is (1/2) × 4 × 12^2 = 2 × 144 = 288 J.

Elastic and Inelastic Collisions

Elastic CollisionInelastic Collision
Both momentum and kinetic energy are conservedMomentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not
Bodies bounce apart without any permanent change of shape, like two billiard ballsPart of the kinetic energy changes into heat, sound and deformation
Examples: collision of billiard balls, hard steel balls in Newton's cradleExamples: two cars colliding and crumpling; a bullet embedding itself in a wooden block and the two moving together

Momentum is conserved in every type of collision provided no external force acts during the short impact, because the internal action and reaction forces cancel. If the bodies stick together after impact, the collision is called perfectly inelastic and the loss of kinetic energy is the maximum possible.

Worked Example 1

A 100 grams bullet is fired from a 10 kg gun with a speed of 1000 m/s. What is the speed of recoil of the gun?

Step 1: Write the conservation of momentum, total momentum after firing = total momentum before firing, so m v + M V = 0 in signed form, i.e. m v = M V in magnitude; here m = 0.1 kg, v = 1000 m/s, M = 10 kg and the initial momentum is 0

Step 2: Substitute, 0.1 × 1000 = 10 × V

Step 3: Solve, 100 = 10 V, so V = 10 m/s

The gun recoils with a speed of 10 m/s in the direction opposite to the bullet.

Worked Example 2

A 50 grams bullet is fired into a 10 kg block that is suspended by a long cord so that it can swing as a pendulum. If the block is displaced so that its centre of gravity rises by 10 cm, what was the speed of the bullet?

Step 1: Find the speed V of the block plus bullet just after impact from the pendulum rise, V = √(2 g h)

Step 2: Substitute, V = √(2 × 9.8 × 0.10) = √1.96 = 1.4 m/s

Step 3: Apply conservation of momentum for the impact, m × v = (M + m) × V, with m = 0.05 kg and M = 10 kg

Step 4: Substitute, 0.05 × v = (10 + 0.05) × 1.4 = 10.05 × 1.4 = 14.07

Step 5: Solve, v = 14.07 / 0.05 = 281.4 m/s

The speed of the bullet was 281.4 m/s.

Worked Example 3

A 70-gram ball collides with another ball of mass 140 gram. The initial velocity of the first ball is 9 m/s to the right while the second ball is at rest. If the collision is perfectly elastic, what would be the velocity of the two balls after the collision?

Step 1: Write the elastic collision formula for the first ball, v1 = [(m1 − m2) / (m1 + m2)] × u1

Step 2: Substitute, v1 = [(70 − 140) / (70 + 140)] × 9 = (−70 / 210) × 9 = −3 m/s

Step 3: Write the formula for the second ball, v2 = [2 m1 / (m1 + m2)] × u1

Step 4: Substitute, v2 = [140 / 210] × 9 = 6 m/s

Step 5: Interpret the signs: the minus sign means the first ball rebounds to the left, while the second ball moves to the right

The first ball moves at −3 m/s (3 m/s to the left) and the second ball at 6 m/s to the right.

Worked Example 4

A truck weighing 2500 kg and moving with a velocity of 21 m/s collides with a stationary car weighing 1000 kg. The truck and car move together after the impact. Calculate their common velocity.

Step 1: Write the conservation of momentum, m1 u1 + m2 u2 = (m1 + m2) V

Step 2: Substitute, 2500 × 21 + 1000 × 0 = (2500 + 1000) V

Step 3: Calculate the left side, 52500 = 3500 V

Step 4: Solve, V = 52500 / 3500 = 15 m/s

The common velocity of the truck and car after the impact is 15 m/s in the original direction of the truck.

mcqs.q: The motion of a rocket in space is according to the law of conservation of:
mcqs.why: The rocket throws exhaust gases backwards with momentum in one direction, so the rocket gains equal momentum in the forward direction. The total momentum of the rocket and gases stays constant, which is why a rocket works even in empty space.

mcqs.q: The total linear momentum of a system remains constant when:
options: the bodies stick together after colliding
no external force acts on the system
mcqs.why: The law of conservation of momentum states that when no external force acts on a system, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant, so the total momentum before a collision or explosion equals the total momentum after it.

mcqs.q: A bomb of mass 12 kg, initially at rest, explodes into two pieces of masses 4 kg and 8 kg. The speed of the 8 kg mass is 6 m/s. The kinetic energy of the 4 kg mass is:
mcqs.why: Working: by conservation of momentum, 4 x v = 8 x 6, so the 4 kg piece moves at v = 12 m/s. Its kinetic energy is (1/2) x 4 x 12^2 = 2 x 144 = 288 J.

mcqs.q: A 100 gram bullet is fired from a 10 kg gun with a speed of 1000 m/s. The speed of recoil of the gun is:
mcqs.why: Working: the total momentum before firing is zero, so m v = M V in magnitude: 0.1 x 1000 = 10 x V, giving 100 = 10 V and V = 10 m/s, in the direction opposite to the bullet.

mcqs.q: A truck of mass 2500 kg moving at 21 m/s collides with a stationary car of mass 1000 kg, and the two move together after the impact. Their common velocity is:
mcqs.why: Working: m1 u1 + m2 u2 = (m1 + m2) V, so 2500 x 21 + 1000 x 0 = 3500 V, that is 52500 = 3500 V, and V = 52500 / 3500 = 15 m/s in the original direction of the truck.

mcqs.q: In an elastic collision, which quantities are conserved?
mcqs.why: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, and the bodies bounce apart without any permanent change of shape, like two billiard balls or hard steel balls in Newton's cradle.

mcqs.q: If two bodies stick together after impact, the collision is called:
mcqs.why: If the bodies stick together after impact, the collision is called perfectly inelastic. Momentum is conserved, but the loss of kinetic energy is the maximum possible, the rest changing into heat, sound and deformation.

mcqs.q: A 70 gram ball moving at 9 m/s to the right collides elastically with a stationary ball of mass 140 gram. The velocity of the second ball after the collision is:
mcqs.why: Working: for a perfectly elastic collision, v2 = [2 m1 / (m1 + m2)] x u1 = [140 / 210] x 9 = 6 m/s, so the second ball moves off at 6 m/s to the right.

mcqs.q: A 50 gram bullet is fired into a 10 kg block suspended as a pendulum. The block rises so that its centre of gravity goes up by 10 cm. The speed of the bullet was:
mcqs.why: Working: the speed of block plus bullet just after impact is V = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 0.10) = sqrt(1.96) = 1.4 m/s. Conservation of momentum gives 0.05 x v = (10 + 0.05) x 1.4 = 14.07, so v = 14.07 / 0.05 = 281.4 m/s.

mcqs.q: In the same elastic collision (70 gram ball at 9 m/s striking a stationary 140 gram ball), the velocity of the first ball after the collision is:
