mcqs.why: Working: v1 = [(m1 - m2) / (m1 + m2)] x u1 = [(70 - 140) / 210] x 9 = -3 m/s. The minus sign means the first ball rebounds to the left at 3 m/s.

lessons.title: Angular Displacement, Angular Velocity and Angular Acceleration
lessons.notes_html:
The Radian

Angles in circular motion are measured in radians. The radian is the angle for which the arc length equals the radius of the circle. One full circle is 2π radians = 360°, so 1 radian = 360 / (2π) = 57.3°, which is about 57°.

1 radian = 57.3° (about 57°)

Constant Angular Speed

When a wheel turns with constant angular speed, it turns through equal angles in equal times, because the angular displacement per second never changes. A point on its rim still changes the direction of its velocity as it goes round, so its velocity is not constant even though its speed is.

Angular Quantities and Linear Quantities

Rotation about a fixed axis is the direct analogue of straight-line motion. In the kinematics equations the angular quantities replace the linear ones: θ replaces s, ω replaces v, and α replaces a.

Circular MotionLinear Motion
ω = ω_o + α tv = u + a t
θ = ω_o t + (1/2) α t^2s = u t + (1/2) a t^2
ω^2 = ω_o^2 + 2 α θv^2 = u^2 + 2 a s

The equations have exactly the same form because of this analogy. Here ω_o is the initial angular velocity, ω the final angular velocity, α the angular acceleration and θ the angular displacement in time t.

Worked Example 1

A car accelerates uniformly from rest and reaches a speed of 22 m/s in 9 s. If the diameter of a tire is 58 cm, find (a) the number of revolutions the tire makes during this motion, assuming no slipping, and (b) the final rotational speed of the tire in revolutions per second.

Given: u = 0, v = 22 m/s, t = 9 s, diameter = 0.58 m so radius r = 0.29 m

Step 1: Find the distance travelled using average speed, s = ((u + v) / 2) × t = (22 / 2) × 9 = 99 m

Step 2: Find the circumference of the tire, C = 2 π r = 2 × 3.14 × 0.29 = 1.82 m

Step 3: For (a), number of revolutions = s / C = 99 / 1.82 = 54.3, about 55 rev

Step 4: For (b), final rotational speed = v / C = 22 / 1.82 = 12.1 rev/s, about 12 rev/s

Final answer: (a) about 55 rev, (b) about 12 rev/s.

mcqs.q: One radian is about:
mcqs.why: One full circle is 2 pi radians = 360 degrees, so 1 radian = 360 / (2 pi) = 57.3 degrees, which is about 57 degrees.

mcqs.q: The radian is the angle for which:
options: the arc length equals the diameter
the arc length equals the radius of the circle
the arc length equals the circumference
the chord length equals the radius
mcqs.why: The radian is defined as the angle for which the arc length equals the radius of the circle, so an arc of length equal to r subtends an angle of one radian at the centre.

mcqs.q: One full circle, expressed in radians, is:
mcqs.why: Angles in circular motion are measured in radians, and one full circle is 2 pi radians, which equals 360 degrees.

mcqs.q: A wheel turns with constant angular speed. Then:
options: each point on its rim moves with constant velocity
the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times
the angle turned in each second increases as time goes on
each point on its rim moves with constant acceleration
mcqs.why: Constant angular speed means the angular displacement per second never changes, so the wheel turns through equal angles in equal times. A point on the rim still changes the direction of its velocity, so its velocity is not constant even though its speed is.

mcqs.q: In the analogy between circular motion and linear motion, the angular displacement theta replaces:
mcqs.why: Rotation about a fixed axis is the direct analogue of straight-line motion: theta replaces s, omega replaces v, and alpha replaces a, so the kinematics equations keep exactly the same form.

mcqs.q: In the equations of circular motion, the quantity that takes the place of v in linear motion is:
mcqs.why: In the analogy, omega (angular velocity) replaces v (linear velocity), just as theta replaces s and alpha replaces a in the equations of motion.

mcqs.q: Which equation is the rotational form of v = u + a t?
mcqs.why: The equation omega = omega_o + alpha t has exactly the same form as v = u + a t, with omega replacing v, omega_o replacing u and alpha replacing a.

mcqs.q: A car accelerates uniformly from rest to 22 m/s in 9 s. Its tire has diameter 58 cm. The number of revolutions the tire makes during this motion (no slipping) is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the distance travelled is s = ((u + v) / 2) x t = (22 / 2) x 9 = 99 m. The circumference is C = 2 pi r = 2 x 3.14 x 0.29 = 1.82 m. Number of revolutions = s / C = 99 / 1.82 = 54.3, about 55 rev.

mcqs.q: For the same tire, the final rotational speed at 22 m/s is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the final rotational speed is v / C = 22 / 1.82 = 12.1 rev/s, about 12 rev/s, where C = 1.82 m is the circumference of the tire.

mcqs.q: A point on the rim of a wheel turning at constant angular speed has:
options: a velocity that is not constant, because its direction keeps changing
mcqs.why: Even at constant angular speed, a point on the rim keeps changing the direction of its velocity as it goes round, so its velocity is not constant, although its speed stays the same.

lessons.title: Centripetal Acceleration and Centripetal Force
lessons.notes_html:
Why Circular Motion Needs a Centre-Seeking Acceleration

A body moving with constant speed v in a circle of radius r is still accelerating, because the direction of its velocity keeps changing. The acceleration is directed towards the centre of the circle and is called centripetal acceleration.

Derivation of Centripetal Acceleration

Consider a body moving with constant speed v in a circle of radius r. In a small time Δt it moves through a small angle Δθ, and its velocity vector turns by the same angle Δθ. The change in velocity Δv forms a small triangle similar to the position triangle, giving Δv / v = Δs / r = v Δt / r, so Δv / Δt = v^2 / r. Taking the limit as Δt goes to zero gives the instantaneous acceleration.

a_c = v^2 / r

Using v = r ω, it can also be written in terms of angular velocity:

a_c = r ω^2

The centripetal force is the net inward force that provides this acceleration. Work done by the centripetal force is always zero, because it acts at right angles to the instantaneous displacement (see Unit 5).

Worked Example 1

An ordinary workshop grindstone has a radius of 7.5 cm and rotates 6500 rev/min. (a) Calculate the magnitude of centripetal acceleration at its edge in m/s^2 and convert it into multiples of g. (b) What is the linear speed of a point on its edge?

Given: r = 7.5 cm = 0.075 m, rotation rate = 6500 rev/min = 6500 / 60 = 108.3 rev/s

Step 1: Find the angular velocity, ω = 2 π × 108.3 = 681 rad/s

Step 2: For (a), a_c = r ω^2 = 0.075 × (681)^2 = 0.075 × 4.64 × 10^5 = 3.47 × 10^4 m/s^2

Step 3: Express in multiples of g, 3.47 × 10^4 / 9.8 = 3.55 × 10^3, so a_c = 3.55 × 10^3 g

Step 4: For (b), v = r ω = 0.075 × 681 = 51 m/s

Final answer: (a) 3.47 × 10^4 m/s^2, equal to 3.55 × 10^3 g, (b) 51 m/s.

Net Force in Orbit — Apparent Weightlessness

A space station revolves around the Earth as a satellite, 100 km above the Earth's surface. Gravity still acts on an astronaut inside and provides the centripetal force that keeps her in orbit, and at only 100 km height g is only slightly smaller than at the surface, so the net force on her is a little less than her weight on Earth. Her apparent weight is zero because she and the station fall together, but the real net (gravitational) force on her is not zero.

mcqs.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body moving with speed v in a circle of radius r is:
mcqs.why: In a small time the velocity vector turns through the same small angle as the position, giving delta v / delta t = v^2 / r. So the centripetal acceleration is a_c = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre of the circle.

mcqs.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion is directed:
options: towards the centre of the circle
mcqs.why: The centripetal acceleration is directed towards the centre of the circle, because the change in velocity points inward even though the speed of the body stays constant.

mcqs.q: Using v = r omega, the centripetal acceleration can also be written as:
mcqs.why: Substituting v = r omega into a_c = v^2 / r gives a_c = (r omega)^2 / r = r omega^2, the form of centripetal acceleration in terms of angular velocity.

mcqs.q: A workshop grindstone of radius 7.5 cm rotates at 6500 rev/min. The centripetal acceleration at its edge is about:
The linear speed of a point on the edge of the same grindstone is:
mcqs.why: Working: the linear speed at the edge is v = r omega = 0.075 x 681 = 51 m/s, using r = 7.5 cm = 0.075 m and omega = 681 rad/s.

mcqs.q: Expressed as a multiple of g, the centripetal acceleration at the grindstone's edge (3.47 x 10^4 m/s^2) is about:
mcqs.why: Working: dividing by g = 9.8 m/s^2 gives 3.47 x 10^4 / 9.8 = 3.55 x 10^3, so the acceleration at the edge is about 3.55 x 10^3 g.

mcqs.q: The work done by the centripetal force on a body in circular motion is:
mcqs.why: The centripetal force acts at right angles to the instantaneous displacement of the body, so the work done by the centripetal force is always zero.

mcqs.q: A space station revolves around the Earth 100 km above the surface. The net force on an astronaut at rest inside the station is:
options: a little less than her weight on Earth
equal to her weight on Earth
less than half her weight on Earth
mcqs.why: Gravity still acts on the astronaut and provides the centripetal force that keeps her in orbit, and at only 100 km height g is only slightly smaller than at the surface, so the net force is a little less than her weight on Earth. Her apparent weight is zero because she and the station fall together, but the real force is not zero.

mcqs.q: A body moving with constant speed in a circle is still accelerating because:
options: the direction of its velocity keeps changing
mcqs.why: A body in uniform circular motion accelerates because the direction of its velocity keeps changing, even though its speed is constant. This centre-seeking acceleration has magnitude v^2 / r.

mcqs.q: The angular velocity of the grindstone rotating at 6500 rev/min is:
mcqs.why: Working: 6500 rev/min = 6500 / 60 = 108.3 rev/s, and omega = 2 pi x 108.3 = 681 rad/s.

lessons.title: Banking of Roads and Orbital Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
Turning on a Flat Road

On a flat, horizontal curve friction alone provides the centripetal force. The fastest safe speed is set by the maximum static friction between the tires and the road.

v_max = √(μ_s r g)

Forces on a Banked Curve

On a road banked at angle θ, the weight m g acts vertically down and the normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface. Resolving N: the vertical component N cos θ balances the weight, and the horizontal component N sin θ points towards the centre of the curve and supplies the centripetal force.

N cos θ = m g

N sin θ = m v^2 / r

Dividing the two equations gives the ideal banking relation. At this speed the vehicle can take the curve without relying on friction.

tan θ = v^2 / (r g)

v = √(r g tan θ)

Orbital Velocity

For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, which gives the orbital speed in terms of the orbital radius r, the gravitational constant G and the mass M of the Earth.

v = √(G M / r)

Worked Example 1

What is the ideal banking angle for a gentle turn of 1.20 km radius on a highway with a 105 km/h speed limit (about 65 mi/h), assuming everyone travels at the limit?

Given: r = 1.20 km = 1200 m, v = 105 km/h = 105 × 1000 / 3600 = 29.2 m/s, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: Write the banking relation, tan θ = v^2 / (r g)

Step 2: Calculate v^2 = (29.2)^2 = 851

Step 3: Calculate r g = 1200 × 9.8 = 11760

Step 4: tan θ = 851 / 11760 = 0.0724

Step 5: θ = arctan(0.0724) = 4.14°

Final answer: 4.14°.

Worked Example 2

A 1500-kg car moving on a flat, horizontal road negotiates a curve. If the radius of the curve is 35 m and the coefficient of static friction between the tires and dry pavement is 0.523, find the maximum speed the car can have and still make the turn successfully.

Given: m = 1500 kg, r = 35 m, μ_s = 0.523, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: On a flat curve friction alone provides the centripetal force, m v^2 / r = μ_s m g

Step 2: Cancel m and rearrange, v_max = √(μ_s r g)

Step 3: Substitute, v_max = √(0.523 × 35 × 9.8) = √(179.4)

Step 4: Take the square root, v_max = 13.4 m/s, about 13.5 m/s

Final answer: 13.5 m/s.

Worked Example 3

A satellite is orbiting the Earth with an orbital velocity of 3200 m/s. What is the orbital radius?

Given: v = 3200 m/s, G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N.m^2/kg^2, M_earth = 5.98 × 10^24 kg

Step 1: For a circular orbit, v = √(G M / r), so r = G M / v^2

Step 2: Calculate G M = 6.67 × 10^-11 × 5.98 × 10^24 = 3.99 × 10^14 m^3/s^2

Step 3: Calculate v^2 = (3200)^2 = 1.024 × 10^7 m^2/s^2

Step 4: Divide, r = 3.99 × 10^14 / 1.024 × 10^7 = 3.90 × 10^7 m

Final answer: 3.897 × 10^7 m (about 3.9 × 10^7 m).

Worked Example 4

A satellite wishes to orbit the earth at a height of 100 km (approximately 60 miles) above the surface of the earth. Determine the speed, acceleration and orbital period of the satellite. (Given: M_earth = 5.98 × 10^24 kg, R_earth = 6.37 × 10^6 m)

Given: h = 100 km = 1.0 × 10^5 m, R = 6.37 × 10^6 m, M = 5.98 × 10^24 kg, G = 6.67 × 10^-11 N.m^2/kg^2

Step 1: Find the orbital radius, r = R + h = 6.37 × 10^6 + 0.10 × 10^6 = 6.47 × 10^6 m

Step 2: Find the speed, v = √(G M / r) = √(3.99 × 10^14 / 6.47 × 10^6) = √(6.17 × 10^7) = 7.85 × 10^3 m/s

Step 3: Find the acceleration, a = v^2 / r = (7.85 × 10^3)^2 / 6.47 × 10^6 = 6.17 × 10^7 / 6.47 × 10^6 = 9.53 m/s^2

Step 4: Find the period, T = 2 π r / v = 2 × 3.14 × 6.47 × 10^6 / 7.85 × 10^3 = 5177 s

Step 5: Convert the period to hours, T = 5177 / 3600 = 1.44 hours

Final answer: speed 7.85 × 10^3 m/s, acceleration 9.53 m/s^2, period 1.44 hours.

mcqs.q: On a flat, horizontal curve, the maximum safe speed of a car is given by:
mcqs.why: On a flat curve friction alone provides the centripetal force, so m v^2 / r = mu_s m g. Cancelling m and rearranging gives v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g), set by the maximum static friction between the tires and the road.

mcqs.q: A 1500 kg car negotiates a flat curve of radius 35 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.523. The maximum speed for a successful turn is about:
mcqs.why: Working: v_max = sqrt(mu_s r g) = sqrt(0.523 x 35 x 9.8) = sqrt(179.4) = 13.4 m/s, about 13.5 m/s. The mass of the car cancels out of the relation.

mcqs.q: For a vehicle on a road banked at angle theta, the ideal banking relation is:
mcqs.why: Resolving the normal reaction gives N cos theta = m g and N sin theta = m v^2 / r. Dividing the second equation by the first gives tan theta = v^2 / (r g), so at this speed the vehicle can take the curve without relying on friction.

mcqs.q: The ideal banking angle for a turn of radius 1.20 km on a highway with a speed limit of 105 km/h is about:
mcqs.why: Working: v = 105 km/h = 29.2 m/s, so tan theta = v^2 / (r g) = 851 / (1200 x 9.8) = 851 / 11760 = 0.0724, and theta = arctan(0.0724) = 4.14 degrees.

mcqs.q: On a banked curve, the component of the normal reaction N that supplies the centripetal force is:
mcqs.why: The horizontal component N sin theta of the normal reaction points towards the centre of the curve and supplies the centripetal force, while the vertical component N cos theta balances the weight m g.

mcqs.q: On a banked curve, the vertical force balance is written as:
options: N cos theta = m v^2 / r
mcqs.why: The weight m g acts vertically down and the normal reaction N acts perpendicular to the road surface. Its vertical component N cos theta balances the weight, so N cos theta = m g, while N sin theta provides the centripetal force.

mcqs.q: The orbital velocity of a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around the Earth (mass M) is:
mcqs.why: For a satellite in a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force, which gives the orbital speed v = sqrt(G M / r) in terms of the orbital radius r, the gravitational constant G and the mass M of the Earth.

mcqs.q: A satellite is orbiting the Earth with an orbital velocity of 3200 m/s. Its orbital radius is about:
A satellite orbits at a height of 100 km above the Earth's surface (R = 6.37 x 10^6 m, M = 5.98 x 10^24 kg). Its orbital speed is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the orbital radius is r = R + h = 6.37 x 10^6 + 0.10 x 10^6 = 6.47 x 10^6 m. Then v = sqrt(G M / r) = sqrt(3.99 x 10^14 / 6.47 x 10^6) = sqrt(6.17 x 10^7) = 7.85 x 10^3 m/s.

mcqs.q: The orbital period of the same satellite (speed 7.85 x 10^3 m/s, radius 6.47 x 10^6 m) is about:
mcqs.why: Working: T = 2 pi r / v = 2 x 3.14 x 6.47 x 10^6 / 7.85 x 10^3 = 5177 s, and converting to hours, 5177 / 3600 = 1.44 hours. Its acceleration in orbit is v^2 / r = 9.53 m/s^2.

lessons.title: Moment of Inertia and Angular Momentum
lessons.notes_html:
Moment of Inertia

Moment of inertia, also called rotational inertia, is the rotational analogue of mass. For a particle it is m r^2, and for a body it is the sum of m r^2 over all its particles.

I = Σ m r^2

  • Total mass — a heavier body has a larger moment of inertia
  • Distribution of mass — mass lying farther from the axis counts much more, because it enters as r^2
  • Position and direction of the axis — the same body has different moments of inertia about different axes

Moment of inertia does not depend on the speed of rotation, on angular velocity, on torque or on angular acceleration. It is a property of the body and the axis. The standard results obtained by dividing the body into small elements and integrating x^2 dm are:

Uniform rod (about centre, perpendicular): I = (1/12) M L^2

Solid sphere: I = (2/5) M R^2

Solid cylinder / disk: I = (1/2) M R^2

Angular Momentum

Angular momentum is L = I ω. It is a vector along the rotation axis, found by the right-hand rule: curling the fingers in the direction of rotation makes the thumb point along the axis. For the Earth rotating west to east, the angular momentum vector about its rotation axis points north.

L = I ω

Conservation of Angular Momentum

Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, τ = dL / dt. When no resultant external torque acts on a body or system, its total angular momentum remains constant, that is I ω = constant. The angular momentum itself need not be zero; the body may keep spinning at a steady rate.

For an isolated rotating body, since I grows with the square of the size (for a particle I = m r^2), a larger radius means a larger I and therefore a smaller ω; in simple form ω is inversely related to r^2 for a given mass. When the body spreads out it spins slower, and when it contracts it spins faster. If the moment of inertia is halved, I1 ω1 = I2 ω2 gives ω2 = 2 ω1, so the angular velocity doubles.

Applications of Angular Momentum

  • Ice skaters and divers — pulling the arms and legs in reduces I and increases the spin rate, while stretching out slows the spin for a safe landing; a diver who tucks into a ball completes more somersaults before entering the water
  • Gyroscopes and satellites — the fixed direction of angular momentum keeps them stable and holding their orientation in space; bicycle and motorcycle wheels likewise resist tipping
  • Planets — the planets keep orbiting the Sun with constant angular momentum because gravity acts along the line joining them to the Sun and exerts no torque about the Sun

A stone of 2 kg tied to a 0.50 m string and swung at constant angular velocity of 12 rad/s has zero net torque about the centre: its angular acceleration α is zero so τ = I α = 0, and the tension acts along the string towards the centre, so its moment arm about the centre is zero. A man spinning on a frictionless turntable who extends his arms increases I, so his angular velocity decreases, but his angular momentum remains the same because there is no external torque.

Worked Example 1

A thin disk with a 0.3 m diameter and a total moment of inertia of 0.45 kg.m^2 is rotating about its center of mass. There are three rocks with masses of 0.2 kg on the outer part of the disk. Find the total moment of inertia of the system.

Given: I_disk = 0.45 kg.m^2, diameter = 0.3 m so r = 0.15 m, three rocks each m = 0.2 kg at the rim

Step 1: Moment of inertia of one rock about the center, I_rock = m r^2 = 0.2 × (0.15)^2 = 0.2 × 0.0225 = 0.0045 kg.m^2

Step 2: For three rocks, I_rocks = 3 × 0.0045 = 0.0135 kg.m^2

Step 3: Add the disk and the rocks, I_total = 0.45 + 0.0135 = 0.4635 kg.m^2

Final answer: 0.464 kg.m^2.

Worked Example 2

A system of points is shown in figure 4.22, with three particles each of mass 0.3 kg lying in the same plane at distances of 40 cm, 20 cm and 50 cm from a central particle on the given axis. What is the moment of inertia of the system about the given axis?

Given: each particle m = 0.3 kg, distances r1 = 0.40 m, r2 = 0.20 m, r3 = 0.50 m, the central particle lies on the axis so its distance is zero

Step 1: Write I = sum of m r^2 for all particles

Step 2: Calculate the squares, (0.40)^2 = 0.16, (0.20)^2 = 0.04, (0.50)^2 = 0.25, sum = 0.45 m^2

Step 3: Multiply by the mass, I = 0.3 × 0.45 = 0.135 kg.m^2

Final answer: 0.135 kg.m^2.

Worked Example 3

(a) What is the angular momentum of a 2.9 kg uniform cylindrical grinding wheel of radius 20 cm when rotating 1550 rpm? (b) How much torque is required to stop it in 6 s?

Given: M = 2.9 kg, R = 20 cm = 0.20 m, rotation rate = 1550 rpm, stopping time t = 6 s

Step 1: Moment of inertia of a solid cylinder, I = (1/2) M R^2 = 0.5 × 2.9 × (0.20)^2 = 0.5 × 2.9 × 0.04 = 0.058 kg.m^2

Step 2: Angular velocity, ω = 1550 × 2 π / 60 = 162 rad/s

Step 3: For (a), L = I ω = 0.058 × 162 = 9.4 kg.m^2/s, about 9.5 kg.m^2/s

Step 4: For (b), torque = rate of change of angular momentum, τ = ΔL / t = 9.4 / 6 = 1.6 N.m, applied opposite to the rotation

Final answer: (a) 9.5 kg.m^2/s, (b) 1.6 N.m opposing the rotation.

Worked Example 4

Determine the angular momentum of the Earth (a) about its rotation axis (assume the Earth as a uniform sphere), and (b) in its orbit around the Sun (take Earth as a particle orbiting the Sun). The Earth has mass 6 × 10^24 kg and radius 6.4 × 10^6 m, and is 1.5 × 10^8 km from the Sun.

Given: M = 6 × 10^24 kg, R = 6.4 × 10^6 m, orbital radius r = 1.5 × 10^8 km = 1.5 × 10^11 m, one day = 86400 s, one year = 3.16 × 10^7 s

Step 1: For (a), I of a uniform sphere = (2/5) M R^2 = 0.4 × 6 × 10^24 × (6.4 × 10^6)^2 = 0.4 × 6 × 10^24 × 4.10 × 10^13 = 9.8 × 10^37 kg.m^2

Step 2: Spin angular velocity, ω = 2 π / 86400 = 7.27 × 10^-5 rad/s

Step 3: Spin angular momentum, L = I ω = 9.8 × 10^37 × 7.27 × 10^-5 = 7.1 × 10^33 kg.m^2/s, about 7.3 × 10^33 kg.m^2/s

Step 4: For (b), orbital speed, v = 2 π r / T = 2 × 3.14 × 1.5 × 10^11 / 3.16 × 10^7 = 2.98 × 10^4 m/s

Step 5: Orbital angular momentum, L = M v r = 6 × 10^24 × 2.98 × 10^4 × 1.5 × 10^11 = 2.7 × 10^40 kg.m^2/s

Final answer: (a) 7.3 × 10^33 kg.m^2/s, (b) 2.7 × 10^40 kg.m^2/s.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a single particle of mass m at distance r from the axis is:
mcqs.why: For a particle the moment of inertia is m r^2, and for a whole body it is the sum of m r^2 over all its particles, I = sum of m r^2. Mass lying farther from the axis counts much more because it enters as r^2.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a body does NOT depend on its:
mcqs.why: Moment of inertia depends on the total mass, the distribution of mass about the axis and the position and direction of the axis. It does not depend on the speed of rotation, angular velocity, torque or angular acceleration; it is a property of the body and the axis.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to the rod, is:
mcqs.why: Dividing the uniform rod into small elements of mass dm = (M / L) dx and integrating x^2 dm from -L/2 to +L/2 gives the standard result I = (1/12) M L^2.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a solid sphere of mass M and radius R is:
mcqs.why: Slicing the solid sphere into thin discs perpendicular to the axis and integrating their moments of inertia over the sphere gives the standard result I = (2/5) M R^2.

mcqs.q: The moment of inertia of a solid cylinder (disk) of mass M and radius R about its central axis is:
mcqs.why: The standard result for a solid cylinder or disk about its central axis is I = (1/2) M R^2, obtained by dividing the body into small elements and summing m r^2 over them.

mcqs.q: Angular momentum L of a rotating body is given by:
mcqs.why: Angular momentum is L = I omega, where I is the moment of inertia and omega the angular velocity. It is a vector along the rotation axis, found by the right-hand rule.

mcqs.q: The angular momentum vector of the Earth about its rotation axis, due to its daily rotation, is directed:
options: tangent to the equator towards east
tangent to the equator towards west
mcqs.why: By the right-hand rule, curling the fingers in the direction of rotation (west to east) makes the thumb point along the axis towards the north pole, so the angular momentum vector points north.

mcqs.q: If the external torque acting on a body is zero, then its:
mcqs.why: Torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, tau = dL / dt, so zero net torque means dL / dt = 0 and L stays constant. The angular momentum itself need not be zero; the body may keep spinning at a steady rate.

mcqs.q: When the moment of inertia of a rotating body (with no external torque) is halved, its angular velocity:
mcqs.why: With no external torque, angular momentum is conserved, so I1 omega1 = I2 omega2. If I2 = I1 / 2, then omega2 = 2 omega1, so the angular velocity doubles. This is why a spinning skater rotates much faster when the arms are pulled in.

mcqs.q: A thin disk has moment of inertia 0.45 kg m^2 and diameter 0.3 m. Three rocks, each of mass 0.2 kg, sit on its outer rim. The total moment of inertia of the system is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the rim radius is r = 0.15 m, so one rock has I = m r^2 = 0.2 x (0.15)^2 = 0.2 x 0.0225 = 0.0045 kg m^2. Three rocks give 3 x 0.0045 = 0.0135 kg m^2, and adding the disk, I_total = 0.45 + 0.0135 = 0.4635, about 0.464 kg m^2.

mcqs.q: Three particles, each of mass 0.3 kg, lie at distances 40 cm, 20 cm and 50 cm from an axis. The moment of inertia of the system about the axis is:
A 2.9 kg uniform cylindrical grinding wheel of radius 20 cm rotates at 1550 rpm. Its angular momentum is about:
mcqs.why: Working: I = (1/2) M R^2 = 0.5 x 2.9 x (0.20)^2 = 0.058 kg m^2, and omega = 1550 x 2 pi / 60 = 162 rad/s. So L = I omega = 0.058 x 162 = 9.4, about 9.5 kg m^2/s.

mcqs.q: The torque required to stop that grinding wheel (angular momentum about 9.4 kg m^2/s) in 6 s is:
mcqs.why: Working: torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, tau = delta L / t = 9.4 / 6 = 1.6 N m, applied opposite to the rotation to bring the wheel to rest.

mcqs.q: A man spinning on a frictionless turntable extends his arms. As a result:
options: his angular momentum remains the same
mcqs.why: There is no external torque about the vertical axis, so L = I omega is conserved. Extending the arms increases I, so his angular velocity actually decreases, but his angular momentum remains the same.

mcqs.q: A stone of 2 kg tied to a 0.50 m string is swung in a circle at a constant angular velocity of 12 rad/s. The net torque on the stone about the centre of the circle is:
mcqs.why: The stone moves with constant angular velocity, so its angular acceleration alpha is zero and tau = I alpha = 0. Also, the tension acts along the string towards the centre, so its moment arm about the centre is zero and it can produce no torque about that point.

lessons.title: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
lessons.notes_html:
What is Torque?

Torque is the turning effect of a force about an axis, defined as τ = r × F with magnitude:

τ = r F sin θ

Here r is the moment arm from the axis to the point of application and θ is the angle between r and F. Torque is largest when both the moment arm r and sin θ are largest: applying the force at the rim gives the greatest r, and applying it tangentially makes θ = 90° so sin θ = 1. A force applied near the axle, or radially outward, gives little or no torque.

Torque is Not the Same as Force

In linear motion a force alone changes the linear momentum and produces linear acceleration through F = m a, regardless of where it is applied. Torque, by contrast, depends on both the force and where and at what angle it is applied, and it produces angular acceleration. A force through the axis causes translation effects only, while an off-axis force also causes rotation. A small force can therefore exert a greater torque than a larger force, because torque depends on the moment arm as well as the force: a small force applied far from the axis and at right angles to the arm can give a larger r F product than a big force applied close to the axis or nearly along the arm. This is why a long spanner loosens a tight nut more easily than a short one.

Torque and Angular Acceleration

Consider a particle of mass m moving in a circle of radius r under a tangential force F. Newton's second law gives F = m a_tan = m r α, since a_tan = r α. Multiplying both sides by r gives r F = m r^2 α, and r F is the torque τ while m r^2 is the moment of inertia I of the particle. Summing over all particles of a rigid body gives the general result:

τ = I α

This relation follows directly from Newton's second law — it is the rotational form of F = m a, not a definition of torque, of rotational inertia or of angular acceleration.

Worked Example 1

A car mechanic applies a force of 800 N to a wrench for the purpose of loosening a bolt. He applies the force which is perpendicular to the arm of the wrench. The distance from the bolt to the mechanic's hand is 0.40 m. Find out the magnitude of the torque applied.

Given: F = 800 N, r = 0.40 m, force perpendicular to the arm so θ = 90° and sin θ = 1

Step 1: Write the torque formula, τ = r F sin θ

Step 2: Substitute the values, τ = 0.40 × 800 × 1

Step 3: Multiply, τ = 320 N.m

Final answer: 320 N.m.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of the torque produced by a force F applied at distance r from an axis, at angle theta to the arm, is:
mcqs.why: Torque is the turning effect of a force about an axis, tau = r x F, with magnitude tau = r F sin theta, where r is the moment arm from the axis to the point of application and theta is the angle between r and F.

mcqs.q: A force of given magnitude is to be applied to a wheel. The torque is maximized by:
options: applying the force near the axle, radially outward
applying the force at the rim, tangent to the rim
applying the force near the rim, radially outward
applying the force near the axle, parallel to a tangent
mcqs.why: Torque tau = r F sin theta is largest when both the moment arm r and sin theta are largest. Applying the force at the rim gives the greatest r, and applying it tangentially makes theta = 90 degrees so sin theta = 1.

mcqs.q: A mechanic applies a force of 800 N perpendicular to the arm of a wrench, at a distance of 0.40 m from the bolt. The magnitude of the torque applied is:
mcqs.why: Working: the force is perpendicular to the arm, so theta = 90 degrees and sin theta = 1. Then tau = r F sin theta = 0.40 x 800 x 1 = 320 N m.

mcqs.q: For an object rotating about a fixed axis, with moment of inertia I and angular acceleration alpha, the relation tau = I alpha:
options: is the definition of rotational inertia
follows directly from Newton's second law
is the definition of angular acceleration
mcqs.why: Applying F = m a to each particle of the rotating body and summing the moments gives sum of tau = I alpha. It is the rotational form of Newton's second law, not a definition of any single quantity.

mcqs.q: Can a small force ever exert a greater torque than a larger force?
options: No, torque depends only on the force
No, a larger force always gives a larger torque
Yes, because torque does not depend on the point of application
Yes, because torque depends on the moment arm as well as the force
mcqs.why: Torque depends on the moment arm as well as the force: tau = r F sin theta. A small force applied far from the axis and at right angles to the arm can give a larger r F product than a big force applied close to the axis or nearly along the arm. This is why a long spanner loosens a tight nut more easily than a short one.

mcqs.q: A force applied radially outward from the axle of a wheel produces no torque because:
options: the angle between r and F is 0 degrees, so sin theta = 0
the radius of the wheel is zero
the mass of the wheel is zero
mcqs.why: A radial force points along the arm, so the angle between r and F is theta = 0 degrees and sin theta = 0, giving tau = r F sin theta = 0. A force applied through the axis likewise produces no torque, only translation effects.

mcqs.q: How does torque differ from force in linear motion?
options: Torque depends on where and at what angle the force is applied, and it produces angular acceleration
Torque acts regardless of the point of application
mcqs.why: In linear motion a force alone changes the linear momentum and produces linear acceleration through F = m a, regardless of where it is applied. Torque, by contrast, depends on both the force and where and at what angle it is applied, and it produces angular acceleration through tau = I alpha.

mcqs.q: In deriving tau = I alpha for a particle moving in a circle of radius r, the tangential acceleration is written as:
mcqs.why: Newton's second law gives F = m a_tan = m r alpha, since a_tan = r alpha. Multiplying both sides by r gives r F = m r^2 alpha, and r F is the torque tau while m r^2 is the moment of inertia I of the particle, so tau = I alpha.

mcqs.q: Applying a force very close to the axis of a wheel gives little or no torque mainly because:
options: the moment arm r is very small
mcqs.why: Torque is tau = r F sin theta, so when r is very small the product r F is small even for a large force. This is why a force applied near the axle, or radially outward, gives little or no torque.

mcqs.q: For given r and F, torque is greatest when the force is applied at theta = 90 degrees to the arm because:
options: cos theta is then equal to 1
sin theta is then 1, its maximum value
mcqs.why: Sin theta reaches its maximum value of 1 at theta = 90 degrees, so for given r and F the torque tau = r F sin theta is greatest when the force is applied tangentially, at right angles to the moment arm.

lessons.title: Work Done by a Force
lessons.notes_html:
Work and the Transfer of Energy

Work is the process by which energy is transferred from one body or system to another: when a force does work on a body, energy equal to that work is transferred to the body. If the work is positive the body gains energy, and if negative (for example by friction) it loses energy. For a constant force at angle θ to the displacement:

W = F s cos θ

Work done by the centripetal force is always zero: the centripetal force always acts at right angles to the instantaneous displacement, so θ = 90° and W = F s cos 90° = 0. It changes only the direction of motion, never the speed or kinetic energy.

Work Done by a Variable Force

For a variable force the work is found by dividing the displacement into very small parts, over each of which the force is nearly constant, and adding up all the small amounts F Δx; in calculus form W = integral of F dx. Graphically it is the area under the force-displacement curve between the starting and finishing positions. This method works for forces such as a spring force that change with position. For example, if the force rises steadily from 0 to 10 N over 4 m the graph is a triangle, and the work is (1/2) × 4 × 10 = 20 J.

Work in a Gravitational Field is Independent of Path

Gravity is a conservative force, so the work it does depends only on the vertical height difference between the start and finish, W = m g h. Along any sloping or curved path, only the vertical component of each small displacement contributes to the work, and these vertical parts always add up to the same total height change. Horizontal parts contribute nothing because gravity is vertical. On an incline of angle θ and length L, gravity's component along the path is m g sin θ and the work is m g sin θ × L = m g h, since L sin θ = h. Hence a body gains or loses the same potential energy whether it is lifted straight up or moved along any other route between the same two levels.

Worked Example 1

A man pulls a trolley through a distance of 10 m by applying a force of 50 N which makes an angle of 60° with the horizontal. Calculate the work done by the man.

Given: F = 50 N, s = 10 m, θ = 60°, cos 60° = 0.5

Step 1: Write the work formula, W = F s cos θ

Step 2: Substitute the values, W = 50 × 10 × 0.5

Step 3: Multiply, W = 250 J

Final answer: 250 J.

Worked Example 2

A 70 kg man runs up a hill through a height of 3 m in 2 seconds. (a) How much work does he do against gravitational field? (b) What is the average power output?

Given: m = 70 kg, h = 3 m, t = 2 s, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: For (a), work against gravity, W = m g h = 70 × 9.8 × 3 = 2058 J, about 2060 J

Step 2: For (b), average power, P = W / t = 2058 / 2 = 1029 W, about 1030 W

Final answer: (a) 2060 J, (b) 1030 Watt.

mcqs.q: What does work represent in physics, as described in this lesson?
options: The rate at which energy is used
The process by which energy is transferred from one body or system to another
The energy stored inside a body at rest
The force needed to stop a moving body
mcqs.why: Work is the process by which energy is transferred from one body or system to another. When a force does work on a body, energy equal to that work is transferred to the body.

mcqs.q: A constant force F acts at an angle theta to a displacement s. The work done is given by:
mcqs.why: For a constant force at angle theta to the displacement, W = F s cos theta. Only the component of force along the displacement, F cos theta, does work.

mcqs.q: Why is the work done by the centripetal force always zero?
options: Because the centripetal force is very small
Because there is no displacement in circular motion
Because the speed of the body keeps changing
Because the centripetal force acts at right angles to the instantaneous displacement
mcqs.why: The centripetal force acts at right angles to the instantaneous displacement, so theta = 90 degrees and W = F s cos 90 degrees = 0. It changes only the direction of motion, never the speed.

mcqs.q: How is the work done by a variable force represented on a force-displacement graph?
options: By the area under the force-displacement curve
By the slope of the force-displacement curve
By the length of the curve
By the highest point of the curve
mcqs.why: For a variable force the work equals the area under the force-displacement curve between the starting and finishing positions, which is the graphical form of W = integral of F dx.

mcqs.q: A force rises steadily from 0 to 10 N as the displacement increases from 0 to 4 m. The work done is:
mcqs.why: The force-displacement graph is a triangle, so work = area of triangle = (1/2) x base x height = (1/2) x 4 x 10 = 20 J.

mcqs.q: Why does the work done by gravity not depend on the path taken between two levels?
options: Because gravity becomes weaker along a sloping path
Because only the vertical parts of the displacement contribute, and they always add up to the same height change
Because friction is absent on every path
Because the length of every path is the same
mcqs.why: Gravity is a conservative force and is vertical, so horizontal parts of the path contribute nothing and the vertical parts always add up to the same total height change, giving W = m g h for every path.

mcqs.q: A body slides down a smooth incline of angle theta and length L, dropping through height h where L sin theta = h. The work done by gravity is:
options: zero, because the path is sloping
mcqs.why: Gravity's component along the incline is m g sin theta, so work = m g sin theta x L = m g h, since L sin theta = h. The result is the same as for a vertical drop.

mcqs.q: A man pulls a trolley through 10 m with a force of 50 N at 60 degrees to the horizontal. The work done by the man is:
mcqs.why: Using W = F s cos theta with cos 60 degrees = 0.5: W = 50 x 10 x 0.5 = 250 J.

mcqs.q: If the work done on a body is negative, for example the work done by friction, what happens to the body?
mcqs.why: If the work done on a body is positive the body gains energy, and if it is negative, as with friction opposing the motion, the body loses energy equal to that work.

mcqs.q: A 70 kg man runs up a hill through a vertical height of 3 m. How much work does he do against the gravitational field? (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Work against gravity is W = m g h = 70 x 9.8 x 3 = 2058 J, which is about 2060 J.

lessons.title: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
lessons.notes_html:
Kinetic Energy, Momentum and Energy Units

Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, KE = (1/2) m v^2. Momentum and kinetic energy are related by:

p = √(2 m KE)

KE = p^2 / (2 m)

For the same kinetic energy, the momentum is larger for the larger mass, so a heavy object has greater momentum than a light object of the same KE even though it moves more slowly. For equal momentum, KE = p^2 / (2 m) is inversely proportional to mass: bodies of mass 1 kg and 2 kg with equal momentum have kinetic energies in the ratio 2 : 1, the lighter body having twice the kinetic energy. The energy equivalent of mass is given by Einstein's relation E = m c^2.

The Work-Energy Theorem

The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body by all the forces acting on it equals the change in its kinetic energy. It follows directly from Newton's second law combined with the equations of motion, and it holds even when the force is not constant.

W = ΔKE = (1/2) m v^2 - (1/2) m u^2

Here u is the initial and v the final velocity. A body of mass 5 kg moving with momentum 10 kg m/s has initial velocity 2 m/s and initial KE 10 J; an impulse of 2 kg m/s raises its momentum to 12 kg m/s and its KE to 14.4 J, an increase of 4.4 J — exactly the net work done.

Worked Example 1

A neutron travels a distance of 12 m in a time interval of 3.6 × 10^-4 sec. Assuming its speed was constant, find its kinetic energy. Take the mass of neutron 1.7 × 10^-27 kg.

Given: s = 12 m, t = 3.6 × 10^-4 s, m = 1.7 × 10^-27 kg, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J

Step 1: Find the speed, v = s / t = 12 / 3.6 × 10^-4 = 3.33 × 10^4 m/s

Step 2: Square the speed, v^2 = (3.33 × 10^4)^2 = 1.11 × 10^9 m^2/s^2

Step 3: Calculate KE = (1/2) m v^2 = 0.5 × 1.7 × 10^-27 × 1.11 × 10^9 = 9.4 × 10^-19 J

Step 4: Convert to electron volts, KE = 9.4 × 10^-19 / 1.6 × 10^-19 = 5.9 eV, about 5.78 eV

Final answer: 5.78 eV (about 5.9 eV).

Worked Example 2

Find the energy equivalent of 1 gram.

Given: m = 1 gram = 1 × 10^-3 kg, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s

Step 1: Write Einstein's relation, E = m c^2

Step 2: Calculate c^2 = (3 × 10^8)^2 = 9 × 10^16 m^2/s^2

Step 3: Substitute, E = 1 × 10^-3 × 9 × 10^16 = 9 × 10^13 J

Final answer: 9 × 10^13 J.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is:
mcqs.why: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion and is given by KE = (1/2) m v^2, so it depends on the mass and on the square of the speed.

mcqs.q: Which relation correctly connects momentum p, mass m and kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: Momentum and kinetic energy are related by p = sqrt(2 m KE), which rearranges to KE = p^2 / (2 m).

mcqs.q: A light object and a heavy object have the same kinetic energy. Which one has the greater momentum?
mcqs.why: From p = sqrt(2 m KE), for the same KE the momentum is larger for the larger mass, so the heavy object has the greater momentum even though it moves more slowly.

mcqs.q: Two bodies of mass 1 kg and 2 kg have equal momentum. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg body : 2 kg body) is:
mcqs.why: For equal momentum, KE = p^2 / (2 m) is inversely proportional to mass, so KE of the 1 kg body : KE of the 2 kg body = 2 : 1, the lighter body having twice the kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals:
options: The change in its kinetic energy
The total time for which the force acts
mcqs.why: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body by all the forces acting on it equals the change in its kinetic energy, W = (1/2) m v^2 - (1/2) m u^2.

mcqs.q: A body of mass 5 kg moves with momentum 10 kg m/s. A force of 0.2 N acts along its motion for 10 s. The increase in its kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: Initial KE = p^2 / (2 m) = 100 / 10 = 10 J. Impulse = F t = 0.2 x 10 = 2 kg m/s, so final momentum = 12 kg m/s and final KE = 144 / 10 = 14.4 J. Increase = 14.4 - 10 = 4.4 J.

mcqs.q: According to Einstein's relation, the energy equivalent of a mass m is:
mcqs.why: The energy equivalent of mass is given by Einstein's relation E = m c^2, where c = 3 x 10^8 m/s is the speed of light.

mcqs.q: What is the energy equivalent of 1 gram of mass? (c = 3 x 10^8 m/s)
mcqs.why: Convert the mass: 1 gram = 1 x 10^-3 kg. Then E = m c^2 = 1 x 10^-3 x (3 x 10^8)^2 = 1 x 10^-3 x 9 x 10^16 = 9 x 10^13 J.

mcqs.q: A neutron of mass 1.7 x 10^-27 kg travels 12 m in 3.6 x 10^-4 s at constant speed. Its kinetic energy is about: (1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J)
A body of mass 5 kg has momentum 10 kg m/s. Its initial speed and initial kinetic energy are:
mcqs.why: Speed v = p / m = 10 / 5 = 2 m/s. Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 = 0.5 x 5 x (2)^2 = 0.5 x 5 x 4 = 10 J.

lessons.title: Potential Energy and Conservation of Energy
lessons.notes_html:
Gravitational Potential Energy

To raise a mass m slowly through a height h, an upward force equal to its weight m g must be applied over the distance h. The work done against gravity is W = F × s = m g h. This work is not lost; it is stored in the body as gravitational potential energy. For example, a 2 kg body raised 5 m gains U = 2 × 9.8 × 5 = 98 J of potential energy.

U = m g h

Gravitational potential energy is directly proportional to both the mass and the height above the reference level: doubling the mass doubles the stored energy, and lifting a body twice as high doubles it as well. The absolute potential energy of an object therefore depends on the object's mass and height (more exactly, on mass and distance from the Earth's centre); speed belongs to kinetic energy.

Reference Level — Positive and Negative Potential Energy

Potential energy has no absolute zero of its own, so it is always measured from an agreed reference level, commonly the ground or a tabletop, where U is taken as zero. A body above the reference level has positive PE, U = +m g h, because work must be done to lift it there. A body below the reference level (for example in a basement or a well) has negative PE, U = -m g h, relative to that level. Only differences in potential energy between two positions have physical meaning, and they are the same whatever reference level is chosen.

Law of Conservation of Energy

Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, so the total energy of an isolated system remains constant. In mechanical problems without friction, the sum of kinetic and potential energy stays the same at every point. When friction acts, the missing mechanical energy appears as heat, and the total including heat is still conserved. A body fallen from height h has, after it has fallen a height h / 2, PE = m g (h / 2), exactly half of its initial m g h; by conservation of energy the other half has been converted into kinetic energy, so the two forms are equal at the halfway point.

Energy Efficiency

Efficiency is the ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, usually expressed as a percentage, and it is always less than 100 percent in real devices. In every transformation some energy is wasted, mostly as heat due to friction, electrical resistance or sound. Knowing the efficiency helps us compare machines and fuels and guides designs that waste less energy, for example in engines, bulbs and power stations.

Worked Example 1

When an object is thrown upwards, it rises to a height 'h'. How high is the object in terms of h, when it has lost one third of its original kinetic energy?

Given: maximum height = h, fraction of original KE lost = 1/3

Step 1: At the maximum height all the original KE has become PE, so original KE = m g h

Step 2: Losing one third of the KE means the PE gained is (1/3) m g h

Step 3: If the body is now at height h1, then m g h1 = (1/3) m g h

Step 4: Cancel m g, giving h1 = h / 3

Final answer: h / 3.

Worked Example 2

A stone is thrown vertically upwards and can reach to a height of 10 m, find the speed of stone, when it is just 2 m above the ground.

Given: maximum height H = 10 m, height of the point = 2 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: By energy conservation, the KE at 2 m equals the PE difference between 10 m and 2 m, (1/2) m v^2 = m g (10 - 2)

Step 2: Cancel m and rearrange, v^2 = 2 g × 8 = 2 × 9.8 × 8 = 156.8

Step 3: Take the square root, v = √(156.8) = 12.5 m/s

Final answer: 12.5 m/s.

Worked Example 3

The potential energy of a body at the top of a building is 200 Joules when it is dropped its kinetic energy just before striking the ground is 160 Joules, find the work done against the air resistance.

Given: PE at top = 200 J, KE just before ground = 160 J, PE at ground = 0

Step 1: Without air resistance the KE at the ground would equal the full 200 J of PE lost

Step 2: The shortfall is the energy used against air resistance, W = 200 - 160

Step 3: Subtract, W = 40 J

Final answer: 40 J.

Worked Example 4

A rocket of mass 2 kg is launched in air, when it attains height of 15 m the 400 Joules of its chemical fuel burns. Find the speed of rocket at that height.

Given: m = 2 kg, fuel energy E = 400 J, h = 15 m, g = 10 m/s^2

Step 1: Potential energy at 15 m, PE = m g h = 2 × 10 × 15 = 300 J

Step 2: The rest of the fuel energy is kinetic, KE = E - PE = 400 - 300 = 100 J

Step 3: From KE = (1/2) m v^2, v^2 = 2 × 100 / 2 = 100

Step 4: Take the square root, v = 10 m/s

Final answer: 10 m/s.

mcqs.q: The gravitational potential energy stored in a body of mass m raised through height h is:
mcqs.why: To raise the mass slowly, an upward force equal to its weight m g acts over the distance h, so the work done against gravity, W = m g h, is stored as gravitational potential energy, U = m g h.

mcqs.q: A 2 kg body is raised 5 m above the ground. The potential energy it gains is: (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: U = m g h = 2 x 9.8 x 5 = 98 J. This is the work done against gravity in lifting the body, stored as potential energy.

mcqs.q: A body is taken to a point below the chosen reference level, for example into a well. Relative to that level its potential energy is:
mcqs.why: Potential energy is measured from an agreed reference level where U is taken as zero. Above the level U = +m g h, while below the level, as in a basement or a well, U = -m g h, and only differences in PE have physical meaning.

mcqs.q: A body at the top of a building has potential energy 200 J. Dropped from there, its kinetic energy just before striking the ground is 160 J. The work done against air resistance is:
mcqs.why: Without air resistance the KE at the ground would equal the full 200 J of PE lost. The shortfall, 200 - 160 = 40 J, is the energy used in doing work against air resistance.

mcqs.q: Which statement expresses the law of conservation of energy correctly?
options: Energy can be created but not destroyed
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it only changes from one form to another
Mechanical energy is always destroyed by friction
The total energy of a system increases during every change
mcqs.why: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form into another, so the total energy of an isolated system remains constant. With friction, the missing mechanical energy appears as heat and the total is still conserved.

mcqs.q: A body falls freely from height h. After it has fallen a height h/2, it possesses:
options: More kinetic and less potential energy
Half potential and half kinetic energy
mcqs.why: At height h/2 the body still holds PE = m g (h/2), exactly half of its initial m g h. By conservation of energy the other half has become kinetic energy, so the two forms are equal at the halfway point.

mcqs.q: The efficiency of a real device is:
options: The ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, and always less than 100 percent in real devices
The ratio of total energy input to useful energy output
mcqs.why: Efficiency is the ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, usually expressed as a percentage. In every real transformation some energy is wasted, mostly as heat due to friction, resistance or sound, so efficiency is always less than 100 percent.

mcqs.q: An object thrown upwards rises to a maximum height h. At what height has it lost one third of its original kinetic energy?
mcqs.why: At maximum height all the original KE has become PE, so original KE = m g h. Losing one third of the KE means the PE gained is (1/3) m g h, so m g h1 = (1/3) m g h and h1 = h / 3.

mcqs.q: A stone thrown vertically upwards can reach a height of 10 m. Its speed when it is just 2 m above the ground is: (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: By energy conservation, (1/2) m v^2 = m g (10 - 2), so v^2 = 2 x 9.8 x 8 = 156.8 and v = sqrt(156.8) = 12.5 m/s.

mcqs.q: A rocket of mass 2 kg uses 400 J of fuel energy to reach a height of 15 m. Its speed at that height is: (g = 10 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Potential energy at 15 m: PE = m g h = 2 x 10 x 15 = 300 J. The remaining fuel energy is kinetic: KE = 400 - 300 = 100 J. From (1/2) m v^2 = 100, v^2 = 2 x 100 / 2 = 100, so v = 10 m/s.

lessons.title: Escape Velocity and Power
lessons.notes_html:
Escape Velocity

The escape velocity is the minimum velocity given to an object so that it emerges out from the gravitational field of the Earth. For the Earth it is about 11.2 km/s: given this speed at the surface, the object just reaches infinity with zero speed and never falls back.

v = √(2 g R)

v = √(2 G M / R)

The escape velocity of a planet depends on both the mass and the radius of the planet: it increases with the planet's mass and decreases with its radius. Neither mass alone nor radius alone is enough to fix its value.

Power

Power is the rate at which work is done, so it tells how quickly energy is transferred. Two machines may do the same total work, but the one that does it in less time has the greater power. Its SI unit is the watt, where 1 watt = 1 joule per second: when one joule of work is done on a body in one second, the power is one watt. Power can also be calculated by multiplying force and velocity, P = F . v.

P = W / t

P = F . v

Average Power and Instantaneous Power

Average PowerInstantaneous Power
Total work divided by total time, P_avg = W / t; describes performance over a whole intervalRate of doing work at one particular instant, P = F . v; can change from moment to moment

For a car accelerating, the instantaneous power keeps changing while the average is a single value for the whole journey.

Worked Example 1

A 100 kg man runs up a long flight of stairs in 9.8 second. The vertical height of the stair is 10 m. Calculate its power.

Given: m = 100 kg, h = 10 m, t = 9.8 s, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: Work done against gravity, W = m g h = 100 × 9.8 × 10 = 9800 J

Step 2: Write the power formula, P = W / t

Step 3: Substitute, P = 9800 / 9.8 = 1000 W

Final answer: 1000 Watts.

Worked Example 2

A 1 Kilowatt motor pump, pumps the water from the ground to a height of 10 m. Find, how much litres of water it can pump in one hour.

Given: P = 1 kW = 1000 W, t = 1 hour = 3600 s, h = 10 m, g = 10 m/s^2, density of water = 1000 kg/m^3 so 1 litre has mass 1 kg

Step 1: Total energy supplied, E = P t = 1000 × 3600 = 3.6 × 10^6 J

Step 2: This energy becomes PE of the water, m g h = E, so m = E / (g h) = 3.6 × 10^6 / (10 × 10) = 3.6 × 10^4 kg

Step 3: Convert mass of water to litres, volume = 3.6 × 10^4 litres

Final answer: 3.6 × 10^4 litre.

Worked Example 3

A motor pumps the water at the rate 500 gram/minute to the height of 120 m. If the motor is 50% efficient then how much input electric power is needed?

Given: mass rate = 500 gram/minute = 0.5 kg per 60 s, h = 120 m, g = 10 m/s^2, efficiency = 50% = 0.5

Step 1: Useful work per minute, W = m g h = 0.5 × 10 × 120 = 600 J

Step 2: Useful output power, P_out = 600 / 60 = 10 W

Step 3: Input power = P_out / efficiency = 10 / 0.5 = 20 W

Final answer: 20 watt.

mcqs.q: Escape velocity is defined as:
options: The speed needed to orbit the Earth
The minimum velocity given to an object so that it emerges out of the gravitational field of the Earth
The velocity of a falling object at the ground
The maximum velocity an object can have in air
mcqs.why: The escape velocity is the minimum velocity given to an object so that it emerges out from the gravitational field of the Earth; given this speed at the surface, the object just reaches infinity with zero speed and never falls back.

mcqs.q: The escape velocity from the Earth is about:
mcqs.why: For the Earth, v = sqrt(2 g R) works out to about 11.2 km/s. An object given this speed at the surface escapes the Earth's gravitational field and never falls back.

mcqs.q: Which formula gives the escape velocity of a planet of mass M and radius R?
mcqs.why: The escape velocity is v = sqrt(2 g R), equivalently v = sqrt(2 G M / R). It therefore depends on both the mass and the radius of the planet.

mcqs.q: The escape velocity of a planet depends on:
options: The mass of the planet only
The radius of the planet only
Both the mass and the radius of the planet
The mass of the escaping object
mcqs.why: From v = sqrt(2 G M / R), escape velocity increases with the planet's mass and decreases with its radius, so both mass and radius are needed to fix its value; neither alone is enough.

mcqs.q: Power is best defined as:
options: The total work a machine can do
The force multiplied by the displacement
The rate at which work is done
The energy stored in a body
mcqs.why: Power is the rate at which work is done, P = W / t, so it tells how quickly energy is transferred. Of two machines doing the same work, the one taking less time has the greater power.

mcqs.q: Which product gives the (instantaneous) power of a force?
mcqs.why: Power can be calculated by multiplying force and velocity, P = F . v. Force times displacement gives work, not power, so that option is ruled out.

mcqs.q: How does average power differ from instantaneous power?
options: Average power is total work divided by total time; instantaneous power is the rate of doing work at one particular instant
Average power is measured in watts but instantaneous power is not
Instantaneous power is total work divided by total time
There is no difference between them
mcqs.why: Average power is the total work divided by the total time, P_avg = W / t, describing a whole interval. Instantaneous power, P = F . v, is the rate of doing work at one instant and can change from moment to moment, as for an accelerating car.

mcqs.q: A 100 kg man runs up stairs of vertical height 10 m in 9.8 s. His power is: (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Work against gravity W = m g h = 100 x 9.8 x 10 = 9800 J. Power P = W / t = 9800 / 9.8 = 1000 W.

mcqs.q: A 1 kW motor pump lifts water to a height of 10 m. How many litres can it pump in one hour? (g = 10 m/s^2, 1 litre of water has mass 1 kg)
mcqs.why: Energy supplied E = P t = 1000 x 3600 = 3.6 x 10^6 J. Setting m g h = E gives m = 3.6 x 10^6 / (10 x 10) = 3.6 x 10^4 kg, and since 1 litre has mass 1 kg this is 3.6 x 10^4 litres.

mcqs.q: A motor pumps water at 500 gram/minute to a height of 120 m and is 50 percent efficient. The input electric power needed is: (g = 10 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Useful work per minute W = m g h = 0.5 x 10 x 120 = 600 J, so output power = 600 / 60 = 10 W. Input power = output / efficiency = 10 / 0.5 = 20 W.

lessons.title: Pascal's Law and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Pressure in a Liquid

Pressure is force per unit area, P = F / A. The pressure exerted on the ground by a man is greatest when he stands on the toes of one foot, because the force (his weight) is the same in every case but the contact area is then smallest; lying down gives the largest area and the least pressure. In a stationary homogeneous liquid the pressure depends only on depth:

P = P_o + ρ g h

All points at the same depth (same level) have the same pressure, while points at different depths have different pressures. The pressure at the bottom of a pond does not depend on the surface area of the pond: a wide pond and a narrow tank of the same depth have the same pressure at the bottom.

Pascal's Principle

Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container. When the pressure at the smaller piston of a hydraulic lift is increased by Δp, the pressure at the larger piston also increases by Δp; it is the force that grows, because its area is larger.

p = F1 / A1 = F2 / A2

Applications of Pascal's Principle

  • Hydraulic press / car lift — a small force on a small piston produces a large force on a large piston
  • Hydraulic brakes — pressure applied at the master cylinder is transmitted through brake oil to operate all the wheel brakes together
  • Hydraulic jack — its mechanical advantage (load lifted / applied force) lets a small applied force lift a heavy automobile

Why a Liquid is Used in Hydraulic Machines

A liquid is practically incompressible, so the pressure applied to it is transmitted at once and the piston movement is passed on without being wasted in compressing the fluid; a gas would simply compress and absorb the push. Hydraulic machines also depend on the liquid being able to flow and take the shape of the connecting pipes, carrying the pressure to every piston. In practice the liquid must also not corrode the machine parts, which is why special hydraulic oils are used.

Worked Example 1

In a hydraulic press a force of 20 N is applied to a piston of area 0.20 m^2. The area of the other piston is 2.0 m^2. What is (a) the pressure transmitted through the fluid; (b) the force on the piston?

Given: F1 = 20 N, A1 = 0.20 m^2, A2 = 2.0 m^2

Step 1: For (a), pressure at the small piston, p = F1 / A1 = 20 / 0.20 = 100 Pa

Step 2: By Pascal's principle this same pressure is transmitted through the fluid

Step 3: For (b), force on the large piston, F2 = p × A2 = 100 × 2.0 = 200 N

Final answer: (a) 100 Pa, (b) 200 N.

Worked Example 2

The pressure in a water pipe in the ground floor of a building is 4 × 10^5 Pa but three floors up it is only 2 × 10^5 Pa. What is the height between the ground floor and the third floor? The water in the pipe may be assumed to be stationary; density of water = 1 × 10^3 kg/m^3

Given: p_ground = 4 × 10^5 Pa, p_third = 2 × 10^5 Pa, ρ = 1 × 10^3 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2

Step 1: Pressure difference, Δp = 4 × 10^5 - 2 × 10^5 = 2 × 10^5 Pa

Step 2: This difference is due to the water column of height h, Δp = ρ g h

Step 3: Rearrange, h = Δp / (ρ g) = 2 × 10^5 / (1 × 10^3 × 10)

Step 4: Divide, h = 2 × 10^5 / 1 × 10^4 = 20 m

Final answer: 20 m.

Worked Example 3

The small piston of hydraulic press has an area of 10.0 cm^2. If the applied force is 50.0 N, what must the area of the large piston to exert a pressing force of 4800 N?

Given: A1 = 10.0 cm^2, F1 = 50.0 N, F2 = 4800 N

Step 1: Pressure at the small piston, p = F1 / A1 = 50.0 / 10.0 = 5.0 N/cm^2

Step 2: The same pressure acts on the large piston, so A2 = F2 / p

Step 3: Substitute, A2 = 4800 / 5.0 = 960 cm^2

Final answer: 960 cm^2.

Worked Example 4

Mechanical advantage of a hydraulic jack is 420. Find the weight of the heaviest automobile that can be lifted by an applied force of 55 N.

Given: mechanical advantage = 420, applied force = 55 N

Step 1: Mechanical advantage = load lifted / applied force

Step 2: Rearrange, load = mechanical advantage × applied force = 420 × 55

Step 3: Multiply, load = 23100 N, about 23000 N

Final answer: 23000 N (23100 N).

Worked Example 5

A canal lock gate is 20 m wide and 10 m deep. Calculate the thrust acting on it assuming that the water in the canal is in level with the top of the gate. Density of water is 1000 kg/m^3

Given: width = 20 m, depth h = 10 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: Pressure grows with depth, so use the average pressure at the mean depth h / 2 = 5 m

Step 2: Average pressure, p_avg = ρ g (h / 2) = 1000 × 9.8 × 5 = 49000 Pa

Step 3: Area of the gate, A = 20 × 10 = 200 m^2

Step 4: Thrust = p_avg × A = 49000 × 200 = 9.8 × 10^6 N

Final answer: 9.8 × 10^6 N.

Worked Example 6

A tank 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2 m deep is filled to the brim with paraffin (density 800 kg/m^3). Calculate the pressure on the base. What is the thrust on the base?

Given: length = 4 m, width = 3 m, depth h = 2 m, ρ = 800 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2

Step 1: Pressure on the base, p = ρ g h = 800 × 10 × 2 = 16000 Pa

Step 2: Area of the base, A = 4 × 3 = 12 m^2

Step 3: Thrust = p × A = 16000 × 12 = 192000 N = 1.92 × 10^5 N

Final answer: 16000 Pa, 192000 N (the book's printed 19200 N misses a zero).

mcqs.q: Pressure is defined as:
options: Force per unit area, P = F / A
mcqs.why: Pressure is force per unit area, P = F / A. For the same force, a smaller area gives a greater pressure.

mcqs.q: The pressure exerted on the ground by a man is greatest when he:
options: Stands with both feet flat on the ground
Stands on the toes of one foot
mcqs.why: The force is his weight in every case, but standing on the toes of one foot gives the smallest contact area, so P = F / A is greatest; lying down gives the largest area and the least pressure.

mcqs.q: In a stationary homogeneous liquid, the pressure at depth h below a surface at pressure P_o is:
mcqs.why: In a stationary homogeneous liquid the pressure depends only on depth: P = P_o + rho g h, where rho is the liquid density and h is the depth below the surface.

mcqs.q: In a stationary homogeneous liquid, pressure is the same at:
options: All points at the same level (same depth)
mcqs.why: Because pressure depends only on depth, all points at the same depth (same level) have the same pressure, while points at different depths have different pressures.

mcqs.q: The pressure at the bottom of a pond does NOT depend on:
options: The surface area of the pond
mcqs.why: Pressure at depth is P = rho g h, fixed by the density and the depth only. A wide pond and a narrow tank of the same depth have the same pressure at the bottom, so surface area does not matter.

mcqs.q: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:
options: Lost in the walls of the container
Increased in proportion to the area
Transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container
Transmitted only in the downward direction
mcqs.why: Pascal's principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of the container. This is the basis of all hydraulic machines.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic lift, one piston has twice the area of the other. When the pressure at the smaller piston increases by delta p, the pressure at the larger piston increases by:
mcqs.why: By Pascal's principle the pressure change is transmitted undiminished, so the larger piston also increases by delta p. It is the force that grows at the larger piston, because its area is larger.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic brake system, Pascal's principle is used so that:
options: The brake oil is compressed to store energy
Pressure applied at the master cylinder is transmitted through brake oil to operate all the wheel brakes together
Each wheel needs its own separate pedal
The brakes work only on the front wheels
mcqs.why: In hydraulic brakes, pressure applied at the master cylinder is transmitted through the brake oil to operate all the wheel brakes together, an application of Pascal's principle.

mcqs.q: Why must a liquid, and not a gas, be used as the fluid in a hydraulic machine?
options: Because a liquid is heavier than a gas
Because a liquid is practically incompressible, so the applied pressure is transmitted at once instead of being wasted in compressing the fluid
Because a gas cannot flow through pipes
Because a liquid has a lower density than a gas
mcqs.why: A liquid is practically incompressible, so the pressure applied to it is transmitted at once and piston movement is passed on without being wasted in compressing the fluid; a gas would simply compress and absorb the push.

mcqs.q: Apart from being incompressible, hydraulic machines also depend on the liquid being able to:
options: Flow and take the shape of the connecting pipes, carrying the pressure to every piston
mcqs.why: Hydraulic machines also depend on the liquid being able to flow and take the shape of the connecting pipes, carrying the pressure to every piston. In practice the liquid must also not corrode the parts, which is why special hydraulic oils are used.

mcqs.q: In a hydraulic press, a force of 20 N is applied to a piston of area 0.20 m^2 and the other piston has area 2.0 m^2. The force on the large piston is:
mcqs.why: Pressure at the small piston p = F1 / A1 = 20 / 0.20 = 100 Pa. This same pressure acts on the large piston, so F2 = p x A2 = 100 x 2.0 = 200 N.

mcqs.q: The pressure in a water pipe is 4 x 10^5 Pa at the ground floor and 2 x 10^5 Pa three floors up. The height between the floors is: (density of water 1 x 10^3 kg/m^3, g = 10 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Pressure difference delta p = 4 x 10^5 - 2 x 10^5 = 2 x 10^5 Pa. From delta p = rho g h, h = 2 x 10^5 / (1 x 10^3 x 10) = 2 x 10^5 / 1 x 10^4 = 20 m.

mcqs.q: The small piston of a hydraulic press has area 10.0 cm^2 and the applied force is 50.0 N. To exert a pressing force of 4800 N, the large piston must have area:
mcqs.why: Pressure at the small piston p = F1 / A1 = 50.0 / 10.0 = 5.0 N/cm^2. The same pressure acts on the large piston, so A2 = F2 / p = 4800 / 5.0 = 960 cm^2.

mcqs.q: The mechanical advantage of a hydraulic jack is 420. The heaviest load it can lift with an applied force of 55 N is:
mcqs.why: Mechanical advantage = load lifted / applied force, so load = mechanical advantage x applied force = 420 x 55 = 23100 N, about 23000 N.

mcqs.q: A tank 4 m long, 3 m wide and 2 m deep is filled to the brim with paraffin of density 800 kg/m^3. The thrust on the base is: (g = 10 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Pressure on the base p = rho g h = 800 x 10 x 2 = 16000 Pa. Base area A = 4 x 3 = 12 m^2. Thrust = p x A = 16000 x 12 = 192000 N = 1.92 x 10^5 N.

lessons.title: Archimedes' Principle, Upthrust and Flotation
lessons.notes_html:
Archimedes' Principle and Displaced Fluid

When a body is immersed in a fluid it experiences an upthrust equal to the weight of the fluid displaced, so the apparent loss of weight of the body equals the weight of the displaced fluid. A completely submerged object always displaces its own volume of fluid, whatever its shape or weight, and this displaced volume is what fixes the buoyant force. A rock that weighs 5 N out of water and 3 N when submerged in water experiences a buoyant force equal to the apparent loss of weight, 5 N - 3 N = 2 N.

Buoyancy in Liquids and Gases

Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid on a body immersed in it, caused by the pressure of the fluid increasing with depth, so the upward push on the lower surface exceeds the downward push on the upper surface. In liquids the effect is strong because liquids are dense: ships float, swimmers are supported, and submerged objects feel lighter. In gases the same effect exists but is much weaker because air is about 800 times less dense; still, it lifts hot-air balloons and helium balloons, and precision weighing must allow for the small upthrust of air. In a vacuum, with no fluid around it, an object experiences no buoyant force, although it still has its mass and, near the Earth, its weight.

Immersed and Submerged

  • Immersed — the body is placed in the water and may be only partly below the surface; part of it can remain above the water
  • Submerged — the body is completely under the water, entirely surrounded by it

A floating ship is immersed but not submerged, while a stone resting on the bottom is fully submerged.

Law of Flotation

Upthrust (buoyant force) is the upward force that a fluid exerts on any body partly or wholly immersed in it, equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. Flotation is the special condition in which a body rests in equilibrium because the upthrust exactly balances its weight. So upthrust is a force, while flotation is the resulting state; a sinking body also experiences upthrust but does not float. The law of flotation states that a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats.

In liquids this explains why a ship floats at a depth where the displaced water weighs as much as the ship, and why the submerged fraction of a floating body equals the ratio of its density to the liquid's density. In gases the same law applies to balloons: a balloon rises until the weight of displaced air equals the total weight of the balloon, its gas and its load, and then it floats at that level. Hydrometers and lactometers are practical instruments based on this law.

Why Iron Ships Float, and Floating Higher in Salt Water

Iron itself is denser than water, but a ship is not a solid block of iron: its hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the whole ship is less than the density of water. The hollow hull displaces a weight of water equal to the ship's total weight before it is fully submerged, so by the law of flotation it floats with only part of the hull below the waterline. Salt water is denser than fresh water, so a floating body displaces the weight equal to its own weight with a smaller submerged volume and sits higher; the buoyant force on a floating boat is equal to its weight in both fresh and salt water — only the displaced volume changes. Floating ice displaces a volume of water whose weight equals the weight of the ice, so when it melts it produces exactly that same volume of water and the water level stays at the rim. When a swimmer dives off a raft, the raft then supports only its own weight, displaces less water and rises, while the swimmer in the pool displaces his own weight of water, so the pool level stays unchanged.

Finding Gold Purity with Archimedes' Principle

To test the purity of gold, the ornament is weighed in air (W1) and then weighed fully immersed in water (W2); the loss W1 - W2 is the weight of water displaced. The relative density is then W1 / (W1 - W2), and multiplying by 1000 kg/m^3 gives the density of the sample. Pure gold has a density of about 19300 kg/m^3; if the measured density matches this value the gold is pure, while a lower value shows it is mixed with a lighter metal such as copper or silver.

Worked Example 1

A flat-bottom river barge is 30 ft wide, 85 ft long and 15 ft. deep, (a) how many m^3 of water will displace while the top stays 1 m above the water? (b) What load in tons will the barge contain under these conditions if the empty barge weighs 160 tons in dry dock?

Given: width = 30 ft = 9.14 m, length = 85 ft = 25.9 m, depth = 15 ft = 4.57 m, top stays 1 m above water, empty barge = 160 tons, density of water = 1000 kg/m^3

Step 1: Submerged depth = 4.57 - 1 = 3.57 m

Step 2: For (a), displaced volume V = length × width × submerged depth = 25.9 × 9.14 × 3.57 = 845 m^3 (about 3.0 × 10^4 ft^3)

Step 3: Weight of displaced water = 845 m^3 × 1000 kg/m^3 = 8.45 × 10^5 kg = 845 tons, which by flotation equals barge plus load

Step 4: For (b), load = 845 - 160 = 685 tons, roughly 7 × 10^2 tons (the book's rough ft-based estimate is about 800 tons)

Final answer: (a) about 8.5 × 10^2 m^3, (b) about 685 tons.

Worked Example 2

A rectangular boat is 4.0 m wide, 8.0 m long, and 3.0 m deep. (a) How much water will it displace if the top stays 1.0 m above the water? (b) What load will the boat contain under these conditions if the empty boat weighs 8.60 × 10^4 N in dry dock? (Weight density of water = 9800 N/m^3)

Given: width = 4.0 m, length = 8.0 m, depth = 3.0 m, top stays 1.0 m above water, empty boat weight = 8.60 × 10^4 N, weight density of water = 9800 N/m^3

Step 1: Submerged depth = 3.0 - 1.0 = 2.0 m

Step 2: For (a), displaced volume V = 8.0 × 4.0 × 2.0 = 64.0 m^3

Step 3: Weight of displaced water = 64.0 × 9800 = 627200 N, which equals boat weight plus load

Step 4: For (b), load = 627200 - 8.60 × 10^4 = 541200 N = 5.41 × 10^5 N

Final answer: (a) 64.0 m^3, (b) 5.41 × 10^5 N.

Worked Example 3

A hot air balloon has a volume of 2200 m^3. The density of air at temperature of 20°C is 1.205 kg/m^3. The density of the hot air inside the balloon at a temperature of 100°C is 0.946 kg/m^3. How much weight can the hot air can lift?

Given: V = 2200 m^3, ρ_out = 1.205 kg/m^3, ρ_in = 0.946 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: Density difference, Δρ = 1.205 - 0.946 = 0.259 kg/m^3

Step 2: Net lifting mass = Δρ × V = 0.259 × 2200 = 569.8 kg

Step 3: Liftable weight = 569.8 × 9.8 = 5584 N, about 5590 N

Final answer: 5590 N.

Worked Example 4

A spherical balloon has a radius of 7.15 m and is filled with helium. How large a cargo can it lift, assuming that the skin and structure of the balloon have a mass of 930 kg? Neglect the buoyant force on the cargo volume itself.

Given: r = 7.15 m, skin and structure mass = 930 kg, density of air = 1.29 kg/m^3, density of helium = 0.179 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: Volume of the sphere, V = (4/3) π r^3 = (4/3) × 3.14 × (7.15)^3 = 4.19 × 365.5 = 1531 m^3

Step 2: Mass of displaced air = 1.29 × 1531 = 1975 kg

Step 3: Mass of helium = 0.179 × 1531 = 274 kg

Step 4: Net lift in mass = 1975 - 274 - 930 = 771 kg, about 770 kg

Step 5: As a weight this is 771 × 9.8 = 7.6 × 10^3 N

Final answer: about 770 kg, weight about 7.6 × 10^3 N (the book's printed 920 kg does not follow from these standard densities).

mcqs.q: Archimedes' principle states that a body immersed in a fluid experiences an upthrust equal to:
options: The weight of the fluid displaced
The pressure at the bottom of the fluid
mcqs.why: By Archimedes' principle the upthrust equals the weight of the fluid displaced, so the apparent loss of weight of the immersed body equals the weight of the displaced fluid.

mcqs.q: A completely submerged object always displaces its own:
mcqs.why: A completely submerged object takes the place of a volume of fluid exactly equal to its own volume, whatever its shape or weight, and this displaced volume is what fixes the buoyant force.

mcqs.q: A rock weighs 5 N out of water and 3 N when submerged in water. The buoyant force on the rock is:
mcqs.why: The buoyant force equals the apparent loss of weight, which is 5 N - 3 N = 2 N.

mcqs.q: Buoyancy arises because, as fluid pressure increases with depth:
options: The downward push on the upper surface exceeds the upward push on the lower surface
The upward push on the lower surface exceeds the downward push on the upper surface
The pressure is the same on all surfaces
mcqs.why: Buoyancy is caused by the pressure of the fluid increasing with depth, so the upward push on the lower surface of the body exceeds the downward push on its upper surface, giving a net upward force.
