mcqs.q: In a vacuum, an object experiences:
mcqs.why: Buoyant force is the upthrust from the surrounding fluid, so in a vacuum, with no fluid around it, an object experiences no buoyant force, although it still has its mass and, near the Earth, its weight.

mcqs.q: Buoyancy in gases is much weaker than in liquids mainly because:
options: Air is about 800 times less dense than a liquid such as water
Balloons are too heavy to lift
mcqs.why: The same buoyancy effect exists in gases but is much weaker because air is about 800 times less dense; still, it lifts hot-air balloons and helium balloons, and precision weighing must allow for the small upthrust of air.

mcqs.q: A floating ship is best described as:
mcqs.why: Immersed means the body is placed in the water and may be only partly below the surface, while submerged means it is completely under the water. A floating ship is immersed but not submerged; a stone resting on the bottom is fully submerged.

mcqs.q: The law of flotation states that a floating body displaces:
options: Its own volume of the fluid
Its own weight of the fluid in which it floats
Twice its own weight of fluid
A weight of fluid equal to the container's weight
mcqs.why: The law of flotation states that a floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats, so a ship floats at the depth where the displaced water weighs as much as the ship.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes upthrust from flotation?
options: Upthrust is a state and flotation is a force
Both are forces of equal size in all cases
Upthrust is a force, while flotation is the state in which that force exactly balances the body's weight
A sinking body experiences no upthrust
mcqs.why: Upthrust is the upward force a fluid exerts on a partly or wholly immersed body, equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Flotation is the resulting state when that force exactly balances the weight; a sinking body also experiences upthrust but does not float.

mcqs.q: Why does a ship made of iron float, even though iron is denser than water?
options: Because iron becomes lighter in water
Because the hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the whole ship is less than that of water
Because the ship's engines hold it up
Because salt in the water pushes it up
mcqs.why: A ship is not a solid block of iron: its hollow hull encloses a large volume of air, so the average density of the whole ship is less than the density of water, and it displaces a weight of water equal to its total weight before it is fully submerged.

mcqs.q: A boat floats in both fresh water and salt water. The buoyant force on the boat in salt water is, compared with that in fresh water:
mcqs.why: A floating boat is in equilibrium, so the buoyant force equals its weight in either liquid. In denser salt water it simply displaces a smaller volume and floats higher, while the buoyant force stays equal to its weight.

mcqs.q: A glass is filled with ice and water up to the rim, with some ice floating above the rim. When the ice melts, the water level:
options: Depends on the size of the glass
mcqs.why: Floating ice displaces a volume of water whose weight equals the weight of the ice. When it melts it produces exactly that same volume of water, so it just refills the space it had displaced and the level stays at the rim.

mcqs.q: A swimmer dives off a raft floating in a pool. What happens to the raft and to the pool's water level?
options: The raft sinks lower and the level rises
The raft rises and the water level stays unchanged
The raft rises and the water level falls
The raft stays at the same depth and the level falls
mcqs.why: Once the swimmer dives off, the raft supports only its own weight, displaces less water and rises. The swimmer in the pool displaces his own weight of water, so the total displaced volume is unchanged and the pool level stays the same.

mcqs.q: To test gold purity with Archimedes' principle, an ornament is weighed in air (W1) and fully immersed in water (W2). Its relative density is:
mcqs.why: The loss W1 - W2 is the weight of water displaced, and the relative density is W1 / (W1 - W2). Multiplying by 1000 kg/m^3 gives the sample density; pure gold has a density of about 19300 kg/m^3, and a lower measured value shows a lighter metal is mixed in.

mcqs.q: A hot air balloon of volume 2200 m^3 has outside air density 1.205 kg/m^3 and inside hot air density 0.946 kg/m^3. The weight it can lift is about: (g = 9.8 m/s^2)
mcqs.why: Density difference = 1.205 - 0.946 = 0.259 kg/m^3. Net lifting mass = 0.259 x 2200 = 569.8 kg. Liftable weight = 569.8 x 9.8 = 5584 N, about 5590 N.

lessons.title: Surface Tension
lessons.notes_html:
What is Surface Tension?

Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface that makes it behave like a stretched elastic membrane; it is defined as the force per unit length acting along the surface, with unit N/m. Equivalently, it is the tangential force per unit length with which a liquid surface contracts, making the surface act like a stretched membrane.

Surface tension = force / length, unit N/m

Experiments and Observations

  • Needle on water — a greased needle or a razor blade placed gently on water floats although the metal is denser than water, held up by the stretched surface film
  • Thread loop on a soap film — a loop of thread on a soap film stays circular once the film inside it is pricked, showing that the outer film pulls it equally in all directions
  • Capillary rise — water rises in a fine capillary tube and forms a concave surface, showing the surface pulling the liquid up the walls
  • Spherical drops — rain drops and falling water droplets are nearly spherical, the shape of minimum surface area

Applications of Surface Tension

  • Detergents and cleaning — detergents lower the surface tension, which helps water spread into fabrics for cleaning
  • Paints, inks and sprays — they must spread evenly over a surface, which depends on surface tension
  • Insects on water — small insects can walk on water, supported by the surface film

Together these examples show the same idea from different sides: the surface always tries to contract to the smallest possible area, and the pull acts equally along the surface in every direction.

mcqs.q: Surface tension is defined as:
options: The force per unit length acting along the liquid surface
The force per unit area on a liquid surface
The weight of a liquid drop
The pressure inside a liquid drop
mcqs.why: Surface tension is defined as the force per unit length acting along the surface, the tangential force per unit length with which a liquid surface contracts, making the surface act like a stretched membrane.

mcqs.q: The unit of surface tension is:
mcqs.why: Since surface tension = force / length, its unit is newtons per metre, written N/m.

mcqs.q: Because of surface tension, a liquid surface behaves like:
mcqs.why: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface that makes it behave like a stretched elastic membrane, with the surface always trying to contract to the smallest possible area.

mcqs.q: A greased needle placed gently on water floats even though the metal is denser than water. This shows that:
options: The needle's weight disappears in water
Water pushes the needle up from below like a boat
The stretched surface film holds the needle up
The needle is attracted to the surface by magnetism
mcqs.why: The needle is held up by the stretched surface film of the water, an observation of surface tension, even though the metal itself is denser than water.

mcqs.q: A loop of thread on a soap film becomes circular once the film inside it is pricked. This experiment shows that:
options: The thread is elastic and pulls itself round
The outer film pulls the thread equally in all directions
The film inside was pushing the thread inward
Surface tension acts only in one direction
mcqs.why: Once the inner film is pricked, the outer film pulls the loop equally in all directions, so the loop takes a circular shape. This shows the surface pull acts equally along the surface in every direction.

mcqs.q: Water rising in a fine capillary tube, forming a concave surface, demonstrates:
options: The pressure of the atmosphere alone
Evaporation of water in the tube
The surface pulling the liquid up the walls of the tube
The weight of the water column
mcqs.why: In capillary rise the water climbs a fine tube and forms a concave surface, showing the surface pulling the liquid up the walls, an effect of surface tension.

mcqs.q: Rain drops and falling water droplets are nearly spherical because a sphere is:
options: The shape with the largest surface area
The shape of minimum surface area
The shape water takes only in space
Forced by the pressure of the air
mcqs.why: The liquid surface always tries to contract to the smallest possible area, and a sphere is the shape of minimum surface area for a given volume, so falling drops are nearly spherical.

mcqs.q: Detergents help cleaning because they:
options: Lower the surface tension, which helps water spread into fabrics
Increase the surface tension of water
Remove the surface of the water completely
mcqs.why: Detergents lower the surface tension of water, which helps the water spread into fabrics for cleaning, one of the practical applications of surface tension.

mcqs.q: Small insects can walk on water because they are:
options: Supported by the surface film of the water
Held up by bubbles under their feet
mcqs.why: Small insects can walk on water because they are supported by the surface film, which behaves like a stretched membrane due to surface tension.

mcqs.q: Paints, inks and sprays must spread evenly over a surface. This spreading depends on:
options: The speed of the spray only
mcqs.why: Paints, inks and sprays must spread evenly over a surface, and this spreading depends on surface tension, which is why it is one of the listed applications of the effect.

lessons.title: Viscosity, Stokes' Law and Terminal Velocity
lessons.notes_html:
Viscosity and Viscous Force

When layers of a fluid move relative to each other, internal friction opposes the motion; the tangential force responsible is called the viscous force, and the property is viscosity. For a layer of area A with velocity gradient dv / dx, the viscous force is:

F = η A (dv / dx)

Here η is the coefficient of viscosity, measured in Pa.s. Viscosity is why honey pours slowly while water pours quickly, why lubricating oil must have a suitable viscosity, and why a falling object in a fluid reaches a terminal velocity instead of accelerating forever.

Stokes' Law

Stokes' law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid:

F = 6 π η r v

It is the basis for finding terminal velocity. It is used to measure the viscosity of liquids in the falling-sphere viscometer and to find the size of tiny particles such as droplets in the Millikan oil-drop experiment. It also explains why fine dust and mist settle very slowly through air while larger drops fall quickly.

Terminal Velocity in Liquids

When a small sphere falls through a liquid, three forces act on it: its weight pulling it down, the upthrust of the liquid, and the viscous drag acting upward, which grows with speed according to Stokes' law. At first the sphere accelerates, but as the drag grows the net force falls to zero and the sphere then falls at a constant maximum speed called its terminal velocity.

v_t = (2 g r^2 (ρ - σ)) / (9 η)

Here ρ is the density of the sphere and σ that of the liquid. In air the same balance holds: a sky diver falling at terminal velocity falls at constant speed, so the net force on him is zero and the upward air resistance is equal to his weight — the defining condition of terminal velocity. Terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, so larger drops fall faster than smaller ones.

Worked Example 1

Two spherical raindrops of equal size are falling through air at a velocity of 0.08 m/s. If the drops join together forming a large spherical drop, what will be the new terminal velocity?

Given: terminal velocity of each small drop v1 = 0.08 m/s, two drops of equal radius r join to form one drop of radius R

Step 1: Volume doubles, (4/3) π R^3 = 2 × (4/3) π r^3, so R^3 = 2 r^3 and R = 2^(1/3) r = 1.26 r

Step 2: Terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, v proportional to r^2

Step 3: v2 / v1 = (R / r)^2 = (2^(1/3))^2 = 2^(2/3) = 1.587

Step 4: v2 = 1.587 × 0.08 = 0.127 m/s, about 0.13 m/s

Final answer: 0.13 m/s.

Worked Example 2

Calculate the viscous drag on a drop of oil of 0.1 mm radius falling through air at its terminal velocity. (Viscosity of air = 1.8 × 10^-5 Pa.s; density of oil = 850 kg/m^3)

Given: r = 0.1 mm = 1.0 × 10^-4 m, ρ_oil = 850 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2, air density about 1.29 kg/m^3

Step 1: At terminal velocity the viscous drag balances the effective weight of the drop, F = (weight - upthrust) = (4/3) π r^3 (ρ_oil - ρ_air) g

Step 2: Volume factor, (4/3) π r^3 = 4.19 × (1.0 × 10^-4)^3 = 4.19 × 10^-12 m^3

Step 3: Density difference = 850 - 1.29 = 848.7 kg/m^3

Step 4: F = 4.19 × 10^-12 × 848.7 × 9.8 = 3.48 × 10^-8 N

Final answer: 3.48 × 10^-8 N.

mcqs.q: What is the viscous force for a fluid layer of area A with velocity gradient dv/dx?
mcqs.why: The viscous force is F = eta A (dv/dx), where eta is the coefficient of viscosity. It is the tangential internal friction force that opposes relative motion between fluid layers.

mcqs.q: What is the SI unit of the coefficient of viscosity eta?
mcqs.why: The coefficient of viscosity eta in F = eta A (dv/dx) is measured in Pa.s, as stated in the notes on viscosity and viscous force.

mcqs.q: Stokes law gives the viscous drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a fluid as:
mcqs.why: Stokes law is F = 6 pi eta r v, where r is the sphere radius and v its speed. It gives the drag that grows with speed and leads to terminal velocity.

mcqs.q: At terminal velocity, a sphere falling through a liquid falls with:
options: increasing speed and increasing net force
constant maximum speed and zero net force
mcqs.why: At terminal velocity the weight is balanced by upthrust plus viscous drag, so the net force is zero and the sphere falls at a constant maximum speed.

mcqs.q: The terminal velocity of a small sphere in a liquid is given by:
mcqs.why: Terminal velocity is v_t = (2 g r^2 (rho - sigma)) / (9 eta), where rho is the density of the sphere and sigma is the density of the liquid.

mcqs.q: Terminal velocity is proportional to which power of the sphere radius r?
mcqs.why: From v_t = (2 g r^2 (rho - sigma)) / (9 eta), terminal velocity is proportional to r^2. That is why larger drops fall faster than smaller ones.

mcqs.q: Two equal raindrops falling at 0.08 m/s join to form one larger drop. What is the new terminal velocity?
mcqs.why: Volume doubles so R^3 = 2 r^3 and R = 2^(1/3) r. Since v is proportional to r^2, v2/v1 = 2^(2/3) = 1.587, so v2 = 1.587 x 0.08 = 0.127 m/s, about 0.13 m/s.

mcqs.q: What is the viscous drag on an oil drop of radius 0.1 mm falling through air at terminal velocity? (density of oil 850 kg/m^3, air density 1.29 kg/m^3)
mcqs.why: At terminal velocity drag = (4/3) pi r^3 (rho_oil - rho_air) g = 4.19 x 10^-12 x 848.7 x 9.8 = 3.48 x 10^-8 N, balancing the effective weight of the drop.

mcqs.q: A sky diver falls through air at terminal velocity. The force of air resistance on him is:
mcqs.why: At terminal velocity the diver falls at constant speed so the net force is zero. The upward air resistance must therefore be equal to his downward weight.

mcqs.q: Stokes law is used in the falling-sphere viscometer and the Millikan oil-drop experiment to:
options: measure flow speed in a venturi meter
measure viscosity and find the size of tiny particles such as droplets
measure atmospheric pressure on a hilltop
find the lift on an aeroplane wing
mcqs.why: Stokes law is the basis for finding terminal velocity. It is used to measure the viscosity of liquids in the falling-sphere viscometer and to find the size of tiny droplets in the Millikan oil-drop experiment.

lessons.title: Fluid Flow and the Equation of Continuity
lessons.notes_html:
Fluid Dynamics and Fluid Statics

Fluid dynamics is the branch of physics that deals with fluids in motion: their speeds, pressures, flow rates and the forces involved in flow. It is significant because almost every practical use of fluids, from water supply and blood circulation to flight and weather, involves moving fluids, and laws such as the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation let us predict and design for these flows. Fluid statics, in contrast, deals with fluids at rest and concerns pressure at a depth, Pascal's principle and buoyancy. The two together give the complete description of fluid behaviour.

Streamline and Turbulent Flow

Streamline (Laminar) FlowTurbulent Flow
Every particle follows a smooth path; streamlines never cross; layers slide over one another in an orderly way, as at low speedsMotion is irregular and disorderly, with eddies and whirls; streamlines change from moment to moment

Turbulence sets in at high speeds or past obstacles and wastes more energy in friction. In most practical situations speeds are high and passages are large, so the Reynolds number far exceeds the critical value of about 2000 and the flow becomes turbulent: smoke rising from a cigarette flows smoothly for a short distance and then breaks into swirls, and rivers, winds, blood in arteries during exertion and water in household pipes all show eddies and mixing, which confirms that everyday fluid flow is mostly turbulent rather than laminar.

Steady Flow and Incompressible Flow

  • Steady flow — the velocity at any given point does not vary with time; every particle arriving at a fixed point has the same velocity as the particles that passed that point earlier, although the velocity may still differ from one point to another
  • Incompressible flow — the density cannot change with time or location; pressure and velocity may still vary from point to point, as is nearly true for liquids

Reynolds Number

The Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial effects to viscous effects in a flow, where L is a characteristic length such as the pipe diameter; it has no units.

Re = ρ v L / η

Its significance is that flows with the same Reynolds number behave similarly, so it is used in model testing of aircraft, ships and pipelines, and to design pipelines, aircraft and ships, because turbulent flow causes much greater drag and energy loss than laminar flow. For pipe flow, when Re is below about 2000 viscous forces dominate and the flow stays laminar and orderly. When Re rises above about 4000 inertia dominates, the streamlines break up into eddies, and the flow becomes turbulent; between these values the flow is in an unstable transition state.

Equation of Continuity

Consider an incompressible fluid flowing through a pipe of varying cross-section, with area A1 and speed v1 at one section and A2 and v2 at another. In time Δt the mass entering is ρ A1 v1 Δt and the mass leaving is ρ A2 v2 Δt; since no fluid accumulates inside, these masses are equal, giving the equation of continuity. It is derived from the conservation of mass: the mass of fluid entering a pipe section must equal the mass leaving it, since fluid is neither created nor stored inside.

A1 v1 = A2 v2

Its physical significance is that the volume flow rate A v is constant throughout the pipe — the flow rate is the same at every section. Where the pipe is narrow the speed is high and where it is wide the speed is low, but their product stays constant. If the cross-sectional area decreases, the fluid velocity increases, which is why water speeds up at the narrow nozzle of a hose.

Worked Example 1

What area must a heating duct have if air moving 3.0 m/s along it can replenish the air every 15 minutes in a room of volume 300 m^3. Assume air density remains constant.

Given: room volume V = 300 m^3, time = 15 minutes = 900 s, air speed v = 3.0 m/s

Step 1: Required volume flow rate, Q = V / t = 300 / 900 = 0.333 m^3/s

Step 2: From Q = A v, area A = Q / v = 0.333 / 3.0 = 0.111 m^2

Step 3: If the duct is square, its side is √(0.111) = 0.33 m

Final answer: 0.11 m^2 (a square duct of side 0.33 m).

Worked Example 2

A liquid flows through a pipe with a diameter of 0.50 m at a speed of 4.20 m/s. What is the rate of flow in L/min?

Given: d = 0.50 m, v = 4.20 m/s, 1 m^3 = 1000 L

Step 1: Radius r = 0.25 m, area A = π r^2 = 3.14 × (0.25)^2 = 0.196 m^2

Step 2: Volume flow rate, Q = A v = 0.196 × 4.20 = 0.825 m^3/s

Step 3: Convert to litres per second, 0.825 × 1000 = 825 L/s

Step 4: Convert to per minute, 825 × 60 = 49500 L/min

Final answer: 49500 L/min.

Worked Example 3

Calculate the average speed of blood flow in the major arteries of the body, which have a total cross-sectional area of about 2.1 cm^2. Use the data of example 7.3 (aorta radius 1.2 cm, blood speed in the aorta 40 cm/s).

Given: aorta radius = 1.2 cm, aorta blood speed = 40 cm/s (Worked Example 7.3 of this unit), total area of major arteries A2 = 2.1 cm^2

Step 1: Area of the aorta, A1 = π r^2 = 3.14 × (1.2)^2 = 4.52 cm^2

Step 2: Volume flow rate from the aorta, Q = A1 v1 = 4.52 × 40 = 181 cm^3/s

Step 3: By continuity the same flow rate passes through the arteries, v2 = Q / A2 = 181 / 2.1 = 86 cm/s

Final answer: 86 cm/s (the book's printed 13.6 cm/s does not follow from the data of its own Example 7.3).

mcqs.q: Fluid dynamics deals with fluids in motion, while fluid statics deals with:
options: fluids at rest, including pressure at a depth, Pascal principle and buoyancy
mcqs.why: Fluid statics deals with fluids at rest and concerns pressure at a depth, Pascal principle and buoyancy, while fluid dynamics deals with speeds, pressures and flow rates of moving fluids.

mcqs.q: In streamline (laminar) flow:
options: the motion has eddies and whirls
every particle follows a smooth path and streamlines never cross
the flow wastes the most energy in friction
mcqs.why: In streamline flow every particle follows a smooth path, streamlines never cross, and layers slide over one another in an orderly way, as at low speeds.

mcqs.q: Turbulent flow is characterised by:
options: smooth paths with layers sliding in order
irregular disorderly motion with eddies and whirls
velocity at a point never changing
mcqs.why: Turbulent flow is irregular and disorderly, with eddies and whirls, and streamlines change from moment to moment. It sets in at high speeds or past obstacles.

mcqs.q: Steady flow means that:
options: the velocity is the same at every point
the density cannot change with location
the pressure is the same everywhere
the velocity at any given point does not vary with time
mcqs.why: In steady flow the velocity at any given point does not vary with time; every particle arriving at a fixed point has the same velocity as earlier particles, though velocity may differ from point to point.

mcqs.q: Incompressible flow means that:
options: the density cannot change with time or location
the velocity at a point cannot change with time
the pressure must be the same everywhere
the velocity must be the same everywhere
mcqs.why: Incompressible flow is defined by the density remaining constant with time and location, as is nearly true for liquids. Pressure and velocity may still vary from point to point.

mcqs.q: The Reynolds number is given by:
mcqs.why: The Reynolds number is Re = rho v L / eta, the ratio of inertial effects to viscous effects, where L is a characteristic length such as the pipe diameter. It has no units.

mcqs.q: For flow in a pipe, the flow stays laminar and orderly when the Reynolds number is:
mcqs.why: When Re is below about 2000 viscous forces dominate and the flow stays laminar. Above about 4000 inertia dominates and the flow becomes turbulent, with a transition state between.

mcqs.q: The equation of continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2 is derived from the conservation of:
mcqs.why: The equation of continuity follows from conservation of mass: the mass entering a pipe section in a given time must equal the mass leaving it, since fluid is neither created nor stored inside.

mcqs.q: For an incompressible fluid, the volume flow rate A v is:
options: greater in the larger parts of the pipe
mcqs.why: By the equation of continuity A v = constant, the volume flow rate is the same at every section. Where the pipe is narrow the speed is high and where it is wide the speed is low.

mcqs.q: If the cross-sectional area of a pipe decreases, the fluid velocity:
options: depends only on the fluid density
mcqs.why: From A1 v1 = A2 v2, a smaller area must be compensated by a larger velocity so the same volume passes each second, which is why water speeds up at the narrow nozzle of a hose.

mcqs.q: Air moving at 3.0 m/s must replenish a room of volume 300 m^3 every 15 minutes. What duct area is needed?
mcqs.why: Flow rate Q = V/t = 300/900 = 0.333 m^3/s. Area A = Q/v = 0.333/3.0 = 0.111 m^2, about 0.11 m^2, a square duct of side 0.33 m.

mcqs.q: A liquid flows at 4.20 m/s through a pipe of diameter 0.50 m. What is the flow rate in L/min?
Blood leaves the aorta (radius 1.2 cm) at 40 cm/s. If the total area of the major arteries is 2.1 cm^2, the average speed there is about:
mcqs.why: Aorta area A1 = 3.14 x (1.2)^2 = 4.52 cm^2, so Q = 4.52 x 40 = 181 cm^3/s. By continuity v2 = Q/A2 = 181/2.1 = 86 cm/s in the major arteries.

mcqs.q: Flows with the same Reynolds number behave similarly, so the Reynolds number is used for:
options: model testing of aircraft, ships and pipelines
finding terminal velocity of spheres only
mcqs.why: Because flows with the same Reynolds number behave similarly, it is used in model testing of aircraft, ships and pipelines, and to design pipelines, aircraft and ships.

mcqs.q: Why is everyday fluid flow mostly turbulent rather than laminar?
options: because speeds are always very low
because in practical situations speeds are high and passages large, so Re far exceeds about 2000
mcqs.why: In most practical situations speeds are high and passages are large, so the Reynolds number far exceeds the critical value of about 2000 and the flow becomes turbulent, as in rivers, winds and household pipes.

lessons.title: Bernoulli's Equation and Its Applications
lessons.notes_html:
Bernoulli's Principle

Bernoulli's principle states that for the steady flow of an ideal (incompressible, non-viscous) fluid, the sum of the pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume remains constant along a streamline. For horizontal flow the sum of the pressure and the energy of motion per unit volume is constant, so as the speed of a moving fluid increases, the pressure in the fluid decreases. Wind speeding up as it blows over the top of a hill therefore decreases the atmospheric pressure there.

P + (1/2) ρ v^2 + ρ g h = constant

Bernoulli's principle is associated with the law of conservation of energy in fluids: the equation is derived by applying the work-energy theorem to a flowing fluid, so it is a statement of conservation of energy per unit volume. The equation of continuity instead expresses conservation of mass, and Pascal's and Archimedes' principles belong to fluid statics.

Derivation of Bernoulli's Equation

Take an ideal fluid flowing through a pipe from point 1 (pressure P1, height h1, speed v1) to point 2 (P2, h2, v2). The pressure forces do net work (P1 - P2) times the volume V of fluid that passes. This work equals the gain in kinetic energy (1/2) ρ V (v2^2 - v1^2) plus the gain in potential energy ρ V g (h2 - h1), by the work-energy theorem. Dividing by V and rearranging gives P1 + (1/2) ρ v1^2 + ρ g h1 = P2 + (1/2) ρ v2^2 + ρ g h2, that is P + (1/2) ρ v^2 + ρ g h = constant along a streamline.

Applications of Bernoulli's Principle

  • Aeroplane wing and lift — air moves faster over the curved upper surface, so the pressure above the wing is lower than below it and the difference provides lift; airplanes also take off into the wind so that air flows over the wings faster, reaching the lift needed at a lower ground speed over a shorter runway
  • Venturi meter, carburetor and atomizer — fluid speeding through a narrow throat has reduced pressure, which is used to measure flow speed or to draw up fuel or perfume spray
  • Spin of a ball (Magnus effect) — a spinning ball drags a layer of air around with it, so on one side the air speed increases and on the other it decreases; the side with faster air has lower pressure, and this pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, curving its path, as used in cricket and football
  • Drinking straw — a straw works because atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up when the air inside is sucked out, creating a pressure difference; gravity itself is not what drives the drink upward

Worked Example 1

Water circulates throughout a house in a hot-water heating system. If the water is pumped at a speed of 0.50 m/s through a 4.0 cm diameter pipe in the basement under a pressure of 3.0 atm, what will be the flow speed and pressure in a 2.6 cm diameter pipe on the second floor 5.0 m above? Assume the pipes do not divide into branches.

Given: v1 = 0.50 m/s, d1 = 4.0 cm, d2 = 2.6 cm, P1 = 3.0 atm = 3.04 × 10^5 Pa, h = 5.0 m, ρ = 1000 kg/m^3, g = 9.8 m/s^2, 1 atm = 1.01 × 10^5 Pa

Step 1: By continuity A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = v1 (d1 / d2)^2 = 0.50 × (4.0 / 2.6)^2 = 0.50 × 2.37 = 1.18 m/s, about 1.2 m/s

Step 2: Apply Bernoulli, P2 = P1 + (1/2) ρ (v1^2 - v2^2) - ρ g h

Step 3: (1/2) ρ (v1^2 - v2^2) = 500 × (0.25 - 1.40) = -575 Pa, and ρ g h = 1000 × 9.8 × 5.0 = 49000 Pa

Step 4: P2 = 304000 - 575 - 49000 = 254425 Pa = 2.5 atm

Final answer: flow speed 1.2 m/s, pressure 2.5 atm.

Worked Example 2

What is the volume rate of flow of water from a 1.85 cm diameter faucet if the pressure head is 12 m?

Given: diameter d = 1.85 cm = 0.0185 m, pressure head h = 12 m, g = 9.8 m/s^2

Step 1: By Torricelli's theorem the speed of efflux is v = √(2 g h) = √(2 × 9.8 × 12) = √(235.2) = 15.3 m/s

Step 2: Cross-sectional area, A = π d^2 / 4 = 3.14 × (0.0185)^2 / 4 = 2.69 × 10^-4 m^2

Step 3: Volume flow rate, Q = A v = 2.69 × 10^-4 × 15.3 = 4.1 × 10^-3 m^3/s

Final answer: 4.1 × 10^-3 m^3/s (the book prints 4.6 × 10^-3 m^3/s).

Worked Example 3

The stream of water emerging from a faucet 'neck down' as it falls. The cross-sectional area is 1.2 cm^2 and 0.35 cm^2. The two levels are separated by a vertical distance of 45 mm as shown in figure. At what rate does water flow from the tap?

Given: A1 = 1.2 cm^2, A2 = 0.35 cm^2, vertical separation h = 45 mm = 4.5 cm, g = 980 cm/s^2

Step 1: By continuity the flow rate Q is the same at both levels, v1 = Q / A1 and v2 = Q / A2

Step 2: By Bernoulli (or free fall through h), v2^2 - v1^2 = 2 g h = 2 × 980 × 4.5 = 8820 cm^2/s^2

Step 3: Substitute the speeds, Q^2 (1 / A2^2 - 1 / A1^2) = 8820, so Q^2 (1 / 0.1225 - 1 / 1.44) = Q^2 (8.163 - 0.694) = 7.47 Q^2 = 8820

Step 4: Q^2 = 1181, so Q = 34 cm^3/s

Final answer: 34 cm^3/s.

Worked Example 4

Water leaves the jet of a horizontal hose at 10 m/s. If the velocity of water within the hose is 0.40 m/s, calculate the pressure within the hose. Density of water is 1000 kg/m^3 and atmospheric pressure is 100000 Pa.

Given: jet speed v1 = 10 m/s, speed inside hose v2 = 0.40 m/s, ρ = 1000 kg/m^3, atmospheric pressure = 100000 Pa, hose is horizontal so heights are equal

Step 1: Apply Bernoulli between the jet (at atmospheric pressure) and the inside of the hose, P_atm + (1/2) ρ v1^2 = P_hose + (1/2) ρ v2^2

Step 2: Rearrange, P_hose = 100000 + (1/2) × 1000 × (10^2 - 0.40^2)

Step 3: Calculate, (1/2) × 1000 × (100 - 0.16) = 500 × 99.84 = 49920 Pa

Step 4: Add, P_hose = 100000 + 49920 = 149920 Pa, about 1.5 × 10^5 Pa

Final answer: 1.5 × 10^5 Pa.

Worked Example 5

What is the maximum weight of an aircraft with a wing area of 50 m^2 flying horizontally, is the velocity of the air over the upper surface of the wing is 150 m/s and that the lower surface 140 m/s? Density of air is 1.29 kg/m^3

Given: wing area A = 50 m^2, v_upper = 150 m/s, v_lower = 140 m/s, ρ = 1.29 kg/m^3

Step 1: Pressure difference from Bernoulli, ΔP = (1/2) ρ (v_upper^2 - v_lower^2)

Step 2: Calculate the squares, 150^2 = 22500 and 140^2 = 19600, difference = 2900

Step 3: ΔP = 0.5 × 1.29 × 2900 = 1870 Pa

Step 4: Lift force = ΔP × A = 1870 × 50 = 9.35 × 10^4 N, about 9.3 × 10^4 N

Step 5: For horizontal flight the maximum weight equals the lift

Final answer: 9.3 × 10^4 N.

mcqs.q: Bernoulli equation for steady flow of an ideal fluid along a streamline is:
options: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant
mcqs.why: Bernoulli principle states that P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant along a streamline: the sum of pressure, kinetic and potential energy per unit volume remains constant.

mcqs.q: For horizontal flow, Bernoulli principle says the sum of pressure and energy of motion per unit volume is:
mcqs.why: For horizontal flow the height term is constant, so P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant along a streamline. If speed rises, pressure falls to keep the sum unchanged.

mcqs.q: As the speed of a moving fluid increases, the pressure in the fluid:
mcqs.why: From P + (1/2) rho v^2 = constant for horizontal flow, greater speed means greater kinetic energy per unit volume, so the pressure must decrease to keep the total constant.

mcqs.q: Bernoulli principle is associated with which conservation law in fluids?
mcqs.why: Bernoulli equation is derived by applying the work-energy theorem to a flowing fluid, so it is a statement of conservation of energy per unit volume. Continuity instead expresses conservation of mass.

mcqs.q: Wind speeds up as it blows over the top of a hill. The atmospheric pressure there:
mcqs.why: By Bernoulli principle, faster-moving air has lower pressure. Wind moving faster over the hilltop therefore decreases the atmospheric pressure there.

mcqs.q: Lift on an aeroplane wing arises because:
options: air moves faster over the curved upper surface, so pressure above is lower than below
air moves slower over the upper surface, giving higher pressure above
the wing pushes air upward by gravity
pressure is equal on both surfaces
mcqs.why: Air moves faster over the curved upper surface, so by Bernoulli principle the pressure above the wing is lower than below it, and the pressure difference provides lift.

mcqs.q: In a venturi meter, carburetor and atomizer, the useful effect is that fluid speeding through a narrow throat has:
options: higher pressure that pushes fuel down
reduced pressure used to measure flow speed or draw up fuel or spray
mcqs.why: Fluid speeding through a narrow throat has reduced pressure by Bernoulli principle. This is used to measure flow speed or to draw up fuel in a carburetor or perfume in an atomizer.

mcqs.q: The curving of a spinning ball (Magnus effect) happens because:
options: gravity acts sideways on a spinning ball
the ball loses mass as it spins
on the side where air speed increases the pressure is lower, pushing the ball sideways
air resistance becomes zero on one side
mcqs.why: A spinning ball drags air around with it, so air speed increases on one side and decreases on the other. The faster side has lower pressure, and the pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, as in cricket and football.

mcqs.q: A drinking straw works mainly because:
options: Bernoulli lift pulls the drink up
atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up when air inside is sucked out
mcqs.why: A straw works because atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up when the air inside is sucked out, creating a pressure difference. Gravity itself is not what drives the drink upward.

mcqs.q: Airplanes take off into the wind because:
options: the wind reduces the weight of the plane
air then flows over the wings faster, so lift is reached at lower ground speed over a shorter runway
it removes the need for lift
mcqs.why: Taking off into the wind makes air flow over the wings faster, so the lift needed is reached at a lower ground speed and over a shorter runway distance, with better control.

mcqs.q: Water pumped at 0.50 m/s through a 4.0 cm pipe reaches a 2.6 cm pipe 5.0 m above. Its flow speed there is about:
mcqs.why: By continuity v2 = v1 (d1/d2)^2 = 0.50 x (4.0/2.6)^2 = 0.50 x 2.37 = 1.18 m/s, about 1.2 m/s in the narrower upper pipe.

mcqs.q: For the same house heating system (basement pressure 3.0 atm), the pressure in the upper 2.6 cm pipe is about:
mcqs.why: Bernoulli: P2 = P1 + (1/2) rho (v1^2 - v2^2) - rho g h = 304000 - 575 - 49000 = 254425 Pa, which is about 2.5 atm.

mcqs.q: Water flows from a 1.85 cm diameter faucet with a pressure head of 12 m. The volume flow rate is about:
mcqs.why: Speed of efflux v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 12) = 15.3 m/s. Area A = pi d^2/4 = 2.69 x 10^-4 m^2. Flow rate Q = A v = 2.69 x 10^-4 x 15.3 = 4.1 x 10^-3 m^3/s.

mcqs.q: Water leaves a horizontal hose jet at 10 m/s while its speed inside the hose is 0.40 m/s. With atmospheric pressure 100000 Pa, the pressure inside the hose is about:
An aircraft has wing area 50 m^2, air speeds 150 m/s above and 140 m/s below the wing, air density 1.29 kg/m^3. Its maximum weight in horizontal flight is about:
mcqs.why: Pressure difference = (1/2) rho (150^2 - 140^2) = 0.5 x 1.29 x 2900 = 1870 Pa. Lift = 1870 x 50 = 9.35 x 10^4 N, so maximum weight is about 9.3 x 10^4 N.

lessons.title: Coulomb's Law
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Charge

Electric charge is the basic property of matter due to which it experiences electric forces. It exists in two kinds, positive and negative, with like charges repelling and unlike charges attracting. Ordinary matter is made of atoms, and each neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons, so bulk objects are normally electrically neutral. Any large imbalance creates very strong electric forces that quickly attract opposite charges from the surroundings and neutralise the excess. That is why everyday objects contain almost equal numbers of positive and negative charges and show no net charge.

Fundamental Properties of Charge

  • Conservation of charge — in any isolated system the total charge remains constant; charge can be transferred but never created or destroyed
  • Quantisation of charge — charge always occurs in whole multiples of the elementary charge
  • Additive and invariant — charges add algebraically, and charge has the same value in all frames of reference

Q = n e

Here e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C is the charge of one electron or proton. The smallest free charge an object can carry is one elementary charge, so no charge smaller than 1.6 × 10^-19 C can occur.

Coulomb's Law

Coulomb's law states that the force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them, acting along the line joining them.

F = (1 / 4πε0) q1 q2 / r^2

The constant (1 / 4πε0) is often written as k = 9 × 10^9 N m^2 C^-2. Because the force is proportional to q1 × q2, doubling both charges multiplies the product by 2 × 2 = 4, so the force becomes four times its original value at the same separation.

Equal and Opposite Forces

By Newton's third law the two charges exert equal and opposite forces on each other. The force on the first charge due to the second, F12, and the force on the second due to the first, F21, therefore have the same magnitude whatever the sizes of the charges, and the ratio of their magnitudes F12 / F21 is 1.

Effect of a Medium

In a dielectric medium the force is reduced. If the force in air is F, then in a medium of relative permittivity εr the force becomes:

F_medium = F / εr

The permittivity in the denominator of Coulomb's law increases by the factor εr. A medium with larger relative permittivity therefore weakens the force more strongly.

Worked Example 1

(a) Calculate the value of two equal charges if they repel one another with a force of 0.1 N when situated 50 cm apart in a vacuum. (b) What would be the size of the charges if they were situated in an insulating liquid whose permittivity was ten times that of a vacuum?

Step 1: Given: F = 0.1 N, r = 50 cm = 0.50 m, q1 = q2 = q, k = 9 × 10^9 N m^2 / C^2. In vacuum F = k q^2 / r^2, so q^2 = F r^2 / k

Step 2: q^2 = 0.1 × (0.50)^2 / (9 × 10^9) = 0.025 / 9 × 10^9 = 2.78 × 10^-12 C^2

Step 3: q = √(2.78 × 10^-12) = 1.7 × 10^-6 C = 1.7 μC

Step 4: In the liquid the force is reduced by εr = 10, so to keep the same force q^2 must increase 10 times, q_liquid = q × √(10) = 1.7 × 3.16 = 5.3 μC

The two equal charges are 1.7 μC each in vacuum, and 5.3 μC each in the liquid.

Worked Example 2

How far apart must two protons be if the magnitude of the electrostatic force acting on either one due to the other is equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force on a proton at Earth's surface? (mass of proton = 1.67 × 10^-27 kg, charge of proton = 1.6 × 10^-19 C)

Step 1: Given: m = 1.67 × 10^-27 kg, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, g = 9.8 m/s^2. Set electrostatic force equal to weight, k e^2 / r^2 = m g

Step 2: r^2 = k e^2 / (m g) = 9 × 10^9 × (1.6 × 10^-19)^2 / (1.67 × 10^-27 × 9.8)

Step 3: r^2 = 2.30 × 10^-28 / 1.64 × 10^-26 = 1.41 × 10^-2 m^2

Step 4: r = √(1.41 × 10^-2) = 0.119 m

The two protons must be 0.119 m apart.

mcqs.q: Electric charge exists in two kinds, positive and negative, and:
options: like charges attract and unlike charges repel
like charges repel and unlike charges attract
mcqs.why: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons, so bulk objects are normally electrically neutral.

mcqs.q: Conservation of charge means that in any isolated system:
options: total charge remains constant; charge can be transferred but never created or destroyed
charge can be created but not destroyed
charge disappears when objects are neutral
mcqs.why: By conservation of charge, the total charge in any isolated system remains constant. Charge can be transferred between objects but never created or destroyed.

mcqs.q: Charge is quantised as Q = n e, where the elementary charge e is:
mcqs.why: Quantisation means charge occurs in whole multiples of e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, the charge of one electron or proton. No free charge smaller than this can occur.

mcqs.q: Coulomb law states the force between two point charges is:
options: proportional to q1 q2 and to r^2
proportional to q1 + q2 and inversely to r
inversely proportional to q1 q2 and proportional to r^2
proportional to q1 q2 and inversely proportional to r^2, along the line joining them
mcqs.why: Coulomb law: F = (1/4 pi epsilon0) q1 q2 / r^2, directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation, acting along the line joining them.

mcqs.q: The constant k = 1/(4 pi epsilon0) in Coulomb law has the value:
mcqs.why: The Coulomb constant is written as k = 9 x 10^9 N m^2 C^-2, so the force is F = k q1 q2 / r^2 in vacuum.

mcqs.q: Two charges are placed at a fixed distance. If the magnitude of each charge is doubled, the force becomes:
options: one fourth of its original value
mcqs.why: Since F is proportional to q1 x q2, doubling both charges multiplies the product by 2 x 2 = 4, so the force becomes four times its original value at the same separation.

mcqs.q: A 2 microC charge and a 6 microC charge exert forces F12 and F21 on each other. The ratio F12/F21 is:
mcqs.why: By Newton third law the two charges exert equal and opposite forces on each other, so F12 and F21 have the same magnitude whatever the sizes of the charges, and their ratio is 1.

mcqs.q: The force between two charges in air is F. In a medium of relative permittivity epsilon_r, the force becomes:
mcqs.why: In a dielectric medium the force is reduced to F_medium = F / epsilon_r, because the permittivity in the denominator of Coulomb law increases by the factor epsilon_r.

mcqs.q: Two equal charges repel with a force of 0.1 N when 50 cm apart in vacuum. Each charge is about:
mcqs.why: From F = k q^2 / r^2, q^2 = F r^2 / k = 0.1 x (0.50)^2 / (9 x 10^9) = 2.78 x 10^-12, so q = 1.7 x 10^-6 C = 1.7 microC. In a liquid with epsilon_r = 10 the value would be 5.3 microC.

mcqs.q: How far apart must two protons be so the electrostatic force between them equals the weight of a proton (m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg)?

lessons.title: Electric Field, Field Strength and Field Lines
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Field and Field Strength

The electric field at a point is the force per unit charge at that point. Field strength, or electric field intensity, is defined by placing a small test charge q0 at the point and dividing the force on it by q0.

E = F / q0

A negative test charge can also be used to measure a field, because the ratio F / q is independent of the test charge used. The only difference is that the force on a negative charge acts opposite to the field direction, so the direction must be reversed when finding E. By convention a small positive test charge is preferred simply because the force on it points along the field.

Field of an Isolated Point Charge

To find the field of an isolated charge Q, place a small test charge q0 at distance r. By Coulomb's law the force on it is F = (1 / 4πε0) Q q0 / r^2. Dividing by q0 gives the field strength:

E = (1 / 4πε0) Q / r^2

The field is directed away from Q if Q is positive and towards Q if Q is negative.

Field Lines

Electric field lines point towards a negative charge and away from a positive charge. During fair weather the electric field due to the net charge on Earth points downward, into the Earth. This shows that the Earth's surface carries a net negative charge, balanced by positive charge in the upper atmosphere.

Motion of a Charged Particle in a Field

An electric field exerts a force F = qE only on a charged particle. The electron carries a negative charge so it is deflected in a field, while the neutron and the photon are electrically neutral and pass through undeflected. Straight line motion occurs when the electric force acts along, or opposite to, the direction of motion, so there is no sideways component to curve the path. The field then only changes the speed of the particle, accelerating it if the force is along the motion and slowing it if it is against it. If the velocity had a component perpendicular to the field, the path would bend into a parabola.

Worked Example 1

An electron of charge 1.6 × 10^-19 C is situated in a uniform electric field of intensity 1200 volt cm^-1. Find the force on it, its acceleration, and the time it takes to travel 2 cm from rest (electronic mass, m_e = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg).

Step 1: Given: q = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, E = 1200 V/cm = 1200 × 100 = 1.2 × 10^5 V/m, s = 2 cm = 0.02 m. Force F = qE = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 1.2 × 10^5 = 1.92 × 10^-14 N

Step 2: Acceleration a = F / m = 1.92 × 10^-14 / 9.1 × 10^-31 = 2.12 × 10^16 m/s^2

Step 3: From s = (1/2) a t^2, t = √(2s / a) = √(2 × 0.02 / 2.12 × 10^16)

Step 4: t = √(1.89 × 10^-18) = 1.37 × 10^-9 s

The force is 1.92 × 10^-14 N, the acceleration is 2.12 × 10^16 m/s^2, and the time is 1.37 × 10^-9 s.

Worked Example 2

An alpha particle (the nucleus of a helium atom) has a mass of 6.64 × 10^-27 kg and a charge of 2e. What are the (a) magnitude and (b) direction of the electric field that will balance the gravitational force on the particle?

Step 1: Given: m = 6.64 × 10^-27 kg, q = 2e = 2 × 1.6 × 10^-19 = 3.2 × 10^-19 C, g = 9.8 m/s^2. For balance the electric force must equal the weight, qE = m g

Step 2: E = m g / q = 6.64 × 10^-27 × 9.8 / 3.2 × 10^-19

Step 3: E = 6.51 × 10^-26 / 3.2 × 10^-19 = 2.03 × 10^-7 N/C

Step 4: The alpha particle is positively charged, so the field must push it upward against gravity

The field magnitude is 2.03 × 10^-7 N/C, and the electric field is directed upwards.

Worked Example 3

A proton and an electron form two corners of an equilateral triangle of side length 2.0 × 10^-6 m. What is the magnitude of the net electric field these two particles produce at the third corner?

Step 1: Given: r = 2.0 × 10^-6 m, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C for both particles. Field of each particle at the third corner, E = k e / r^2 = 9 × 10^9 × 1.6 × 10^-19 / (2.0 × 10^-6)^2 = 3.6 × 10^2 N/C

Step 2: The proton's field points away from the proton and the electron's field points towards the electron, and in the equilateral geometry their components perpendicular to the base cancel

Step 3: The components along the base add, giving E_net = 2 × E × cos 60° = 2 × 360 × 0.5 = 360 N/C

The magnitude of the net electric field is 3.6 × 10^2 N/C.

Worked Example 4

Two charged particles lie on an x-axis: -q = -3.20 × 10^-19 C at x = -3.00 m and q = 3.20 × 10^-19 C at x = 3.00 m. What are the (a) magnitude and (b) direction (relative to the positive direction of the x-axis) of the net electric field produced at point P at y = 4.00 m?

Step 1: Given: q = 3.20 × 10^-19 C, charges at x = -3.00 m and x = +3.00 m, P at y = 4.00 m. Distance of each charge from P, r = √(3^2 + 4^2) = 5.00 m

Step 2: Field of each charge, E = k q / r^2 = 9 × 10^9 × 3.20 × 10^-19 / 25 = 1.15 × 10^-10 N/C

Step 3: The y-components of the two fields cancel by symmetry, while the x-components both point in the -x direction and add: E_net = 2 × E × (3/5) = 2 × 1.15 × 10^-10 × 0.6

Step 4: E_net = 1.38 × 10^-10 N/C

The magnitude is 1.38 × 10^-10 N/C, and the net electric field points in the -x direction.

Worked Example 5

A proton and an electron form two corners of an equilateral triangle of side length 5 μm. What is the magnitude of the net electric field these two particles produce at the third corner?

Step 1: Given: r = 5 μm = 5 × 10^-6 m, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C. Field of each particle, E = k e / r^2 = 9 × 10^9 × 1.6 × 10^-19 / (5 × 10^-6)^2 = 57.6 N/C

Step 2: As in the equilateral triangle geometry, the perpendicular components cancel and the components along the base add

Step 3: E_net = 2 × E × cos 60° = 2 × 57.6 × 0.5 = 57.6 N/C

The magnitude of the net electric field is 57.6 N/C (about 5.8 × 10^1 N/C).

mcqs.q: Electric field strength at a point is defined as:
options: E = F / q0, the force per unit charge at that point
mcqs.why: Field strength is defined by placing a small test charge q0 at the point and dividing the force on it by q0: E = F / q0, the force per unit charge.

mcqs.q: Can a negative test charge be used to measure an electric field?
options: No, only a positive charge gives a field
Yes, because F/q is independent of the test charge; only the force direction is opposite to E
Yes, but the field value doubles
No, a negative charge destroys the field
mcqs.why: A negative test charge can be used because the ratio F/q is independent of the test charge. The force on a negative charge acts opposite to the field direction, so the direction must be reversed when finding E.

mcqs.q: The field strength due to an isolated point charge Q at distance r is:
options: E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q q0 / r^2
mcqs.why: Dividing the Coulomb force F = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q q0 / r^2 by q0 gives E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q / r^2, directed away from Q if Q is positive and towards Q if Q is negative.

mcqs.q: Electric field lines point:
options: away from a negative charge and towards a positive charge
towards a negative charge and away from a positive charge
from negative to positive inside the charge only
mcqs.why: Electric field lines point away from a positive charge and towards a negative charge, following the direction of the force on a small positive test charge.

mcqs.q: In fair weather the electric field due to the net charge on Earth points downward. This shows Earth surface is:
options: charged only in the upper atmosphere
mcqs.why: Field lines point towards a negative charge, so a downward field into the Earth shows the Earth surface carries a net negative charge, balanced by positive charge in the upper atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Which particle can be deflected while moving in an electric field?
mcqs.why: An electric field exerts F = qE only on a charged particle. The electron carries a negative charge so it is deflected, while the neutron and photon are neutral and pass through undeflected.

mcqs.q: A charged particle moves in a straight line in an electric field when:
options: the electric force acts along or opposite to the direction of motion
the velocity is perpendicular to the field
mcqs.why: Straight line motion occurs when the electric force acts along or opposite to the motion, so there is no sideways component to curve the path; the field then only changes the speed.

mcqs.q: The force on a charge q placed in an electric field E is:
mcqs.why: From the definition E = F/q, the force on a charged particle in a field is F = qE. This is the force that deflects electrons and other charged particles.

mcqs.q: An electron (q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C) is in a uniform field of 1200 V/cm. The force on it is:
mcqs.why: Convert E = 1200 V/cm = 1.2 x 10^5 V/m. Force F = qE = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 1.2 x 10^5 = 1.92 x 10^-14 N on the electron.

mcqs.q: For the same electron (mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg), its acceleration in that field is:
mcqs.why: Acceleration a = F/m = 1.92 x 10^-14 / 9.1 x 10^-31 = 2.12 x 10^16 m/s^2, using the force F = qE found from the field of 1.2 x 10^5 V/m.

mcqs.q: Starting from rest, the time for that electron to travel 2 cm in the field is about:
An alpha particle (m = 6.64 x 10^-27 kg, q = 2e) is balanced against gravity by an electric field of:
mcqs.why: For balance qE = m g, so E = m g/q = 6.64 x 10^-27 x 9.8 / 3.2 x 10^-19 = 2.03 x 10^-7 N/C. The particle is positive, so the field must push it upward against gravity.

mcqs.q: A proton and an electron sit at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side 2.0 x 10^-6 m. The net field at the third corner is:
mcqs.why: Each field is E = k e / r^2 = 9 x 10^9 x 1.6 x 10^-19 / (2.0 x 10^-6)^2 = 360 N/C. Perpendicular components cancel and base components add: E_net = 2 x 360 x cos 60 = 360 N/C.

mcqs.q: Charges -3.20 x 10^-19 C at x = -3.00 m and +3.20 x 10^-19 C at x = +3.00 m give a net field at P (y = 4.00 m) of:
mcqs.why: Distance r = sqrt(3^2+4^2) = 5.00 m, each E = k q/r^2 = 1.15 x 10^-10 N/C. Y-components cancel and x-components add: E_net = 2 x 1.15 x 10^-10 x (3/5) = 1.38 x 10^-10 N/C in the -x direction.

mcqs.q: A proton and an electron at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side 5 micrometres give a net field at the third corner of:
mcqs.why: Each field is E = k e / r^2 = 9 x 10^9 x 1.6 x 10^-19 / (5 x 10^-6)^2 = 57.6 N/C. As in the equilateral geometry, E_net = 2 x 57.6 x cos 60 = 57.6 N/C.

lessons.title: Electric Dipole and Electric Flux
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Dipole

An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges, +q and -q, separated by a small distance d. In another common form the two charges are separated by a small distance 2a. The dipole moment measures the strength of the dipole and decides the field it produces and the torque it experiences in an external field.

p = q d

The dipole moment is a vector directed from the negative charge to the positive charge along the line joining them. For a separation 2a the moment is written p = q × 2a.

Field of a Dipole on its Axial Line

For a point P on the axis at distance r from the centre of a dipole with half-separation a, the field due to +q is (1 / 4πε0) q / (r - a)^2 away from the dipole, and the field due to -q is (1 / 4πε0) q / (r + a)^2 towards it. Subtracting gives:

E = (1 / 4πε0) × (2 p r) / (r^2 - a^2)^2

For r much greater than a this reduces to the simpler far-field form, along the direction of p:

E = (1 / 4πε0) × 2p / r^3

Electric Flux

Electric flux is a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through a given area. For a uniform field it is defined by:

φ = E A cos θ

Here θ is the angle between E and the normal to the surface, and the unit of flux is N m^2 / C. The flux is maximum when the normal is along E, which means the surface itself is perpendicular to the field lines, so the greatest number of lines pass through it. When the surface is parallel to E, no lines pass through it and the flux is zero. With φ = φ_max cos θ, cos 60° = 0.5, so at 60° the flux falls to exactly one half of its maximum value.

Gauss's Law and Closed Surfaces

The great significance of flux is Gauss's law: the total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε0, whatever the shape of the surface.

φ = Q_enclosed / ε0

By Gauss's law the total flux through a closed surface depends only on the net charge inside the surface. Enlarging the surface spreads the same field lines over a larger area while the field itself becomes weaker, and the two effects cancel exactly. Changing the shape has the same result, because every field line from the enclosed charge still crosses the surface once. This lets us calculate fields of symmetric charge distributions very easily, and in this way flux connects the field spread out in space directly to the charges that produce it.

Worked Example 1

The square surface shown in figure measures 3.2 mm on each side. It is immersed in a uniform electric field with magnitude E = 1800 N/C and with field lines at an angle of θ = 35° with a normal to the surface, as shown. Take that normal to be directed "outward," as though the surface were one face of a box. Calculate the electric flux through the surface.

Step 1: Given: side = 3.2 mm = 3.2 × 10^-3 m, E = 1800 N/C, field lines enter the face so the angle between E and the outward normal is 180° - 35° = 145°. Area A = (3.2 × 10^-3)^2 = 1.024 × 10^-5 m^2

Step 2: Flux φ = E A cos θ = 1800 × 1.024 × 10^-5 × cos 145°

Step 3: φ = 1.843 × 10^-2 × (-0.819) = -1.5 × 10^-2 N m^2 / C

The flux is -1.5 × 10^-2 N m^2 / C, the negative sign showing net flux enters the surface.

mcqs.q: An electric dipole consists of:
options: two equal positive charges far apart
a pair of equal and opposite charges +q and -q separated by a small distance
mcqs.why: An electric dipole is a pair of equal and opposite charges, +q and -q, separated by a small distance d (also written as separation 2a).

mcqs.q: The electric dipole moment is p = q d, and as a vector it is directed:
options: from the positive charge to the negative charge
perpendicular to the line joining the charges
from the negative charge to the positive charge
opposite to the axial field always
mcqs.why: The dipole moment p = q d measures the strength of the dipole and is a vector directed from the negative charge to the positive charge along the line joining them.

mcqs.q: If the two charges of a dipole are separated by a distance 2a, the dipole moment is written as:
mcqs.why: For a separation written as 2a, the dipole moment is p = q x 2a, the product of one charge and the full separation between the charges.

mcqs.q: For a point far from a dipole on its axial line (r much greater than a), the field is:
options: E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) x 2p / r^3, along the direction of p
E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) x p / r^2
E = zero at all far points
mcqs.why: The exact axial field E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) x (2 p r)/(r^2 - a^2)^2 reduces for r much greater than a to E = (1/4 pi epsilon0) x 2p / r^3, along the direction of p.

mcqs.q: Electric flux through a surface in a uniform field is defined by:
options: phi = E A cos theta, where theta is the angle between E and the normal
phi = Q / epsilon0 for any open surface
mcqs.why: Electric flux is phi = E A cos theta, a measure of the number of field lines passing through the area, where theta is the angle between E and the normal to the surface. Its unit is N m^2 / C.

mcqs.q: The flux through a flat surface in a uniform field E is maximum when the surface is:
options: perpendicular to E, so its normal is along E
mcqs.why: Flux phi = E A cos theta is maximum when the normal is along E, which means the surface itself is perpendicular to the field lines, so the greatest number of lines pass through it. When the surface is parallel to E the flux is zero.

mcqs.q: The electric flux through a plane area is half its maximum value when the area is held at an angle of:
mcqs.why: With phi = phi_max cos theta, cos 60 degrees = 0.5, so at 60 degrees the flux falls to exactly one half of its maximum value.

mcqs.q: Gauss law states that the total flux through any closed surface equals:
options: the enclosed charge multiplied by epsilon0
the surface area times the field only
the enclosed charge divided by epsilon0
mcqs.why: Gauss law: phi = Q_enclosed / epsilon0. The total flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by epsilon0, whatever the shape of the surface.

mcqs.q: The flux through a closed surface is independent of the size or shape of the surface because:
options: the field is zero outside the surface
it depends only on the net charge inside; enlarging spreads the same lines over a larger area while the field weakens, and the effects cancel
flux is defined only for spheres
mcqs.why: By Gauss law the flux depends only on the net charge inside. Enlarging the surface spreads the same field lines over a larger area while the field becomes weaker, and the two effects cancel exactly; changing shape has the same result.

mcqs.q: A square surface of side 3.2 mm sits in a field E = 1800 N/C with lines entering at 145 degrees to the outward normal. The flux is about:
mcqs.why: Area A = (3.2 x 10^-3)^2 = 1.024 x 10^-5 m^2. Flux phi = E A cos theta = 1800 x 1.024 x 10^-5 x cos 145 = 1.843 x 10^-2 x (-0.819) = -1.5 x 10^-2 N m^2 / C, negative because net flux enters.

lessons.title: Electric Potential, Potential Difference and the Electron Volt
lessons.notes_html:
Electric Potential

Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point, measured in volts.

V = W / q0

Potential Due to an Isolated Point Charge

For a point charge Q, the field at distance r is E = (1 / 4πε0) Q / r^2, and the work in moving q0 from infinity to r against this field is W = (1 / 4πε0) Q q0 / r. Dividing by q0 gives:

V = (1 / 4πε0) Q / r

The potential is a scalar, positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge, and it falls as 1 / r.

Potential Difference

Potential difference is work done per unit charge:

V = W / q

For example, if 12 J of work is done against an existing electric field to take a charge of 0.01 C from one point A to another point B, the potential difference between B and A is V = W / q = 12 / 0.01 = 1200 V. Point B is at a potential 1200 V higher than point A for this positive charge.

Field as the Negative Gradient of Potential

The field and potential are related by:

E = - dV / dr

The electric field intensity is therefore the negative rate of change of potential with distance — the negative gradient of the potential. The field points in the direction of decreasing potential.

The Electron Volt

The electron volt is an energy unit suited to single particles: 1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J. The kinetic energy of a particle can be found in joules first and then converted by dividing by 1.6 × 10^-19.

Worked Example 1

An electron has a speed of 10^6 m/s. Find its energy in electron volt.

Step 1: Given: v = 10^6 m/s, mass of electron m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10^-19 J. Kinetic energy KE = (1/2) m v^2 = 0.5 × 9.1 × 10^-31 × (10^6)^2

Step 2: KE = 0.5 × 9.1 × 10^-31 × 10^12 = 4.55 × 10^-19 J

Step 3: Convert to electron volts, KE = 4.55 × 10^-19 / 1.6 × 10^-19 = 2.84 eV

The energy of the electron is 2.84 eV.

Worked Example 2

An electron is liberated from the lower of two large parallel metal plates separated by a distance h = 2 cm. The upper plate has a potential of 2400 volts relative to the lower. How long does the electron take to reach it?

Step 1: Given: h = 2 cm = 0.02 m, V = 2400 V, e = 1.6 × 10^-19 C, m = 9.1 × 10^-31 kg. Field between the plates E = V / h = 2400 / 0.02 = 1.2 × 10^5 V/m

Step 2: Acceleration a = eE / m = 1.6 × 10^-19 × 1.2 × 10^5 / 9.1 × 10^-31 = 2.1 × 10^16 m/s^2

Step 3: From h = (1/2) a t^2, t = √(2h / a) = √(2 × 0.02 / 2.1 × 10^16)

Step 4: t = √(1.9 × 10^-18) = 1.4 × 10^-9 s

The electron takes about 1.4 × 10^-9 s to reach the upper plate (field between plates is 1.2 × 10^5 V/m).

Worked Example 3

Two large parallel metal plates are 1.5 cm apart and have charges of equal magnitudes but opposite signs on their facing surfaces. Take the potential of the negative plate to be zero. If the potential halfway between the plates is then 5.0 V, what is the electric field in the region between the plates?

Step 1: Given: separation d = 1.5 cm = 0.015 m, potential at halfway point = 5.0 V, negative plate at 0 V. The field between large parallel plates is uniform, so potential increases linearly from the negative plate

Step 2: Halfway potential is half the total potential difference, so total V = 2 × 5.0 = 10 V

Step 3: E = V / d = 10 / 0.015 = 6.7 × 10^2 V/m

The electric field is 6.7 × 10^2 V/m, directed from the positive plate to the negative plate.

mcqs.q: Electric potential at a point is defined as:
options: the force per unit charge at the point
the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to that point
the charge multiplied by the field
the negative gradient of the field
mcqs.why: Electric potential is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a test charge from infinity to the point: V = W / q0, measured in volts.

mcqs.q: The potential due to an isolated point charge Q at distance r is:
options: V = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q q0 / r
V = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q / r, a scalar falling as 1/r
mcqs.why: Dividing the work W = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q q0 / r by q0 gives V = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q / r. Potential is a scalar and falls as 1/r, unlike the field which falls as 1/r^2.

mcqs.q: The potential due to a point charge is positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge because potential is:
options: a scalar whose sign follows the sign of Q
mcqs.why: From V = (1/4 pi epsilon0) Q / r, potential is a scalar whose sign is the sign of Q: positive for a positive charge and negative for a negative charge.

mcqs.q: 12 J of work is done to take a charge of 0.01 C from point A to point B. The potential difference between B and A is:
mcqs.why: Potential difference is work done per unit charge: V = W/q = 12 / 0.01 = 1200 V, so point B is at a potential 1200 V higher than point A for this positive charge.

mcqs.q: The electric field is the negative gradient of the potential, E = -dV/dr, which means the field points in the direction of:
mcqs.why: Since E = -dV/dr, electric field intensity is the negative rate of change of potential with distance, so the field points in the direction of decreasing potential.

mcqs.q: One electron volt (1 eV) is equal to:
mcqs.why: The electron volt is an energy unit suited to single particles: 1 eV = 1.6 x 10^-19 J. Energy in joules is converted to eV by dividing by 1.6 x 10^-19.

mcqs.q: An electron moving at 10^6 m/s (mass 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) has kinetic energy of about:
An electron is released from the lower of two plates 2 cm apart, the upper plate being 2400 V above the lower. The field between the plates is:
mcqs.why: For parallel plates E = V/h = 2400 / 0.02 = 1.2 x 10^5 V/m. This field gives the electron its acceleration towards the upper plate.

mcqs.q: For the same plates, the time taken by the electron to reach the upper plate is about:
Two parallel plates 1.5 cm apart have the negative plate at zero potential and 5.0 V halfway between them. The field between the plates is:
mcqs.why: The field is uniform so potential rises linearly; halfway 5.0 V means total V = 10 V. Then E = V/d = 10 / 0.015 = 6.7 x 10^2 V/m, directed from the positive plate to the negative plate.

lessons.title: Capacitance and the Parallel Plate Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
Capacitance

Capacitance is charge per unit voltage:

C = Q / V

For example, a capacitor which has a voltage of 4 V and has 16 C of charge has capacitance C = Q / V = 16 / 4 = 4 F. A larger charge stored at the same voltage would mean a larger capacitance.

The Parallel Plate Capacitor

The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is:

C = ε0 εr A / d

It increases with the area A of overlap of the plates and with the relative permittivity εr of the dielectric between them. It decreases as the separation d between the plates increases. Capacitance increases in direct proportion to the overlapping area, because a larger area can hold more charge at the same voltage. It increases when a dielectric of high relative permittivity is inserted, since the dielectric polarises and reduces the effective field for the same charge. It decreases in inverse proportion to the plate separation, because a wider gap gives a smaller field and less induced charge on the opposite plate. It does not depend on the charge stored, the voltage applied, or the thickness and material of the metal plates themselves. Plate thickness in particular has no effect, because it does not appear in the formula.

FactorEffect on Capacitance
Plate area A increasesCapacitance increases
Plate separation d increasesCapacitance decreases
Relative permittivity εr increasesCapacitance increases
Plate thickness changesNo effect

Dielectric Constant (Relative Permittivity)

The dielectric constant, or relative permittivity εr, is the ratio of the capacitance with the dielectric filling the space between the plates to the capacitance with vacuum (or air) in the same space:

εr = C / C0

It tells how many times the material increases the capacitance. A good dielectric should have a high dielectric strength so it can withstand a large voltage without breaking down, and a high relative permittivity so a large capacitance is obtained in a small size; low leakage and low energy loss are also desirable.

Variable Capacitor

In an air variable capacitor one set of plates rotates inside another fixed set. Capacitance can be varied by turning the rotatable plates in or out. Turning them changes the overlapping area A, and since C is proportional to A, the capacitance changes smoothly.

Worked Example 1

A capacitor gets a charge of 50 C when it is connected to a battery of emf 5 V. Calculate the capacity of the capacitor.

Step 1: Given: Q = 50 C, V = 5 V. Capacitance is defined by C = Q / V

Step 2: C = 50 / 5 = 10

The capacity of the capacitor is 10 F.

Worked Example 2

The capacitance of air-filled parallel-plate capacitor is 1.3 pF. If the separation of the plates is doubled and wax is inserted between them, the new capacitance is 2.6 pF. Find the dielectric constant of the wax.

Step 1: Given: C0 = 1.3 pF, separation doubled, C_new = 2.6 pF. Doubling the separation alone would halve the capacitance to C0 / 2, and inserting wax multiplies it by εr, so C_new = εr × C0 / 2

Step 2: εr = 2 × C_new / C0 = 2 × 2.6 / 1.3

Step 3: εr = 4.0

The dielectric constant of wax is 4.0.

mcqs.why: Capacitance is charge per unit voltage, C = Q / V, so a larger charge stored at the same voltage means a larger capacitance.

mcqs.why: C = Q / V. Substituting Q = 50 C and V = 5 V gives C = 50 / 5 = 10 F, so the capacity of the capacitor is 10 F.

mcqs.why: Capacitance varies inversely with plate separation d in C = epsilon_0 epsilon_r A / d, so doubling d halves the capacitance.

mcqs.why: Epsilon_r = C / C_0, the ratio of capacitance with the dielectric filling the space to the capacitance with vacuum or air in the same space.

mcqs.q: An air-filled capacitor has capacitance 1.3 pF. The plate separation is doubled and wax is inserted, giving 2.6 pF. The dielectric constant of wax is:
mcqs.why: Doubling separation halves C and wax multiplies by epsilon_r, so C_new = epsilon_r x C_0 / 2. Hence epsilon_r = 2 x 2.6 / 1.3 = 4.0.

lessons.title: Capacitors in Series and Parallel
lessons.notes_html:
Capacitors in Series

In series the same charge Q sits on each capacitor, and the voltages add: V = V1 + V2 = Q / C1 + Q / C2. This leads to:

1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2

For two capacitors this gives C = C1 C2 / (C1 + C2), always smaller than either capacitor. For more capacitors in series, 1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2 + 1 / C3 + ..., so the combined capacitance is less than the smallest individual capacitance. Series connection therefore reduces capacitance.

Capacitors in Parallel

In parallel both capacitors have the same voltage V and the charges add: Q = Q1 + Q2 = C1 V + C2 V. This gives:

C = C1 + C2

For more capacitors in parallel, C = C1 + C2 + C3 + .... Parallel connection therefore increases capacitance. As a check, 10 μF and 15 μF give 6 μF in series and 25 μF in parallel.

SeriesParallel
Same charge Q on each capacitorSame voltage V across each capacitor
Voltages addCharges add
1 / C = 1 / C1 + 1 / C2 + ...C = C1 + C2 + ...
Combined capacitance decreasesCombined capacitance increases

Worked Example 1

Three capacitors have capacitances 10, 50 and 25 μF respectively. Calculate (i) charge on each when connected in parallel to a 250 V supply (ii) total capacitance and (iii) potential difference across each when connected in series.

Step 1: Given: C1 = 10 μF, C2 = 50 μF, C3 = 25 μF, V = 250 V. In parallel each capacitor has 250 V, so Q1 = C1 V = 10 × 10^-6 × 250 = 2.5 mC, Q2 = 50 × 10^-6 × 250 = 12.5 mC, Q3 = 25 × 10^-6 × 250 = 6.25 mC

Step 2: Total parallel capacitance C = 10 + 50 + 25 = 85 μF

Step 3: In series, 1 / Cs = 1/10 + 1/50 + 1/25 = 0.16, so Cs = 6.25 μF and the common charge is Q = Cs V = 6.25 × 10^-6 × 250 = 1.5625 mC

Step 4: Voltages in series: V1 = Q / C1 = 156.25 V, V2 = Q / C2 = 31.25 V, V3 = Q / C3 = 62.5 V, which add to 250 V

The charges in parallel are 2.5 mC, 12.5 mC and 6.25 mC; the total capacitance is 85 μF in parallel (6.25 μF in series); the potential differences in series are 156.25 V, 31.25 V and 62.5 V.

Worked Example 2

Three capacitors are connected through a potential difference of 100 volts (C1 = 2 μF in series with the parallel combination of C2 = 3 μF and C3 = 5 μF). Find the charges and potential difference across each capacitor.

Step 1: Given: C1 = 2 μF, C2 = 3 μF, C3 = 5 μF, total V = 100 V. C2 and C3 in parallel give C23 = 3 + 5 = 8 μF

Step 2: C23 in series with C1 gives 1 / C = 1/2 + 1/8 = 0.625, so C = 1.6 μF

Step 3: Charge on C1 equals the total charge, Q1 = C V = 1.6 × 100 = 160 μC, so V1 = Q1 / C1 = 160 / 2 = 80 V

Step 4: Voltage across the parallel pair V23 = 100 - 80 = 20 V, so Q2 = 3 × 20 = 60 μC and Q3 = 5 × 20 = 100 μC

The charges are Q1 = 160 μC, Q2 = 60 μC and Q3 = 100 μC, with V1 = 80 V and V2 = V3 = 20 V.

mcqs.why: In parallel C = C1 + C2 + C3 = 10 + 50 + 25 = 85 microF. The charges at 250 V would be 2.5 mC, 12.5 mC and 6.25 mC.

mcqs.why: In series 1 / Cs = 1/10 + 1/50 + 1/25 = 0.16, so Cs = 1 / 0.16 = 6.25 microF, less than the smallest capacitor in the group.

lessons.title: Charging, Discharging and Energy Stored in a Capacitor
lessons.notes_html:
Energy Stored in a Capacitor

While charging, work must be done against the repulsion of the charge already on the plates. Suppose the capacitor is charged step by step; when its charge is q, its potential difference is v = q / C, and adding a small charge dq needs work dW = v dq = q dq / C. Integrating from q = 0 to the final charge Q gives total work W = Q^2 / (2C), and this work is stored as potential energy in the field. Substituting Q = C V gives:

E = (1/2) C V^2

The stored energy can also be written as E = (1/2) Q V, and as E = Q^2 / (2C). The energy resides in the electric field between the plates until the capacitor discharges. Because energy is proportional to the square of the charge, doubling the total charge quadruples the stored energy, provided the capacitance stays the same.

Charging and Discharging: The Time Constant

The charging of a capacitor through a resistance follows an exponential law. During charging the charge grows as:

q = Q0 (1 - exp(-t / RC))

This happens because the charging current falls as the capacitor voltage rises towards the supply voltage. The growth is therefore exponential, not linear. The time constant of the circuit is:

τ = R C

The time constant has the unit of time and sets the speed of charging and discharging. A larger resistance or a larger capacitance makes the circuit respond more slowly. For example, a 100 μF capacitor in series with a 100 ohm resistor has τ = RC = 100 × 100 × 10^-6 = 10^4 × 10^-6 = 0.01 s. In one time constant the charge on the capacitor rises to about 63 percent of its final value.

Capacitor Blocks Direct Current

Once a capacitor is charged to the supply voltage, no steady direct current can flow through its insulating dielectric, so a capacitor blocks DC. Alternating current appears to pass because the capacitor repeatedly charges and discharges on each half cycle.

Uses in Power Supply Systems

Capacitors are used in electric power supply systems to improve power factor. Capacitor banks supply reactive power locally, bringing the current and voltage more nearly in phase. This improves the power factor of the supply system, which also reduces losses, but power factor improvement is their primary purpose in power systems.

Worked Example 1

Capacitor is charged through a large non-reactive resistance by a battery of constant voltage V. For this arrangement, if the capacitor has a capacitance of 10 μF and the resistance is 1 M ohm, calculate the time taken for the capacitor to receive 90% of its final charge.

Step 1: Given: C = 10 μF = 10 × 10^-6 F, R = 1 M ohm = 10^6 ohm, q = 0.90 Q0. Time constant τ = RC = 10^6 × 10 × 10^-6 = 10 s

Step 2: Charging follows q = Q0 (1 - exp(-t / τ)), so 0.90 = 1 - exp(-t / 10) and exp(-t / 10) = 0.10

Step 3: -t / 10 = ln 0.10 = -2.303, so t = 10 × 2.303 = 23.03 s

The time taken is about 23 s.

Worked Example 2

What capacitance is required to store energy of 10 kWh at a potential difference of 1000 V?

Step 1: Given: E = 10 kWh = 10 × 3.6 × 10^6 = 3.6 × 10^7 J, V = 1000 V. Stored energy E = (1/2) C V^2, so C = 2E / V^2

Step 2: C = 2 × 3.6 × 10^7 / (1000)^2 = 7.2 × 10^7 / 10^6

Step 3: C = 72 F

The required capacitance is 72 F.

Worked Example 3

A 2.0 μF capacitor and a 4.0 μF capacitor are connected in parallel across a 300 V potential difference. Calculate the total energy stored in the capacitors.

Step 1: Given: C1 = 2.0 μF, C2 = 4.0 μF, V = 300 V. Parallel combination C = 2.0 + 4.0 = 6.0 μF

Step 2: Total energy E = (1/2) C V^2 = 0.5 × 6.0 × 10^-6 × (300)^2

Step 3: E = 0.5 × 6.0 × 10^-6 × 9 × 10^4 = 0.27 J

The total energy stored is 0.27 J.

Worked Example 4

A 12.0-V battery is connected to a capacitor, resulting in 54.0 μC of charge stored on the capacitor. How much energy is stored in the capacitor?

Step 1: Given: V = 12.0 V, Q = 54.0 μC = 54.0 × 10^-6 C. Stored energy E = (1/2) Q V

Step 2: E = 0.5 × 54.0 × 10^-6 × 12.0 = 3.24 × 10^-4 J

The energy stored in the capacitor is 3.24 × 10^-4 J.

mcqs.why: During charging q = Q0 (1 - exp(-t / RC)), because the charging current falls as the capacitor voltage rises towards the supply voltage.
