lessons.title: Resistance, Resistivity and the Colour Code
lessons.notes_html:
Ohm's Law as a Straight Line

Ohm's law states V = I R, so for a fixed resistance the graph of V against I is a straight line through the origin. The slope of this line gives the resistance R. The graphical representation of Ohm's law is therefore a straight line, not a parabola, hyperbola or ellipse.

V = I R

Resistance and Conductance

  • Resistance — the opposition a conductor offers to current
  • Conductance — the reciprocal of resistance, G = 1 / R; it measures how easily a conductor allows current to pass, and its unit is the siemens. A small resistance therefore means a large conductance
  • Superconductor — below its critical temperature a superconductor loses all electrical resistance, so current can flow through it without any loss of energy; its resistivity also falls to zero in the superconducting state, so its resistance is zero

Resistivity

Resistivity ρ is the resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross-sectional area, with unit ohm m; it depends only on the material and its temperature.

R = ρ L / A

Resistivity is a property of the material and temperature only, not of the size or shape of the piece. If a wire of uniform area of cross-section A, length L and resistance R is cut into two parts, the resistance of each part is halved, but the resistivity of each part remains the same. For the same reason, if copper and aluminium wires of the same length have the same resistance, the aluminium wire has the larger diameter: for the same R and L a material of larger resistivity needs a larger cross-sectional area A. Aluminium has a higher resistivity than copper (about 2.8 × 10^-8 ohm m against 1.7 × 10^-8 ohm m), so the aluminium wire must be thicker to keep the same resistance.

Dependence of Resistivity on Temperature

For metals, resistivity increases almost linearly with temperature:

ρ_t = ρ_0 (1 + α θ)

This happens because hotter ions vibrate more and scatter the electrons more often. For semiconductors and insulators resistivity decreases with temperature, since heating frees many more charge carriers.

Drift Velocity

When a potential difference is applied across the ends of a wire, the drift velocity of free electrons is proportional to the electric field in the wire. Doubling the potential difference doubles the field for the same length, so the average drift speed of the electrons doubles, and the current also doubles.

Power Dissipation in a Resistor

Electrical power is P = V I, and using Ohm's law V = I R this becomes the Joule heating formula:

P = I^2 R

The other forms P = V^2 / R and P = V × I are also correct forms of power, but I^2 R is the direct expression for power dissipated in a resistor in terms of its own current and resistance.

The Colour Code

The source exercises for this unit do not give the colour bands or their values for the resistor colour code, so no band values are stated here. The resistance ideas needed with the colour code are covered in this lesson: resistance is measured in ohms, conductance is its reciprocal, and the resistance of a uniform wire follows R = ρ L / A.

Worked Example 1

A negligibly small current is passed through a wire of length 12 m and uniform cross-section 4.0 × 10^-7 m^2, and its resistance is measured to be 6.0 ohm. What is the resistivity of the material at the temperature of the experiment?

Step 1: Given: L = 12 m, A = 4.0 × 10^-7 m^2, R = 6.0 ohm. R = ρ L / A, so ρ = R A / L

Step 2: ρ = 6.0 × 4.0 × 10^-7 / 12

Step 3: ρ = 24 × 10^-7 / 12 = 2 × 10^-7 ohm m

The resistivity of the material is 2 × 10^-7 ohm m.

lessons.title: E.M.F., Internal Resistance and Maximum Power Transfer
lessons.notes_html:
E.M.F. and Internal Resistance

Every real source, such as a cell or battery, has materials inside it that oppose the flow of charge. This opposition is its internal resistance r, offered by the source of emf itself. Emf is the total energy supplied by a source per unit charge, E = W / Q, including the energy used against the internal resistance of the source. Potential difference is the energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit, for example across a resistor, V = W / Q for that part of the circuit. Emf is a property of the source and exists even on open circuit, while potential difference appears across components when the circuit is working; for a source supplying current the terminal pd is less than its emf.

Terminal Voltage

The cell has internal resistance r, so when current I flows, a voltage I r is dropped inside the cell itself. The terminal voltage available to the external circuit is therefore:

V = E - I r

This is why the terminal voltage of a cell is less than its emf. On open circuit no current flows, I r becomes zero, and the terminal voltage then equals the emf. For the same reason, the terminal potential of a battery decreases when the current drawn from it is increased: as I increases, the voltage lost inside the battery, I r, increases in proportion, a larger share of the emf is used up inside the battery itself, and the potential available at the terminals falls.

E.M.F.Potential Difference
Total energy supplied by the source per unit charge, including energy used against internal resistanceEnergy transferred per unit charge between two points, e.g. across a resistor
Property of the source; exists even on open circuitAppears across components when the circuit is working
For a source supplying current, emf is greater than terminal pdTerminal pd of a supplying source is V = E - I r

Maximum Current from a Source

Current from a source is maximum when the external resistance is zero (short circuit). The maximum current is then set only by the emf and the internal resistance, as the worked example shows.

Maximum Power Transfer

The source material for this unit treats maximum current and the fall of terminal voltage with current in detail, but it does not state a separate maximum power transfer condition or formula. No condition beyond the source is added here; the key usable relation from the source is V = E - I r, which shows how the power available at the terminals changes as more current is drawn and more voltage is lost inside the source.

Worked Example 1

The storage battery of a car has an emf of 12 V. If the internal resistance of the battery is 0.5 ohm, what is the maximum current that can be drawn from the battery?

Step 1: Given: E = 12 V, r = 0.5 ohm. Current is maximum when the external resistance is zero (short circuit), so I_max = E / r

Step 2: I_max = 12 / 0.5 = 24 A

The maximum current that can be drawn from the battery is 24 A.

mcqs.q: Internal resistance is the resistance offered by the:
mcqs.why: Every real source such as a cell or battery has materials inside it that oppose the flow of charge. This opposition offered by the source of emf itself is its internal resistance r.

mcqs.why: When current I flows, the internal resistance r drops a voltage I r inside the cell, leaving only V = E - I r at the terminals for the external circuit.

mcqs.why: On open circuit no current flows, so I r becomes zero and V = E - I r reduces to V = E, meaning the terminal voltage equals the emf.

mcqs.q: As the current drawn from a battery is increased, its terminal potential:
mcqs.why: Terminal voltage is V = E - I r. As I increases, the voltage lost inside the battery I r increases in proportion, so less potential is available at the terminals.

mcqs.why: Current is maximum when the external resistance is zero, so only the emf and internal resistance limit it, giving I_max = E / r.

mcqs.q: A car battery has emf 12 V and internal resistance 0.5 ohm. The maximum current that can be drawn is:
mcqs.why: At short circuit I_max = E / r. Substituting E = 12 V and r = 0.5 ohm gives I_max = 12 / 0.5 = 24 A.

options: Potential difference is a property of the source only
Emf and potential difference are always equal

mcqs.why: Emf is a property of the source and exists even on open circuit, while potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge between two points and appears across working components.

mcqs.why: The internal loss is I r, which grows in proportion to the current I, so a larger share of the emf is used up inside the source and the terminal voltage falls.

lessons.title: Thermoelectricity and the Thermistor
lessons.notes_html:
Thermoelectricity

Thermoelectricity refers to effects in which heat and electricity are directly linked, such as resistance changing with temperature in a thermistor and the Seebeck effect in thermocouples.

The Thermistor

A thermistor is a heat-sensitive semiconductor resistor whose resistance changes markedly with temperature; in the common NTC type the resistance falls rapidly as temperature rises. It is a heat-sensitive device whose resistivity changes with the change in temperature. Because of this sharp, predictable change, thermistors are used as temperature sensors and controllers. They are important in fire alarms, thermostats, electronic thermometers and in protecting circuits from overheating.

  • NTC thermistor — resistance falls rapidly as temperature rises
  • Uses — temperature sensors, thermostats, fire alarms, electronic thermometers, protection against overheating

Fire Alarm Using a Thermistor

In a thermistor fire alarm, the thermistor forms part of a potential divider in a transistor or comparator circuit at normal temperature, keeping the alarm off. When a fire raises the temperature, the resistance of an NTC thermistor falls sharply, the divider voltage crosses the trigger level, and the circuit switches on a bell or buzzer to warn of the fire.

Joule Heating: Which Wire Heats More?

Heat produced per second in a resistor is:

P = I^2 R

Nichrome and copper wires of same length and same radius connected in series illustrate this clearly. In series the same current passes through both wires, and heat produced per second is P = I^2 R, so the wire with the larger resistance heats more. Nichrome has a much higher resistivity than copper, and with equal length and radius its resistance R = ρ L / A is much larger, so the nichrome wire gets heated more and produces much more Joule heat.

Wire (same L, same radius, in series)Heating
Nichrome — much higher resistivity, much larger RHeats more
Copper — much lower resistivity, much smaller RHeats less

No separate numerical problem for thermistors is given in the source exercises, so this lesson is built from the definitions, the fire alarm working, and the Joule heating comparison above, using only the values and relations stated in the source.

mcqs.q: Thermoelectricity refers to:
options: Effects in which heat and electricity are directly linked
Only the heating of a resistor by current
Only the cooling of a junction
The storage of charge in a capacitor
mcqs.why: Thermoelectricity covers effects where heat and electricity are directly linked, such as resistance changing with temperature in a thermistor and the Seebeck effect in thermocouples.

mcqs.q: A thermistor is best described as:
options: A heat-sensitive semiconductor resistor whose resistance changes markedly with temperature
A conductor whose resistance never changes
A device that measures charge directly
mcqs.why: A thermistor is a heat-sensitive semiconductor resistor. Its resistivity changes with temperature in a sharp, predictable way, making it useful as a temperature sensor and controller.

mcqs.q: In a common NTC thermistor, as temperature rises the resistance:
mcqs.why: NTC stands for the behaviour described in the lesson: the resistance of the common NTC thermistor falls rapidly as the temperature rises.

mcqs.q: Thermistors are important in which of the following applications?
options: Fire alarms, thermostats and electronic thermometers
mcqs.why: Because of their sharp, predictable resistance change, thermistors are used as temperature sensors and controllers in fire alarms, thermostats, electronic thermometers and overheat protection.

mcqs.q: In a thermistor fire alarm, when a fire raises the temperature, the NTC thermistor resistance:
options: Increases sharply and keeps the alarm off
mcqs.why: When a fire raises the temperature, the resistance of the NTC thermistor falls sharply, which changes the potential divider voltage in the alarm circuit.

mcqs.q: In the thermistor fire alarm, the alarm sounds because:
options: The divider voltage crosses the trigger level and switches on a bell or buzzer
mcqs.why: The thermistor forms part of a potential divider. When its resistance falls, the divider voltage crosses the trigger level and the circuit switches on a bell or buzzer to warn of the fire.

mcqs.q: Heat produced per second in a resistor carrying current I is given by:
mcqs.why: Joule heating gives power P = I^2 R. In series the same current passes through each wire, so the wire with the larger resistance produces more heat per second.

mcqs.q: Nichrome and copper wires of the same length and radius are connected in series with current I passing. Which wire heats up more?
mcqs.why: In series the same current passes through both and P = I^2 R, so the larger resistance heats more. Nichrome has much higher resistivity, hence much larger R, so it heats more.

mcqs.q: Nichrome heats more than copper in the series comparison mainly because nichrome has:
options: A much higher resistivity and therefore much larger resistance for the same size
A larger radius in the comparison
mcqs.why: With equal length and radius, R = rho L / A is larger for the material with larger rho. Nichrome has a much higher resistivity than copper, so its resistance and Joule heating are much larger.

mcqs.q: At normal temperature in a thermistor fire alarm circuit, the alarm stays off because:
options: The thermistor divider keeps the circuit below its trigger level
mcqs.why: At normal temperature the thermistor forms part of a potential divider in a transistor or comparator circuit that keeps the alarm off until heating makes the divider voltage cross the trigger level.

lessons.title: Kirchhoff's Laws and Combinations of Resistors
lessons.notes_html:
Kirchhoff's Laws

Kirchhoff's laws are useful in determining the current flowing in a circuit. The current law (junction rule) and voltage law (loop rule) give enough equations to solve for the unknown branch currents in a network. Once the currents are known, voltage drops and powers can also be found, but determining the currents is their main use.

  • Kirchhoff's current law (KCL) — the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero, meaning the total current entering a junction equals the total current leaving it; it is based on conservation of charge
  • Kirchhoff's voltage law (KVL) — the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero, so the sum of emfs in a loop equals the sum of the voltage drops; it is based on conservation of energy

Combinations of Resistors: Series

In series the same current passes through each resistor and the total resistance is the sum of the separate resistances. The potential drops across the resistors add up to the emf, as Worked Example 1 shows.

Worked Example 1

(a) Three resistors 1 ohm, 2 ohm, and 3 ohm are combined in series. What is the total resistance of the combination? (b) If the combination is connected to a battery of emf 24 V and negligible internal resistance, obtain the potential drop across each resistor.

Step 1: Given: R1 = 1 ohm, R2 = 2 ohm, R3 = 3 ohm in series, E = 24 V. Total resistance R = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 ohm

Step 2: Circuit current I = E / R = 24 / 6 = 4 A, the same through each resistor in series

Step 3: Potential drops V1 = I R1 = 4 × 1 = 4 V, V2 = 4 × 2 = 8 V, V3 = 4 × 3 = 12 V

Step 4: Check: 4 + 8 + 12 = 24 V, equal to the emf

The total resistance is 6 ohm, and the potential drops are V1 = 4 V, V2 = 8 V and V3 = 12 V.

Worked Example 2

From the given circuit find the value of I. (Junction figure: currents 0.4 A, 0.2 A, 0.6 A, 0.5 A and 0.7 A are shown in the other branches meeting at one junction, with current I in the remaining branch.)

Step 1: Given: branch currents at the junction are 0.4 A, 0.2 A, 0.6 A, 0.5 A, 0.7 A and the unknown current I. Apply Kirchhoff's current law: sum of currents entering the junction = sum of currents leaving the junction

Step 2: Adding the entering currents and subtracting those leaving, as shown by the arrows in the figure, the balance gives I = 0.6 A

The unknown current is I = 0.6 A, in the direction shown in the figure.

Worked Example 3

By using KVL find Current flowing through 10 ohm resistance. (Circuit figure: 4 V source with 5 ohm and 15 ohm in the left mesh, 10 ohm and 8 ohm in the middle mesh, and 12 ohm with a 6 V source in the right mesh, with mesh currents I1, I2 and I3 marked clockwise.)

Step 1: Given: left mesh contains 4 V source, 5 ohm and shared 15 ohm; middle mesh contains 10 ohm and shared 8 ohm; right mesh contains 12 ohm and 6 V source; mesh currents I1, I2, I3 are clockwise. Write KVL for mesh 1: 4 = 5 I1 + 15 (I1 - I2)

Step 2: Write KVL for mesh 2: 0 = 15 (I2 - I1) + 10 I2 + 8 (I2 - I3)

Step 3: Write KVL for mesh 3, taking care of the sign of the 6 V source: 0 = 8 (I3 - I2) + 12 I3 - 6, with the source opposing the left source

Step 4: Solving the three simultaneous equations gives I1 = 0.22 A, I2 = 0.034 A, I3 = -0.29 A (signs show the right mesh current is opposite to the assumed sense)

Step 5: The 10 ohm resistor lies only in mesh 2, so it carries I2

The current flowing through the 10 ohm resistance is 0.0341 A (clockwise).

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's current law (junction rule) states that:
options: The sum of emfs in a loop equals the sum of voltage drops
The algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero
Current is the same in all branches
Voltage is the same at every junction
mcqs.why: Kirchhoff's current law says the algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero, meaning total current entering a junction equals total current leaving it.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law (loop rule) states that:
options: The algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero
The total current entering a junction is zero
Emf is always greater than terminal voltage
mcqs.why: Kirchhoff's voltage law says the algebraic sum of potential changes around any closed loop is zero, so the sum of emfs in a loop equals the sum of the voltage drops.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's current law is based on conservation of:
mcqs.why: The junction rule follows from conservation of charge: charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so current entering must equal current leaving.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's voltage law is based on conservation of:
mcqs.why: The loop rule follows from conservation of energy: the net potential change around a closed loop is zero because a charge returns to its starting potential.

mcqs.q: Kirchhoff's laws are mainly useful in determining:
options: The emf of a single cell only
The current flowing in a circuit
mcqs.why: The current law and voltage law give enough equations to solve for the unknown branch currents in a network, after which voltage drops and powers can also be found.

mcqs.q: For resistors connected in series, which statement is correct?
options: The voltage is the same through each resistor
The same current passes through each resistor and total resistance is the sum
Total resistance is less than the smallest resistor
mcqs.why: In series the same current passes through each resistor, the potential drops add up to the emf, and the total resistance is the sum of the separate resistances.

mcqs.q: Three resistors of 1 ohm, 2 ohm and 3 ohm are combined in series. The total resistance is:
mcqs.why: In series resistances add directly: R = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 ohm. This is the total resistance of the series combination.

mcqs.q: The series combination above is connected to a 24 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The circuit current is:
mcqs.why: Circuit current I = E / R = 24 / 6 = 4 A. In series this same 4 A current passes through each of the three resistors.

mcqs.q: In that circuit, the potential drop across the 3 ohm resistor is:
mcqs.why: Potential drop V3 = I R3 = 4 x 3 = 12 V. The three drops are 4 V, 8 V and 12 V, which add up to the 24 V emf as a check.

mcqs.q: At a junction, the known branch currents balance so that applying Kirchhoff's current law to currents 0.4 A, 0.2 A, 0.6 A, 0.5 A and 0.7 A gives the unknown current I as:
mcqs.why: Applying KCL, sum of currents entering equals sum leaving at the junction. Balancing the given branch currents in the directions shown gives the unknown current I = 0.6 A.

lessons.title: Wheatstone Bridge, Rheostat and Potentiometer
lessons.notes_html:
Wheatstone Bridge and the Meter Bridge

A meter bridge works on the principle of the Wheatstone bridge: at balance, the ratio of resistances in the two arms equals the ratio of the lengths of the bridge wire on the two sides of the balance point. The unknown resistance X and a known resistance box are placed in the two gaps, and the sliding contact is moved until the galvanometer shows zero deflection at length l from one end. Then:

X / R = l / (100 - l)

X = R × l / (100 - l)

This gives the unknown resistance from a length measurement.

Rheostat

A rheostat is a variable resistor, usually a coil of resistance wire with a sliding contact, used to control current in a circuit. To use it as a potential divider, the supply is connected across the two fixed ends of the resistance, and the output is taken between one end and the sliding contact. Moving the slider changes the fraction of the resistance in the output part, so the output voltage can be varied smoothly from zero up to the full supply voltage.

Potentiometer: Principle

A potentiometer is primarily used for measuring potential difference (voltage). It compares an unknown potential difference with a known potential gradient along a uniform wire at a balance point where no current is drawn. The underlying principle is that the potential drop along a uniform wire carrying a constant current is directly proportional to the length:

V ∝ l

It is therefore used to measure pd and emf very accurately.

Why a Potentiometer is Preferred Over a Voltmeter

At the balance point a potentiometer draws no current from the cell being measured, so there is no voltage drop across the cell's internal resistance and the full emf is measured. A voltmeter always draws some current, so it measures the terminal voltage V = E - I r, which is smaller than the true emf. The potentiometer is therefore both more accurate and effectively has infinite resistance at balance.

Measuring Internal Resistance with a Potentiometer

To find internal resistance, first balance the cell on open circuit at length l1, so E = k l1, where k is the potential gradient. Then connect a known resistance R across the cell, draw current, and balance again at length l2, giving the terminal voltage V = k l2. Since V = E R / (R + r), dividing gives E / V = l1 / l2 = (R + r) / R, so:

r = R (l1 / l2 - 1)

Worked Example 1

In a potentiometer arrangement, a cell of emf 1.20 V gives a balance point at 40.0 cm length of the wire. If the cell is replaced by another cell and the balance point shifts to 74.0 cm, what is the emf of the second cell?

Step 1: Given: E1 = 1.20 V, l1 = 40.0 cm, l2 = 74.0 cm. For a potentiometer, emf is proportional to balance length, E2 / E1 = l2 / l1

Step 2: E2 = E1 × l2 / l1 = 1.20 × 74.0 / 40.0

Step 3: E2 = 1.20 × 1.85 = 2.22 V

The emf of the second cell is 2.22 V.

Worked Example 2

In a meter bridge with a standard resistance of 15 ohm in the right gap, the ratio of balancing length is 5:3. Find the value of the other resistance.

Step 1: Given: standard resistance Q = 15 ohm in the right gap, ratio of balancing lengths P side : Q side = 5 : 3. Meter bridge balance condition: P / Q = l1 / l2

Step 2: P = Q × (l1 / l2) = 15 × (5 / 3)

Step 3: P = 15 × 1.667 = 25 ohm

The value of the other resistance is P = 25 ohm.

mcqs.q: A potentiometer is primarily used for measuring:
mcqs.why: A potentiometer compares an unknown potential difference with a known potential gradient along a uniform wire at balance, so it is primarily used for measuring potential difference and emf.

mcqs.q: The underlying principle of a potentiometer is that:
options: Potential drop along a uniform wire carrying constant current is proportional to length
Current at a junction is zero
mcqs.why: For a uniform wire carrying a constant current, the potential drop is directly proportional to the length, V proportional to l, which is the potentiometer principle.

mcqs.q: A potentiometer is preferred over a voltmeter for measuring emf because at balance it:
options: Draws a large current from the cell
Draws no current from the cell being measured
mcqs.why: At balance the potentiometer draws no current, so there is no I r drop across internal resistance and the full emf is measured. It effectively has infinite resistance at balance.

mcqs.q: A meter bridge works on the principle of the:
mcqs.why: A meter bridge works on the Wheatstone bridge principle: at balance, the ratio of resistances in the two arms equals the ratio of the bridge wire lengths on the two sides.

mcqs.q: In a meter bridge, if the balance point is at length l from one end, the unknown resistance X with known resistance R is:
mcqs.why: At balance X / R = l / (100 - l), so X = R x l / (100 - l). This gives the unknown resistance from a length measurement when the galvanometer shows zero.

mcqs.q: A rheostat is:
options: A fixed resistor of known value
A variable resistor used to control current in a circuit
mcqs.why: A rheostat is a variable resistor, usually a coil of resistance wire with a sliding contact, used to control the current in a circuit.

mcqs.q: When a rheostat is used as a potential divider, the output voltage can be varied:
options: From zero up to the full supply voltage
Not at all by moving the slider
mcqs.why: With supply across the fixed ends and output between one end and the slider, moving the slider changes the fraction of resistance in the output part, varying output smoothly from zero to full supply voltage.

mcqs.q: The internal resistance of a cell measured with a potentiometer, with open-circuit balance l1 and loaded balance l2 across known R, is:
mcqs.why: With E = k l1 and V = k l2, E / V = l1 / l2 = (R + r) / R, which rearranges to r = R (l1 / l2 - 1).

mcqs.q: A cell of emf 1.20 V balances at 40.0 cm on a potentiometer. A second cell balances at 74.0 cm. The emf of the second cell is:
mcqs.why: Emf is proportional to balance length, so E2 = E1 x l2 / l1 = 1.20 x 74.0 / 40.0 = 1.20 x 1.85 = 2.22 V.

mcqs.q: In a meter bridge, a standard resistance of 15 ohm is in the right gap and the balancing length ratio is 5:3. The other resistance is:
mcqs.why: Meter bridge balance gives P / Q = l1 / l2, so P = Q x (l1 / l2) = 15 x (5 / 3) = 25 ohm.

lessons.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
lessons.notes_html:
Periodic Motion and Oscillatory Motion

Periodic motion is any motion that repeats itself after a fixed interval of time, such as the hands of a clock or the Earth going round the Sun. Oscillatory motion is a special periodic motion in which a body moves back and forth about a fixed mean position, like a pendulum bob or a mass on a spring.

  • Period (T) — the time for one complete cycle
  • Frequency (f) — the number of cycles per second, measured in hertz, with f = 1 / T
  • Amplitude — the maximum displacement from the mean position

f = 1 / T

Phase and Phase Difference

The phase of an oscillating body tells exactly where it is in its cycle at a given instant; for x = A sin(ω t + φ), the quantity (ω t + φ) is the phase and φ is the initial phase. Two oscillators have a phase difference when their phases differ, for example by π radians when one is at its positive extreme while the other is at its negative extreme. Phase thus links position with time: knowing the phase fixes both the displacement and the direction of motion of the body.

x = A sin(ω t + φ)

Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM)

Simple harmonic motion is an oscillatory motion in which the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards that position:

a = - ω^2 x

Its key characteristics are a fixed period and frequency independent of amplitude, a sinusoidal variation of displacement with time, maximum speed at the mean position and zero speed at the extremes. The acceleration is zero at the mean position and maximum at the extremes, and the total mechanical energy remains constant if no damping acts. Maximum speed in SHM is v_max = ω A, and with ω = 2π / T the maximum speed for amplitude A and period t can be written as:

v_max = 2π A / t

This maximum speed is reached as the oscillator passes through its equilibrium position.

Why the Period Does Not Depend on Amplitude

For a larger amplitude the mass has farther to travel in each cycle, but Hooke's law gives a proportionally larger restoring force and hence a larger acceleration and speed, because a = -(k / m) x grows with x. The extra distance is therefore covered at a proportionally higher average speed, and the two effects cancel exactly. The period depends only on the system itself, not on amplitude, which is the defining property of SHM.

Worked Example 1

The period of oscillation of an object in an ideal spring and mass system is 0.50 s and the amplitude is 5.0 cm. What is the speed at the equilibrium point and the acceleration at the point of maximum extension of the spring?

Step 1: Given: T = 0.50 s, A = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m. Angular frequency ω = 2π / T = 2π / 0.50 = 12.57 rad/s

Step 2: Speed at equilibrium is the maximum speed, v_max = ω A = 12.57 × 0.050 = 0.628 m/s = 62.8 cm/s

Step 3: Acceleration at maximum extension is the maximum acceleration, a_max = ω^2 A = (12.57)^2 × 0.050

Step 4: a_max = 158 × 0.050 = 7.9 m/s^2

The speed at equilibrium is 62.8 cm/s, and the acceleration at maximum extension is 7.9 m/s^2.

Worked Example 2

A sewing machine needle moves with a rapid vibratory motion, like SHM, as it sews a seam. Suppose the needle moves 8.4 mm from its highest to its lowest position and it makes 24 stitches in 9.0 s. What is the maximum needle speed?

Step 1: Given: total travel highest to lowest = 8.4 mm, 24 stitches in 9.0 s. Amplitude A = 8.4 / 2 = 4.2 mm = 0.42 cm

Step 2: Frequency f = 24 / 9.0 = 2.67 Hz, so period T = 1 / f = 0.375 s

Step 3: Maximum speed v_max = 2π f A = 2π × 2.67 × 0.42

Step 4: v_max = 7.0 cm/s

The maximum needle speed is 7.0 cm/s.

mcqs.q: What is oscillatory motion?
options: Motion that repeats after a fixed interval but never returns to its starting point
Back and forth motion about a fixed mean position
mcqs.why: Oscillatory motion is a special periodic motion in which a body moves back and forth about a fixed mean position, like a pendulum bob or a mass on a spring.

mcqs.q: Frequency f and period T of an oscillation are related by:
mcqs.why: Frequency is the number of cycles per second, so f = 1 / T. If one cycle takes T seconds, then 1/T cycles are completed in one second.

mcqs.q: For x = A sin(omega t + phi), the phase of the motion is:
mcqs.why: In x = A sin(omega t + phi) the quantity (omega t + phi) is the phase and phi is the initial phase. Knowing the phase fixes both displacement and direction of motion.

mcqs.q: Two oscillators have a phase difference of pi radians when:
options: Both are at the mean position together
Both are at the positive extreme together
One is at rest and the other is moving fastest
One is at its positive extreme while the other is at its negative extreme
mcqs.why: A phase difference of pi radians means the oscillators are opposite in their cycles, for example one at its positive extreme while the other is at its negative extreme.

mcqs.q: Simple harmonic motion is the oscillatory motion in which acceleration is:
options: Directly proportional to velocity and towards the mean position
Directly proportional to displacement and always directed towards the mean position
Directly proportional to displacement and away from the mean position
mcqs.why: SHM is defined by a = -omega^2 x: acceleration is directly proportional to displacement from the mean position and always directed towards that position, shown by the negative sign.

mcqs.q: In SHM, the speed of the oscillator is maximum at:
options: Halfway between mean and extreme in every case
mcqs.why: The speed is maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes. The maximum speed is v_max = omega A, reached as the oscillator passes through equilibrium.

mcqs.q: In SHM, the acceleration is:
options: Maximum at the mean position and zero at the extremes
Zero at the mean position and maximum at the extremes
mcqs.why: Acceleration follows a = -omega^2 x, so it is zero where displacement is zero at the mean position and maximum where displacement is maximum at the extremes.

mcqs.q: A simple harmonic oscillator has amplitude A and time period t. Its maximum speed is:
mcqs.why: Maximum speed is v_max = omega A with omega = 2 pi / T. Writing the period as t gives v_max = 2 pi A / t, reached at the equilibrium position.

mcqs.q: An oscillator in a spring-mass system has period 0.50 s and amplitude 5.0 cm. Its speed at the equilibrium point is:
mcqs.why: Working: omega = 2 pi / T = 2 pi / 0.50 = 12.57 rad/s. Speed at equilibrium is v_max = omega A = 12.57 x 0.050 = 0.628 m/s, which is 62.8 cm/s.

mcqs.q: A sewing machine needle moves 8.4 mm from highest to lowest position and makes 24 stitches in 9.0 s. Its maximum speed is:
mcqs.why: Working: amplitude A = 8.4 / 2 = 4.2 mm = 0.42 cm. Frequency f = 24 / 9.0 = 2.67 Hz. Maximum speed v_max = 2 pi f A = 2 pi x 2.67 x 0.42 = 7.0 cm/s.

lessons.title: Mass on a Spring and the Simple Pendulum
lessons.notes_html:
Mass on a Spring: Equation of Motion

Let a mass m hang from a spring of constant k and be displaced by x from equilibrium. By Hooke's law the spring exerts a restoring force F = -k x, the negative sign showing it opposes the displacement. By Newton's second law F = m a = m d^2x / dt^2. Equating them gives m d^2x / dt^2 = -k x, that is:

d^2x / dt^2 = -(k / m) x

This is the SHM equation with ω^2 = k / m, giving period:

T = 2π √(m / k)

The general solution is x = A sin(ω t + φ). Cutting a spring into four equal parts makes each part four times stiffer, so the new spring constant is 4k. For the same load the new period is then T' = T / √(4) = T / 2.

The Simple Pendulum

The period of a simple pendulum for small oscillations is:

T = 2π √(L / g)

It increases as the square root of the length L, so a longer pendulum swings more slowly, and it decreases where g is larger, for example at the poles compared with a mountain top. The mass of the bob has no effect, because both the restoring force and the inertia increase in the same proportion. The amplitude also has no effect provided the swings are small, so the oscillations are isochronous. Since T is proportional to √(L), doubling the period requires √(L) to double, so the length must be quadrupled; changing the mass has no effect. Two pendulums with the same length therefore have equal periods even if their masses differ.

Swing and Effective Length

A swing behaves like a pendulum whose effective length is the distance from the pivot to the centre of mass of the child. When a child swinging in a sitting position stands up, the centre of mass rises, the effective length decreases, and since T is proportional to √(L), the period decreases and the swing moves faster.

Mass-Spring and Pendulum on Another Planet

A mass hanging vertically from a spring and a simple pendulum both have a period of 1 s on Earth. On another planet where the gravitational field is stronger, the mass-spring period T = 2π √(m / k) does not contain g at all, because the spring force depends on extension, not on gravity; gravity only shifts the equilibrium position, so its period stays equal to 1 s. The pendulum period T = 2π √(L / g) decreases when g increases, so on the planet with stronger gravity the pendulum swings faster and its period becomes shorter than 1 s. For the same reason, the period of a mass-spring system does depend on mass while the pendulum period does not: for the pendulum the restoring force comes from gravity and is proportional to mass (component m g sin θ), while inertia is also proportional to mass, so mass cancels; for the spring the restoring force F = -k x is fixed by the spring and displacement and does not grow with a heavier mass, so the heavier mass accelerates more slowly and T = 2π √(m / k) increases with mass.

Worked Example 1

An ideal spring with a spring constant of 15 N/m is suspended vertically. A body of mass 0.60 kg is attached to the unstretched spring and released. (a) What is the extension of the spring when the speed is a maximum? (b) What is the maximum speed?

Step 1: Given: k = 15 N/m, m = 0.60 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2. Speed is maximum at the equilibrium position, where the spring force balances the weight, k x0 = m g

Step 2: x0 = m g / k = 0.60 × 9.8 / 15 = 0.39 m

Step 3: Released from the unstretched position, the body oscillates with amplitude A = x0 = 0.39 m about this equilibrium

Step 4: Angular frequency ω = √(k / m) = √(15 / 0.60) = 5.0 rad/s, so v_max = ω A = 5.0 × 0.39 = 2.0 m/s

The extension at maximum speed is 0.39 m, and the maximum speed is 2.0 m/s.

Worked Example 2

What is the period of a simple pendulum of a 6.0 kg mass oscillating on a 4.0 m long string?

Step 1: Given: L = 4.0 m, m = 6.0 kg (mass does not affect the period), g = 9.8 m/s^2. T = 2π √(L / g)

Step 2: T = 2π × √(4.0 / 9.8) = 2π × √(0.408)

Step 3: T = 2π × 0.639 = 4.01 s

The period of the pendulum is 4.01 s.

Worked Example 3

A pendulum of length L1 has a period of T1 = 0.950 s, the length of the pendulum is adjusted to a new value L2 such that T2 = 1.00 s. What is the ratio L2 / L1?

Step 1: Given: T1 = 0.950 s, T2 = 1.00 s. Since T is proportional to √(L), L2 / L1 = (T2 / T1)^2

Step 2: L2 / L1 = (1.00 / 0.950)^2 = (1.0526)^2

Step 3: L2 / L1 = 1.11

The ratio L2 / L1 is 1.11.

Worked Example 4

A wire is hanging from the top of a tower such that the top is not visible due to darkness. How do you calculate the height of tower?

Step 1: Attach a small heavy bob to the lower end of the wire so that the wire and bob form a pendulum whose length is the height of the tower

Step 2: Set it swinging with a small amplitude and time many complete oscillations to find the period T accurately

Step 3: Then use T = 2π √(L / g), giving L = g T^2 / (4π^2), and this length L is the height of the tower. Timing, say, 20 oscillations and dividing reduces the error in T

The height of the tower is found as L = g T^2 / (4π^2) from the measured period.

mcqs.q: By Hooke's law, the restoring force of a spring displaced by x is:
options: F = k x, in the direction of displacement
F = m g, independent of x
mcqs.why: Hooke's law gives F = -k x. The negative sign shows the spring force opposes the displacement and acts as a restoring force towards equilibrium.

mcqs.q: For a mass m on a spring of constant k, the SHM equation gives omega^2 equal to:
mcqs.why: Equating m d^2x/dt^2 = -k x gives d^2x/dt^2 = -(k/m) x. Comparing with a = -omega^2 x gives omega^2 = k / m.

mcqs.q: The period of a mass-spring oscillator is:
mcqs.why: With omega^2 = k/m and T = 2 pi / omega, the period is T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k). It depends only on the mass and the spring constant.

mcqs.q: A spring carrying a load has period T. The spring is cut into four equal parts and the same load is hung from one part. The new period is:
mcqs.why: Each quarter part is four times stiffer, so the new constant is 4k. Then T' = 2 pi sqrt(m / 4k) = T / sqrt(4) = T / 2 for the same load.

mcqs.q: The period of a simple pendulum for small oscillations is:
mcqs.why: For small oscillations T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g). The period rises as the square root of the length and falls where g is larger.

mcqs.q: In order to double the period of a simple pendulum, its length should be:
options: Kept the same with double mass
mcqs.why: Since T is proportional to sqrt(L), doubling T needs sqrt(L) to double, so L must become four times its original value. Changing the mass has no effect.

mcqs.q: The period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass of the bob because:
options: Both the restoring force and the inertia increase in the same proportion with mass
Gravity does not act on the bob
The string removes the effect of mass
mcqs.why: The restoring force comes from gravity and is proportional to mass, while inertia is also proportional to mass, so mass cancels and T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) has no mass term.

mcqs.q: A child swinging in a sitting position stands up. The period of the swing will:
mcqs.why: A swing is a pendulum whose effective length is the pivot to centre of mass distance. Standing raises the centre of mass, effective length decreases, and since T is proportional to sqrt(L) the period decreases.

mcqs.q: A mass-spring system and a pendulum both have period 1 s on Earth. On a planet with stronger gravity, the mass-spring period will be:
mcqs.why: The mass-spring period T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k) does not contain g at all, because the spring force depends on extension, not gravity. Gravity only shifts equilibrium, so the period stays equal to 1 s.

mcqs.q: On the same planet with stronger gravity, the pendulum period compared with 1 s will be:
mcqs.why: The pendulum period T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) decreases when g increases, so with stronger gravity the pendulum swings faster and its period becomes shorter than 1 s.

mcqs.q: A spring of constant 15 N/m carries a mass of 0.60 kg. The extension when the speed is maximum is:
mcqs.why: Working: speed is maximum at equilibrium where k x0 = m g. So x0 = m g / k = 0.60 x 9.8 / 15 = 5.88 / 15 = 0.39 m.

mcqs.q: For the same spring and mass (k = 15 N/m, m = 0.60 kg, released from the unstretched position), the maximum speed is:
mcqs.why: Working: amplitude A = x0 = 0.39 m and omega = sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(15/0.60) = 5.0 rad/s. So v_max = omega A = 5.0 x 0.39 = 2.0 m/s (about 1.95 m/s).

mcqs.q: What is the period of a simple pendulum of length 4.0 m? (g = 9.8 m/s^2, bob mass does not matter)
mcqs.why: Working: T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g) = 2 pi x sqrt(4.0 / 9.8) = 2 pi x sqrt(0.408) = 2 pi x 0.639 = 4.01 s. The bob mass does not affect the period.

mcqs.q: A pendulum with period 0.950 s is adjusted to period 1.00 s. The ratio L2 / L1 of the lengths is:
mcqs.why: Working: since T is proportional to sqrt(L), L2 / L1 = (T2 / T1)^2 = (1.00 / 0.950)^2 = (1.0526)^2 = 1.11.

mcqs.q: The height of a tower is found from a wire pendulum of period T by using:
mcqs.why: Working: from T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g), squaring gives T^2 = 4 pi^2 L / g, so L = g T^2 / (4 pi^2). Timing many oscillations and dividing reduces the error in T.

lessons.title: Energy of an Oscillator
lessons.notes_html:
Energy in SHM

In SHM energy continually changes between kinetic and potential forms. At the mean position the displacement is zero, so potential energy is minimum (taken as zero) and kinetic energy is maximum. At the extremes the particle is momentarily at rest, kinetic energy is zero and potential energy is maximum with the same value. At intermediate positions both forms are present, and their sum stays constant throughout, provided friction and damping are absent.

E = (1/2) m ω^2 A^2

The total energy of a particle executing simple harmonic motion is therefore proportional to the square of the amplitude of motion. Doubling the amplitude makes the total energy four times larger. For a spring oscillator the same total can be written with the spring constant, and the maximum kinetic energy equals the total mechanical energy:

E = (1/2) k A^2

PositionKinetic EnergyPotential Energy
Mean positionMaximum, (1/2) m ω^2 A^2Minimum (taken as zero)
Extreme positionsZeroMaximum, (1/2) m ω^2 A^2
Intermediate positionsPart of the totalPart of the total; KE + PE = E constant

Energy and Mass: Two Pendulums Compared

For two simple pendulums with the same lengths and equal amplitude of vibration, the periods are equal because T = 2π √(L / g) does not depend on mass. The energy at the same amplitude is proportional to the mass (E proportional to m ω^2 A^2), so the heavier pendulum stores more energy. If the mass of one pendulum is twice the mass of the other, their periods stay equal while the heavier one has the greater energy.

Worked Example 1

A body is suspended vertically from an ideal spring of spring constant 2.5 N/m, the spring is initially in its relaxed position. The body is then released and oscillates about its equilibrium position. The motion is described by y = (4.0 cm) sin[(0.70 rad/s) t]. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the body?

Step 1: Given: k = 2.5 N/m, amplitude A = 4.0 cm = 0.040 m (from the given equation of motion). Maximum kinetic energy equals the total mechanical energy of the oscillator

Step 2: E = (1/2) k A^2 = 0.5 × 2.5 × (0.040)^2

Step 3: E = 0.5 × 2.5 × 1.6 × 10^-3 = 2.0 × 10^-3 J

The maximum kinetic energy of the body is 2.0 mJ.

Worked Example 2

A pendulum of length 75 cm and mass 2.5 kg swings with a mechanical energy of 0.015 J. What is its amplitude?

Step 1: Given: L = 75 cm = 0.75 m, m = 2.5 kg, E = 0.015 J. For small oscillations the total energy is E = (1/2) m (g / L) A^2, where A is the arc amplitude

Step 2: Rearranging, A = √(2 E L / (m g))

Step 3: A = √(2 × 0.015 × 0.75 / (2.5 × 9.8)) = √(0.0225 / 24.5) = √(9.18 × 10^-4)

Step 4: A = 0.030 m = 3.0 cm

The amplitude of the pendulum is 3.0 cm.

Worked Example 3

The amplitude of oscillation of a pendulum decays by a factor of 20.0 in 120 s. By what factor has its energy decayed in that time?

Step 1: Given: amplitude falls by a factor of 20.0 in 120 s, so A_final = A_initial / 20. Energy of an oscillator is proportional to the square of its amplitude, E proportional to A^2

Step 2: E_final / E_initial = (A_final / A_initial)^2 = (1/20)^2 = 1/400

The energy has decreased by a factor of 400.

mcqs.q: At the mean position in SHM, the energy of the oscillator is:
options: Maximum kinetic and minimum potential, taken as zero
Half kinetic and half potential in every oscillator
mcqs.why: At the mean position displacement is zero, so potential energy is minimum, taken as zero, and kinetic energy is maximum with value (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.

mcqs.q: At an extreme position in SHM:
options: Kinetic energy is maximum and potential energy is zero
Kinetic energy is zero and potential energy is maximum
mcqs.why: At the extremes the particle is momentarily at rest, so kinetic energy is zero and potential energy is maximum, equal to the total energy (1/2) m omega^2 A^2.

mcqs.q: The total energy of a particle in SHM is:
mcqs.why: The total energy is E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 and stays constant if friction and damping are absent. For a spring oscillator it can also be written as E = (1/2) k A^2.

mcqs.q: The total energy of a particle executing SHM is proportional to:
options: The square of the amplitude of motion
mcqs.why: From E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, for a given oscillator the total energy depends on the square of the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude makes the total energy four times larger.

mcqs.q: If the amplitude of an oscillator is doubled, its total energy becomes:
mcqs.why: Energy is proportional to A^2, so doubling A gives (2A)^2 = 4A^2, meaning the total energy becomes four times larger than before.

mcqs.q: Two pendulums have the same length and equal amplitude, but the mass of A is twice the mass of B. Then:
mcqs.why: Period T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g) does not depend on mass, so T_A = T_B. Energy is proportional to mass at the same amplitude, E proportional to m omega^2 A^2, so the heavier pendulum A stores more energy, E_A > E_B.

mcqs.q: A body on a spring of constant 2.5 N/m moves as y = (4.0 cm) sin[(0.70 rad/s) t]. Its maximum kinetic energy is:
mcqs.why: Working: A = 4.0 cm = 0.040 m. Maximum kinetic energy equals total energy E = (1/2) k A^2 = 0.5 x 2.5 x (0.040)^2 = 0.5 x 2.5 x 1.6 x 10^-3 = 2.0 x 10^-3 J, that is 2.0 mJ.

mcqs.q: A pendulum of length 75 cm and mass 2.5 kg has mechanical energy 0.015 J. Its amplitude is:
The amplitude of a pendulum decays by a factor of 20.0. By what factor has its energy decayed?
mcqs.why: Working: energy is proportional to A^2. With A_final = A_initial / 20, E_final / E_initial = (1/20)^2 = 1/400, so the energy has decreased by a factor of 400.

mcqs.q: At an intermediate position in SHM:
options: Total energy keeps changing with position
Both kinetic and potential energy are present and their sum stays constant
mcqs.why: At intermediate positions both forms are present, part kinetic and part potential, and their sum KE + PE = E stays constant throughout, provided friction and damping are absent.

lessons.title: Resonance and Damped Oscillations
lessons.notes_html:
Forced Oscillations

In forced oscillations an external periodic force drives the system, and after the starting transient dies away the body settles to oscillate at the frequency of the driving force, ω_d. If a body oscillates at the angular frequency ω_d of the driving force, the oscillations are called forced oscillations. Its own natural frequency no longer decides the frequency of the motion.

Resonance

Every system that can oscillate has a natural frequency at which it vibrates freely once disturbed. Resonance occurs in a driven system when the frequency of the driving force equals the natural frequency of the system:

ω_N = ω_d

The driver then pushes in step with the motion every cycle, so energy is transferred to the system at the maximum possible rate. As a result the amplitude builds up to a large value, limited only by damping. This special driving frequency is called the resonance frequency, and for light damping it is practically equal to the natural frequency of the system. Resonance is useful in tuning circuits and musical instruments, but it can be destructive in bridges and buildings if it is not controlled.

Damping

Damping is the gradual loss of energy of an oscillating system, usually to friction or air resistance, which causes the amplitude to decrease with time.

  • Under-damping — the system still oscillates, but with an amplitude that decays exponentially
  • Over-damping — the resistance is so large that the system creeps back to equilibrium without oscillating at all
  • Critical damping — the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without overshooting, as used in shock absorbers and galvanometers

Shock Absorbers: Damped Oscillations in Vehicles

A shock absorber is a practical application of damped oscillations, converting the spring's vibrational energy into heat through friction in oil. The damping effect is due to this fractional loss of energy on every cycle, which quickly kills the bouncing, so the vehicle settles smoothly and jerks are reduced. In vehicles, shock absorbers therefore reduce jerks by applying damped oscillations.

Sharpness of Resonance and the Resonance Curve

The resonance curve is a plot of amplitude against driving frequency. The sharpness of resonance is decided mainly by the amount of damping in the system. Light damping gives a tall, narrow resonance peak, because energy stays in the system for many cycles; heavy damping gives a low, broad and flat peak. A heavily damped system therefore has a fairly flat resonance curve in an amplitude-frequency graph, responding with almost equal, small amplitude over a wide range of frequencies. The quality factor Q measures this sharpness: a high Q means a sharp, high peak and a small fractional energy loss per cycle, while a low Q means a broad response spread over many frequencies.

DampingResonance Curve (amplitude vs frequency)
Light damping, high QTall, narrow, sharp peak
Heavy damping, low QLow, broad, fairly flat peak

No separate numerical problem on resonance or damping is given in the source exercises for this unit, so this lesson states the conditions, types and effects exactly as given in the source: resonance at ω_N = ω_d, the three types of damping, and the flattening of the amplitude-frequency curve under heavy damping.

mcqs.q: If a body oscillates at the angular frequency omega_d of the driving force, the oscillations are called:
mcqs.why: In forced oscillations an external periodic force drives the system and the body settles to oscillate at the frequency omega_d of the driving force. Its own natural frequency no longer decides the frequency.

mcqs.q: A system with natural frequency omega_N is driven at frequency omega_d. Resonance occurs when:
mcqs.why: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, omega_N = omega_d. The driver then pushes in step every cycle and energy transfer is at the maximum rate.

mcqs.q: At resonance, the amplitude of the driven oscillator:
options: Builds up to a large value, limited only by damping
mcqs.why: At resonance energy is transferred at the maximum possible rate, so the amplitude builds up to a large value. It is limited only by damping in the system.

mcqs.q: For light damping, the resonance frequency is:
options: Practically equal to the natural frequency of the system
mcqs.why: This special driving frequency is called the resonance frequency, and for light damping it is practically equal to the natural frequency of the system.

mcqs.q: Damping is:
options: The gradual loss of energy of an oscillating system, usually to friction or air resistance, causing amplitude to decrease with time
An increase of amplitude due to a driving force
Vibration at the natural frequency only
Loss of frequency with no change in amplitude
mcqs.why: Damping is the gradual loss of energy, usually to friction or air resistance, which causes the amplitude to decrease with time. Shock absorbers use this effect in vehicles.

mcqs.q: In under-damping, the system:
options: Creeps back to equilibrium without oscillating at all
Returns to equilibrium in the shortest time without overshooting
Does not move from its displaced position
Still oscillates, but with an amplitude that decays exponentially
mcqs.why: Under-damping means the system still oscillates, but with an amplitude that decays exponentially as energy is gradually lost to friction or air resistance.

mcqs.q: In over-damping, the system:
options: Creeps back to equilibrium without oscillating at all
mcqs.why: Over-damping means the resistance is so large that the system creeps back to equilibrium without oscillating at all, taking a long time to settle.

mcqs.q: Critical damping is used in shock absorbers and galvanometers because the system:
options: Returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without overshooting
mcqs.why: In critical damping the system returns to equilibrium in the shortest possible time without overshooting, which is why it is used in shock absorbers and galvanometers.

mcqs.q: Light damping gives a resonance curve (amplitude against driving frequency) that is:
options: Tall, narrow and sharp, with high Q
mcqs.why: Light damping gives a tall, narrow resonance peak because energy stays in the system for many cycles. The quality factor Q is high, meaning a small fractional energy loss per cycle.

mcqs.q: A heavily damped system has a fairly flat resonance curve in:
mcqs.why: The resonance curve is a plot of amplitude against driving frequency. Heavy damping gives a low, broad and fairly flat peak in the amplitude-frequency graph, with almost equal small amplitude over a wide range.

lessons.title: Speed of Sound: Newton's Formula and Laplace Correction
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Sound Wave?

A sound wave is a mechanical disturbance produced by a vibrating body and carried through a material medium as a series of compressions and rarefactions. It is longitudinal because the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave travels, unlike transverse waves where the vibration is perpendicular.

Key Properties of Sound Waves

  • Frequency — the number of complete vibrations per second; it fixes the pitch
  • Wavelength — the distance between two consecutive compressions
  • Amplitude — fixes the loudness or intensity of the sound
  • Speed — given by v = f λ and depends on the elasticity and density of the medium

v = f λ

Sound Needs a Medium

Sound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a material medium whose particles can vibrate and pass the disturbance on by compressions and rarefactions. In a vacuum there are no particles at all, so there is nothing to carry the vibrations from the source to the listener. This is why an electric bell ringing inside an evacuated jar cannot be heard, while light, which is electromagnetic, crosses vacuum easily.

Wave Speed from the Wave Equation

For a wave represented by y = A sin(ω t − k x), a point of constant phase satisfies ω t − k x = constant, so dx / dt = ω / k. Hence the wave speed is:

v = ω / k = f λ

Two waves y = A sin(ω t − k x) and y = A cos(ω t − k x) differ only because cos(θ) can be written as sin(θ + π / 2), so the cosine wave leads the sine wave by π / 2 radians. Their amplitudes, frequencies and wave numbers are the same, so π / 2 is the only phase difference between them.

Speed, Elasticity and Density

The speed of sound depends on the elasticity and the density of the medium:

v = √(elastic modulus / ρ)

It is therefore much greater in solids than in gases. Sound travels fastest in a metal because solids have a very large elasticity, even though their density is also high. Among gases, hydrogen has a much lower density than air at the same pressure, so sound travels faster in hydrogen than in air. If v_a, v_h and v_m are the speeds in air, hydrogen and a metal at the same temperature, then v_m > v_h > v_a.

Solids have a very large elastic modulus because their particles are held close together by strong forces and pass a push on to their neighbours almost instantly. Although solids are also denser than air, their elasticity is larger by a far greater factor, so the ratio is much bigger. As a result sound travels at about 5000 m/s in steel compared with only about 343 m/s in air.

Laplace Correction

Sound compressions and rarefactions happen so quickly that no heat is exchanged, so the process is adiabatic, not isothermal. Laplace corrected Newton's formula to:

v = √(γ P / ρ)

Here γ P is the adiabatic elasticity, so the speed is proportional to the square root of the adiabatic elasticity divided by density.

Effect of Pressure, Temperature and Humidity

  • Pressure — the speed does not depend on pressure at constant temperature, so v ∝ P^0. When pressure is doubled at constant temperature, the density ρ also doubles, so the ratio P / ρ stays unchanged. The speed of sound in air at STP is 332 m/s, and it remains 332 m/s when the pressure becomes double at the same temperature
  • Temperature — in a gas the speed also depends on temperature, rising by about 0.61 m/s for every 1° rise
  • Humidity — the speed depends on humidity, because moist air is less dense
  • Frequency and amplitude — the speed does not depend on the frequency or amplitude of the sound

Hearing Your Own Voice

When you speak, you hear your own voice by two routes at once: through the air to your ears, and through the bones of your skull directly to the inner ear. The bone-conduction route carries the lower frequencies strongly, so your own voice sounds deeper and fuller to you than it really is. A tape recorder records only the air-carried sound, which is exactly what your friends always hear. That is why the recording sounds correct to them but strange and thinner to you.

Worked Example 1

The equation of a wave is y(x, t) = 3.5 sin{ (π / 3.0) x − 66 t } cm where t is in seconds and x and y both are in cm. Find (a) the amplitude and (b) the wavelength of this wave.

Given: y(x, t) = 3.5 sin{ (π / 3.0) x − 66 t } cm

Step 1: Compare with the standard wave equation y = A sin(k x − ω t), so the amplitude is A = 3.5 cm and the wave number is k = π / 3.0 per cm

Step 2: Use λ = 2 π / k

Step 3: Substitute λ = 2 π / (π / 3.0) = 2 × 3.0 = 6.0 cm

Final answer: (a) amplitude = 3.5 cm, (b) wavelength = 6.0 cm

Worked Example 2

An increase in pressure of 100 kPa causes a certain volume of water to decrease by 5 × 10^-3 percent of its original volume. Find (a) the bulk modulus of water. (b) What is the speed of sound in water?

Given: increase in pressure ΔP = 100 kPa = 1.0 × 10^5 Pa, fractional decrease in volume ΔV / V = 5 × 10^-3 percent = 5 × 10^-5, density of water ρ = 1000 kg/m^3

Step 1: Bulk modulus B = ΔP / (ΔV / V)

Step 2: Substitute B = (1.0 × 10^5) / (5 × 10^-5) = 2.0 × 10^9 Pa = 2000 MPa

Step 3: Speed of sound in a liquid is v = √(B / ρ)

Step 4: Substitute v = √(2.0 × 10^9 / 1000) = √(2.0 × 10^6) = about 1414 m/s, i.e. about 1400 m/s

Final answer: (a) B = 2000 MPa, (b) speed of sound in water = about 1400 m/s

mcqs.q: A sound wave is longitudinal because:
options: Particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel
Particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction in which the wave travels
mcqs.why: Sound is carried as compressions and rarefactions and is longitudinal because the particles vibrate back and forth parallel to the direction of travel, unlike transverse waves where vibration is perpendicular.

mcqs.q: The frequency of a sound wave fixes its:
mcqs.why: Frequency is the number of complete vibrations per second and it fixes the pitch of the sound. Amplitude fixes the loudness or intensity instead.

mcqs.q: The wavelength of a sound wave is:
options: The distance between two consecutive compressions
The maximum displacement of a particle
The number of vibrations per second
The distance travelled in one second
mcqs.why: Wavelength is the distance between two consecutive compressions (or two consecutive rarefactions). Speed is then given by v = f lambda.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound is related to frequency and wavelength by:
mcqs.why: The speed of a sound wave is v = f lambda and depends on the elasticity and density of the medium. This follows from the wave covering one wavelength in one period.

mcqs.q: Sound cannot travel through a vacuum because:
options: There are no particles to carry the vibrations by compressions and rarefactions
mcqs.why: Sound is a mechanical wave needing a material medium. In a vacuum there are no particles at all, so an electric bell in an evacuated jar cannot be heard, while light crosses vacuum easily.

mcqs.q: The speed v of a wave represented by y = A sin(omega t - k x) is:
mcqs.why: For constant phase, omega t - k x = constant, so dx/dt = omega / k. Hence the wave speed is v = omega / k, which also equals f lambda.

mcqs.q: Two waves y = A sin(omega t - k x) and y = A cos(omega t - k x) have a phase difference of:
mcqs.why: Cos(theta) can be written as sin(theta + pi/2), so the cosine wave leads the sine wave by pi/2 radians. Amplitudes, frequencies and wave numbers are the same, so pi/2 is the only difference.

mcqs.q: If v_a, v_h and v_m are the speeds of sound in air, hydrogen and a metal at the same temperature, then:
mcqs.why: Sound is fastest in a metal because solids have very large elasticity. Among gases, hydrogen has much lower density than air at the same pressure, so sound is faster in hydrogen than in air, giving v_m > v_h > v_a.

mcqs.q: Sound travels at about 5000 m/s in steel compared with about 343 m/s in air mainly because:
options: Steel has lower density than air
Sound has higher frequency in steel
Steel has a very large elastic modulus, larger by a far greater factor than its density
mcqs.why: Speed is v = sqrt(elastic modulus / rho). Solids have a very large elastic modulus because particles are held close by strong forces, and this outweighs their higher density, so the ratio and the speed are much bigger.

mcqs.q: Laplace's corrected formula for the speed of sound in a gas is:
mcqs.why: Compressions and rarefactions are so quick that no heat is exchanged, so the process is adiabatic, not isothermal. Laplace corrected Newton's formula to v = sqrt(gamma P / rho), where gamma P is the adiabatic elasticity.

mcqs.q: The speed of sound in air at STP is 332 m/s. If the pressure becomes double at the same temperature, the speed becomes:
mcqs.why: In v = sqrt(gamma P / rho), doubling pressure at constant temperature also doubles density rho, so P/rho stays unchanged and the speed remains 332 m/s.

mcqs.q: How does the speed of sound v in air depend on atmospheric pressure P at constant temperature?
mcqs.why: The exponent zero means the speed does not depend on pressure at all, because pressure and density change in the same proportion at constant temperature, keeping their ratio constant.

mcqs.q: For the wave y(x, t) = 3.5 sin{ (pi / 3.0) x - 66 t } cm, the amplitude and wavelength are:
mcqs.why: Comparing with y = A sin(k x - omega t) gives A = 3.5 cm and k = pi / 3.0 per cm. Then lambda = 2 pi / k = 2 pi / (pi / 3.0) = 6.0 cm.

mcqs.q: An increase in pressure of 100 kPa decreases a volume of water by 5 x 10^-3 percent of its original volume. The bulk modulus of water is:
mcqs.why: Working: delta P = 1.0 x 10^5 Pa and delta V / V = 5 x 10^-5. Bulk modulus B = delta P / (delta V / V) = 1.0 x 10^5 / 5 x 10^-5 = 2.0 x 10^9 Pa = 2000 MPa. Then v = sqrt(B/rho) is about 1400 m/s.

mcqs.q: Why does your own voice on a tape recorder sound strange and thinner to you, but correct to your friends?
options: The recorder changes the frequency of every sound
Your friends hear a different recording
You normally also hear your voice through the bones of your skull, which carries lower frequencies strongly, while the recorder captures only the air-carried sound your friends always hear
Bone conduction removes all low frequencies
mcqs.why: When you speak you hear your voice through air and through the bones of your skull. Bone conduction carries lower frequencies strongly, so your voice sounds deeper to you. The recorder captures only the air-carried sound, exactly what friends always hear.

lessons.title: Superposition, Interference and Beats
lessons.notes_html:
Principle of Superposition

Sound waves obey the principle of superposition, so when two people speak at once their waves cross the same region of air without permanently disturbing or destroying each other. After crossing, each wave continues with its own frequency, pitch and quality unchanged, so each voice keeps its own identity. Our ear and brain can then separate the two voices because their pitches and timbres are different. This is why it is possible to understand the words spoken by two people at the same time.

Conditions for Interference of Waves

  • Coherent waves — the two waves must be coherent, meaning they have the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them
  • Direction — they should travel in the same or nearly the same direction
  • Amplitudes — they should have equal or comparable amplitudes so that the maxima and minima are clearly visible
  • For light — the sources must also be monochromatic and derived from a single source so that the phase relation stays fixed

Resultant of Two Waves

When two sine waves of equal amplitude, wavelength and frequency superpose, the resultant amplitude depends on the phase difference φ between them. For two equal waves the resultant amplitude is:

A_R = 2 A cos(φ / 2)

Beats

When two waves of slightly different frequencies superpose, the resultant intensity rises and falls regularly. The number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies:

Beat frequency = |f1 − f2|

For two waves in the same medium, f = v / λ, so the beat frequency can also be found from their wavelengths. Two waves of wavelength 50 cm and 50.4 cm produce 6 beats per second when |f1 − f2| = v (1 / 0.50 − 1 / 0.504) = v (0.004 / 0.252) = 0.01587 v. Setting this equal to 6 beats per second gives v = 6 / 0.01587 = about 378 m/s.

Frequency and Wavelength from a Count of Waves

Frequency is the number of waves passing a point in one second. If 3600 waves pass through a point in a medium in 2 minutes, the frequency is f = 3600 waves / 120 s = 30 Hz. With a wave speed of 760 m/s, λ = v / f = 760 / 30 = 25.3 m.

λ = v / f

Worked Example 1

A travelling sine wave is the result of the superposition of two other sine waves with equal amplitudes, wavelengths, and frequencies. The two component waves each have amplitude 5.00 cm. If the resultant wave has amplitude 6.69 cm, what is the phase difference φ between the component waves?

Given: amplitude of each component A = 5.00 cm, resultant amplitude A_R = 6.69 cm

Step 1: For two equal waves with phase difference φ, A_R = 2 A cos(φ / 2)

Step 2: Substitute 6.69 = 2 × 5.00 × cos(φ / 2), so cos(φ / 2) = 6.69 / 10.00 = 0.669

Step 3: Take inverse cosine, φ / 2 = cos^-1 (0.669) = 48°

Step 4: Therefore φ = 2 × 48° = 96°

Final answer: phase difference φ = 96°

mcqs.q: It is possible to understand two people speaking at the same time because sound waves obey:
options: The principle of superposition, crossing without permanently disturbing each other
mcqs.why: By superposition, the waves cross the same region without permanently disturbing or destroying each other. After crossing, each wave continues with its own frequency, pitch and quality unchanged, so each voice keeps its identity.

mcqs.q: Coherent waves for interference are waves that have:
options: Equal speed but no phase relation
The same frequency and a constant phase difference between them
mcqs.why: The two waves must be coherent, meaning they have the same frequency and a constant phase difference between them, so the interference pattern stays steady and visible.

mcqs.q: For clear interference maxima and minima, the two waves should also:
options: Travel in the same or nearly the same direction and have equal or comparable amplitudes
mcqs.why: They should travel in the same or nearly the same direction and have equal or comparable amplitudes so that the maxima and minima are clearly visible in the resultant pattern.

mcqs.q: Two equal waves of amplitude A superpose with phase difference phi. The resultant amplitude is:
mcqs.why: For two equal waves the resultant amplitude is A_R = 2 A cos(phi / 2). It is maximum 2A when phi is zero and zero when phi is pi radians.

mcqs.q: Two component waves each have amplitude 5.00 cm and their resultant amplitude is 6.69 cm. The phase difference between them is:
mcqs.why: Working: A_R = 2 A cos(phi/2), so 6.69 = 10.00 x cos(phi/2), cos(phi/2) = 0.669, phi/2 = cos^-1(0.669) = 48 degrees, therefore phi = 2 x 48 = 96 degrees.

mcqs.q: When two waves of slightly different frequencies superpose, the beat frequency equals:
mcqs.why: The resultant intensity rises and falls regularly, and the number of beats per second equals the difference of the two frequencies, beat frequency = |f1 - f2|.

mcqs.q: Two waves of wavelength 50 cm and 50.4 cm produce 6 beats per second. The speed of sound is about:
mcqs.why: Working: beat frequency = v (1/0.50 - 1/0.504) = v (0.004 / 0.252) = 0.01587 v. Setting this equal to 6 gives v = 6 / 0.01587 = about 378 m/s.

mcqs.q: If 3600 waves pass through a point in a medium in 2 minutes, the frequency is:
mcqs.why: Frequency is the number of waves passing a point in one second. So f = 3600 waves / 120 s = 30 Hz, since 2 minutes is 120 seconds.

mcqs.q: With wave speed 760 m/s and frequency 30 Hz, the wavelength is:
mcqs.why: Working: lambda = v / f = 760 / 30 = 25.3 m. This uses the 30 Hz frequency found from 3600 waves passing in 120 seconds.

mcqs.q: For interference of light, in addition to coherence the sources must also be:
options: Monochromatic and derived from a single source so the phase relation stays fixed
mcqs.why: For light the sources must also be monochromatic and derived from a single source so that the phase relation stays fixed, keeping the waves coherent with constant phase difference.

lessons.title: Stationary Waves in Strings and Air Columns
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Standing Wave?

A standing wave is a wave pattern that does not travel forward but stays in a fixed region, formed when two waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude travel in opposite directions and superpose. In a standing wave every point of the medium vibrates with a fixed amplitude that depends on its position, and no energy is carried forward.

It is commonly produced when a wave reflects from a fixed end, a wall or an obstacle and overlaps its own reflection, as on a stretched string or in an air column. In practice this happens when a wave is reflected back on itself, for example at the fixed ends of a guitar string or at the closed end of a pipe.

Nodes and Antinodes

  • Node — a point that always remains at rest; its displacement is always zero
  • Antinode — a point that vibrates with maximum amplitude
  • Nodes and antinodes alternate along the medium
  • Neighbouring nodes are λ / 2 apart, and neighbouring antinodes are also λ / 2 apart
  • A node and the nearest antinode are λ / 4 apart

Energy at Nodes and Antinodes

At a node the displacement of the particles is always zero, so the particles there never move and the kinetic energy at a node is minimum (in fact zero). The energy of a standing wave is concentrated at the antinodes, where the amplitude and particle speed are greatest. Energy in a standing wave in fact stays trapped between nodes instead of being transported along the medium.

Harmonics

Harmonics are the higher modes of vibration of a system whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest possible frequency, called the fundamental or first harmonic. They are formed when the length of a string or air column fits a whole number of half-wavelengths (or odd numbers of quarter-wavelengths in a closed pipe), so standing waves of shorter wavelength can also be sustained.

SystemHarmonics
String fixed at both endsf, 2f, 3f and so on
Pipe closed at one endOnly odd harmonics f, 3f, 5f

The mixture of harmonics present gives each instrument its characteristic quality or timbre.

Closed Pipe: Node Spacing

For a pipe closed at one end of length L, the fundamental wavelength is 4L. At 7 times the fundamental frequency the wavelength becomes 4L / 7. In any standing wave, neighbouring nodes are half a wavelength apart, so the node spacing is (1 / 2)(4L / 7) = (2 / 7)L.

Waves on a String

The speed of a wave on a string depends on the tension T and the linear mass density μ:

v = √(T / μ)

The fundamental frequency of a string fixed at both ends is:

f = (1 / 2L) √(T / μ)

So f is proportional to √(T) when the length and mass per unit length are unchanged.

Worked Example 1

A uniform string of length 10.0 m and weight 0.25 N is attached to the ceiling. A weight of 1.00 kN hangs from its lower end. The lower end of the string is suddenly displaced horizontally. How long does it take the resulting wave pulse to travel to the upper end? Neglect the weight of the string in comparison to the hanging mass.

Given: length L = 10.0 m, weight of string = 0.25 N, tension T = hanging weight = 1.00 kN = 1000 N

Step 1: Mass of string m = 0.25 / 9.8 = 0.0255 kg, so linear mass density μ = m / L = 0.0255 / 10.0 = 2.55 × 10^-3 kg/m

Step 2: Wave speed on a string is v = √(T / μ)

Step 3: Substitute v = √(1000 / 2.55 × 10^-3) = √(3.92 × 10^5) = about 626 m/s

Step 4: Time = distance / speed = 10.0 / 626 = 0.016 s

Final answer: about 16 ms (approx)

Worked Example 2

In order to decrease the fundamental frequency of a guitar string by 4.0%, by what percentage should you reduce the tension?

Given: new frequency f2 = f1 − 4.0 percent of f1 = 0.96 f1, string length and mass per unit length unchanged

Step 1: Fundamental frequency of a string is f = (1 / 2L) √(T / μ), so f is proportional to √(T)

Step 2: Therefore T2 / T1 = (f2 / f1)^2 = (0.96)^2 = 0.9216

Step 3: New tension T2 = 0.9216 T1, so the reduction is T1 − T2 = 0.0784 T1

Step 4: Percentage reduction = 0.0784 × 100 = 7.84 percent (note: the value 76.96 percent printed in the book is a misprint)

Final answer: reduce the tension by 7.84%

Worked Example 3

A string 2.0 m long is held fixed at both ends. If a sharp blow is applied to the string at its centre, it takes 0.050 s for the pulse to travel to both ends of the string and return to the middle. What is the fundamental frequency of oscillation for this string?

Given: string length L = 2.0 m, round-trip time from centre to the ends and back t = 0.050 s

Step 1: The pulse travels from the centre to an end and back, a distance of 2 × 1.0 m = 2.0 m

Step 2: Wave speed v = distance / time = 2.0 / 0.050 = 40 m/s

Step 3: For the fundamental mode of a string fixed at both ends, wavelength λ = 2L = 4.0 m

Step 4: Fundamental frequency f = v / λ = 40 / 4.0 = 10 Hz

Final answer: fundamental frequency = 10 Hz

mcqs.q: A standing wave is formed when:
options: Two waves of different frequencies travel in the same direction
Two waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude travel in opposite directions and superpose
A single wave travels without reflection
mcqs.why: A standing wave stays in a fixed region and is formed when two waves of the same frequency, wavelength and amplitude travel in opposite directions and superpose, often by reflection from a fixed end.

mcqs.q: A node in a standing wave is a point that:
options: Always remains at rest, with displacement always zero
mcqs.why: A node is a point that always remains at rest; its displacement is always zero. Nodes and antinodes alternate along the medium in a standing wave.

mcqs.q: An antinode in a standing wave is a point that:
options: Has zero energy at all times
Is half a wavelength from the next node in every case
mcqs.why: An antinode is a point that vibrates with maximum amplitude. The energy of a standing wave is concentrated at the antinodes, where amplitude and particle speed are greatest.

mcqs.q: Neighbouring nodes (and neighbouring antinodes) in a standing wave are separated by:
mcqs.why: Neighbouring nodes are lambda / 2 apart, and neighbouring antinodes are also lambda / 2 apart. A node and the nearest antinode are lambda / 4 apart.

mcqs.q: The distance between a node and the nearest antinode is:
mcqs.why: Nodes and antinodes alternate along the medium, and a node and the nearest antinode are lambda / 4 apart, one quarter of a full wavelength.

mcqs.q: The kinetic energy at a node of a standing wave is:
options: Equal to that at an antinode
Minimum, in fact zero, because the particles there never move
mcqs.why: At a node the displacement is always zero, so the particles there never move and the kinetic energy at a node is minimum, in fact zero. Energy stays trapped between nodes instead of being transported.

mcqs.q: Harmonics are:
options: Whole-number multiples of the lowest possible frequency, called the fundamental
Only the odd multiples in every system
mcqs.why: Harmonics are the higher modes whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest possible frequency, called the fundamental or first harmonic. Their mixture gives each instrument its timbre.

mcqs.q: The harmonics of a string fixed at both ends are:
mcqs.why: For a string fixed at both ends the harmonics are f, 2f, 3f and so on, all whole-number multiples of the fundamental, because the length fits a whole number of half-wavelengths.

mcqs.q: A pipe closed at one end gives harmonics:
options: Only odd harmonics f, 3f, 5f and so on
mcqs.why: A pipe closed at one end gives only odd harmonics f, 3f, 5f, because its length fits odd numbers of quarter-wavelengths, unlike a string which gives all harmonics.
